claim: The NOAA NWM CONUS Retrospective v3.0 provides 44 years (February 1979 through January 2023) of hourly modeled streamflow plus 3-hourly land-surface output, in NetCDF and Zarr, from public S3 bucket `noaa-nwm-retrospective-3-0-pds` (us-east-1), accessible with `aws s3 ls --no-sign-request` — no AWS account, no authentication, and stated license 'Open Data. There are no restrictions on the use of this data.' v2.1 covers February 1979 through December 2020 (`noaa-nwm-retrospective-2-1-pds`, with a Zarr mirror `noaa-nwm-retrospective-2-1-zarr-pds'). FALSIFIABLE / OPERATIONAL: coverage is CONUS-wide, so it covers the multi-state portions of Iowa basins, and the years fully span the 2008-2026 training window except the post-Jan-2023 tail, which the retrospective does NOT cover (a deployment gap requiring the operational NWM feed, not the retrospective). CAVEAT: the registry page does NOT document the reach identifier — it makes no mention of NHDPlus v2 COMID or `feature_id`. The per-reach join to the project's stored NHDPlus comids is therefore UNVERIFIED from this source and must be confirmed against the NWM route-link file before any effort is spent.
effectSize: v3.0 = Feb 1979–Jan 2023 hourly; v2.1 = Feb 1979–Dec 2020; 2.7 million reaches CONUS

The claim stands as written. Four refinements, one of which materially changes the recommended next action:

1. CAVEAT RESOLVED, DO NOT SPEND EFFORT ON IT. The claim says the COMID join is "UNVERIFIED ... must be confirmed against the NWM route-link file before any effort is spent." I confirmed it in one HTTP GET, no route-link download: chrtout.zarr feature_id carries comment "NHDPlusv2 ComIDs within CONUS, arbitrary Reach IDs outside of CONUS". The per-reach join to the project's stored NHDPlus comids is VALID. Reach count is exactly 2,776,734, not an approximation.

2. SOURCING NIT: the "2.7 million reaches" figure in the reported effect size is NOT on the cited registry page. It comes from water.noaa.gov/about/nwm ("over 2.7 million river reaches") and is corroborated by the Zarr shape. The number is right; the attribution to the registry page is not.

3. TRAIN/SERVE SKEW — the claim understates this. It correctly notes the post-Jan-2023 gap needs "the operational NWM feed, not the retrospective," but does not flag that these are different products: a different bucket (noaa-nwm-pds), and an operational model whose version and calibration drift over time relative to the frozen v3.0 retrospective. A model trained on v3.0 retrospective streamflow and served on operational NWM output is exposed to a feature-distribution shift that is invisible in LOFO CV. If NWM features are adopted, this needs an explicit consistency check on the overlap period, and it is a real deployment risk, not a footnote.

4. TRANSFERABILITY WARNING THE CLAIM DOES NOT RAISE, and the one that matters most here. NWM streamflow is primarily a TIME-VARYING feature. This project has now failed seven consecutive hydrologically-motivated temporal ablations (lagged weather, rolling precip/water balance, travel-time routing, rolling targets, spike targets, antecedent moisture). The stated diagnosis is that the deficit is in BETWEEN-SITE STATIC information, not temporal dynamics. Feeding raw daily NWM discharge into the model lands squarely in the category that has repeatedly failed, and at n=19 independent basin families it is unlikely to be distinguishable from noise. The defensible use is the opposite framing: derive PER-BASIN STATIC HYDROLOGIC SIGNATURES from the 44-year record — mean annual runoff per unit area, baseflow index, flashiness/R-B index, runoff ratio, low-flow percentiles — which are exactly the between-site static descriptors where the remaining headroom is. Those are 19-effective-sample-friendly (a handful of scalars per basin) in a way that 160k rows of daily modeled discharge is not.

5. GENUINE DEPLOYMENT-TARGET FIT (the strongest point, which the claim undersells): unlike the project's observed discharge — present at only 22 of 85 sites and zero of 61 IWQIS sites — NWM covers all 2.7M CONUS reaches. It therefore works at an ARBITRARY UNGAUGED MAP PIN with no local history, and covers the multi-state portions of Iowa basins. It requires no target-site observations and no gauged upstream neighbor. This is one of the few candidate data sources that is actually compatible with the shipped product's constraints.

One thing I could NOT check and am flagging rather than asserting: NWM v3.0 skill specifically in tile-drained Midwest agricultural basins. Tile drainage is the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa and is not explicitly represented in WRF-Hydro's physics, so NWM discharge in these basins may be systematically biased. My web-search budget was exhausted before I could find peer-reviewed regional validation. Treat NWM Iowa skill as an open question, not a given.

claim: Pandit et al. (2025, WRR 61(8), doi:10.1029/2024WR039207) trained an LSTM on daily stream nitrate across the conterminous US and reported a large drop from temporal to spatial validation: median KGE fell from 0.60 (temporal validation, forecasting unseen periods at sites INCLUDED in training) to 0.18 (spatial validation, prediction at basins NOT in training). This is the closest published analogue to our deployment target and says an LSTM does not solve the ungauged-basin nitrate-concentration problem.
effectSize: median KGE 0.60 (temporal) -> 0.18 (spatial holdout); a drop of 0.42 KGE

votes.confidence: high on the KGE numbers and the paper's identity (exact verbatim match from two independent publisher-deposited metadata sources); low on the n=95/148 site counts, which I could not verify at all
votes.evidence:
PRIMARY-SOURCE CHECK — the two headline numbers are EXACT, not paraphrased.

Wiley (agupubs) is Cloudflare-blocked (HTTP 402 via WebFetch, 403 via curl on /doi/, /doi/full/, /doi/pdfdirect/, /doi/epdf/, and via text-extraction proxy). The PMC copy (PMC12425153, EPA Author Manuscript, PMID 40948694) exists but is UNDER EMBARGO until 2026-08-09 — three weeks from today. Europe PMC has no full text. No Zenodo/HydroShare data package found. So I verified against the publisher-deposited abstract, retrieved independently from OpenAlex (inverted-index reconstruction) and the Semantic Scholar Graph API; both returned byte-identical text.

Verbatim from the abstract: "We developed a long short-term memory (LSTM) model using high-frequency sensor data from across the conterminous US to predict daily nitrate concentrations, achieving strong temporal validation performance (median KGE = 0.60). Spatial validation—or prediction in unmonitored basins—yielded lower performance for nitrate concentration (median KGE = 0.18)."

Confirmed: LSTM; conterminous-US high-frequency sensor training data; target = DAILY NITRATE CONCENTRATION; temporal median KGE 0.60; spatial median KGE 0.18; drop 0.42 (arithmetic correct); spatial validation is explicitly glossed by the authors as "prediction in unmonitored basins," which is our deployment target. Bibliographic details confirmed via Crossref: WRR 61(8), e2024WR039207, published 2025-08-09, CC-BY-NC, NSF-funded (EAR-2438017, OIA-2229616, OAC-2117449).

THE ONE MATERIAL PROBLEM — the claim omits the number that actually applies to Iowa. The very next sentence of the abstract reads: "Nonetheless, spatial validation was crucial in quantifying the impact of current data gaps and guiding the model's targeted application to the MRB where spatial validation performance was stronger (median KGE = 0.34)." Iowa sits inside the Mississippi River Basin, and the abstract names Iowa explicitly. The 0.18 is the CONUS-wide figure, diluted by arid-west and non-agricultural basins where a nitrate LSTM transfers badly. The region-matched ungauged-basin number is 0.34, and the region-matched drop is 0.60 -> 0.34 = 0.26, not 0.42.

TITLE MISSTATED: the paper is "Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin" (Pandit, Golden, Christensen, Lane, Husic), not a CONUS-titled paper. The claim's description of the training data as CONUS is nonetheless accurate.

n AND YEARS — UNVERIFIED AND PARTLY CONFLATED. The abstract states no site counts; I could not reach any text that does, so "95 sites drawn from 148" is unsubstantiated by me (plausible, but treat as unconfirmed). Separately, "1980-2022" is NOT the LSTM training period — the abstract assigns those years to the MRB application: "Modeling results for the MRB from 1980 to 2022." Optical in-situ nitrate sensors barely exist before ~2007, so 1980-2022 is a hindcast/simulation window, and attaching it to the training set is a garble.

METHODOLOGY / METRIC — the claim's protocol label is right, but the metric is not comparable to ours. Spatial-holdout is the correct protocol and is used correctly. However KGE on a daily concentration series cannot be set against our LOFO AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 on a binary exceedance target. Note also that KGE decomposes into correlation, bias ratio and variability ratio, so a model with good event timing but a biased mean scores low KGE — which is precisely our project's diagnosed pathology (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21, "a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker"). Pandit's temporal->spatial collapse is very likely the same failure mode in a different metric. That makes the paper corroborative of our diagnosis rather than merely a pessimistic benchmark.

TRANSFERABILITY — unusually strong for our case, with one caveat that cuts against us. Same analyte, same daily timestep, same sensor-derived data, and a holdout definition that literally is our deployment target (no local history at the held-out basin). Much closer than any CAMELS streamflow result. The caveat per the n=19 rule: if the 95/148 figures are right, Pandit had roughly 5-8x more independent spatial units than our 19 basin families, and still landed at KGE 0.18 CONUS-wide / 0.34 in-MRB. A deep model is more data-hungry than our XGBoost, so this is evidence that an LSTM would very likely do WORSE than 0.820 AUC at n=19, not better — the claim's conclusion holds a fortiori.

ACTIONABLE LEAD THE CLAIM MISSES: the abstract reports that Shapley analysis identified the top spatial drivers of MEAN nitrate concentration as "tile drainage, roadway density, wetland cover," with non-linear thresholds. That is independent published confirmation that the between-site term — exactly the term our project fails at — is governed by tile drainage, the single feature our project knows it lacks with no source identified. This paper is therefore a citation trail to a CONUS tile-drainage layer usable in ungauged prediction. (The scratchpad already holds TILES92_CONUS.txt and TILES_Early90s_CONUS.txt, consistent with the USGS Nakagaki/Wieczorek tile-drainage product; worth reconciling against whatever Pandit et al. cite once the PMC embargo lifts on 2026-08-09.)
votes.correction:
The claim is directionally correct and its two quoted numbers are exact, but it should be restated as follows before use.

Pandit et al. (2025), "Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin," WRR 61(8), e2024WR039207, doi:10.1029/2024WR039207 (CC-BY-NC), trained an LSTM on high-frequency nitrate sensor data from across the conterminous US to predict daily nitrate CONCENTRATION. Iowa's out-of-state tails are MN, IL, MO, NE, SD, WI — none flagged. This concern is null. (ii) "Bias worst in the discriminating middle needed for site ranking": the classes 3–5 weakness is a point-level false-negative pattern, and the county area constraint converts misses into within-county reallocation rather than a low area total. Iowa tile sits in classes 6–7, where AgTile-US achieves 91.1% accuracy on 5,253 Iowa ground-truth points — its strongest region, not its weakest.

REPLACEMENT LIMITATION WORTH CARRYING FORWARD. The real constraint on AgTile-US as a between-site ranking feature is not low bias but RESOLUTION CEILING: because the map is disaggregated from county census totals, basin tile fraction is substantially a reallocation of county-level truth, limiting independent sub-county between-site signal. Second, it is a static 2017 snapshot; unlike the failed 2017 N-surplus broadcast this is physically defensible (tile infrastructure changes slowly), but it should be treated as a static geographic covariate alongside lat/lon/log_basin_area, not as a temporal driver.

NET RECOMMENDATION: the biases raised are not a reason to avoid AgTile-US for Iowa basins. Operational details — AgTile-US, 30 m raster, static single-vintage 2017, full CONUS coverage including all multi-state basin tails, free/public, hosted at the NCAR/UCAR Research Data Archive and linked from the Scientific Data paper (DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x), no authentication, open license. Expected use: basin-mean tile fraction, optionally per distance bucket to match the existing feature layout. Test it under LOFO against the between_rate_r2 = 0.24 term specifically, and pre-register that a single static covariate against ~19 independent families has limited power to demonstrate a small improvement.

SOURCE VERIFIED. PMC7406500 = Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis & Franz (2020), "Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach", Scientific Data 7:257, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x. This is the AgTile-US source paper. Not a misattribution.

WHAT THE PAPER ACTUALLY SAYS (verbatim, confirmed across two independent fetches):

1. Cropland mask: "Since tile drainage mapping by the geospatial model is mainly based on the county-level census estimate, soil drainage categories, and topographic slope, a cropland mask is necessary to mask out non-agricultural lands." The mask is NLCD 2016. CONFIRMED.

2. NLCD deficit: "A comparison of cropland from USDA county-level census 2017 and NLCD 2016 indicate an underrepresentation of croplands by -92.00%, -27.45%, and -18.15%, for West Virginia, New Mexico, and the CONUS, respectively." The -18.15% CONUS figure is EXACT and correctly attributed.

3. Tile underestimation: "The AgTile-US shows higher underestimation of tile drainage over the croplands of New Mexico (-79.06%), West Virginia (-42.38%)"; Table 1 also gives Mississippi -15.90%, Oklahoma -14.06%, Texas -11.53%. Paper explicitly attributes the cause: "The underestimation of tile drainage by the AgTile-US is mainly due to underrepresentation of croplands in NLCD land cover 2016." So the causal MECHANISM in the claim is the paper's own stated mechanism, not an inference.

4. SSURGO 3-5: "The AgTile-US failed to identify tile drainage at about 13.97% of ground-truth locations, and most of these points are in marginal drainage categories (category = 3-5)." CONFIRMED, and it is an OMISSION (false-negative) error as claimed. Overall CONUS accuracy 86.03%, omission error 13.97%, ~16,000 ground-truth points.

5. Slope cap: "using the extracted slope values, we have identified the upper limit of slope (=20%) in the geospatial model." CONFIRMED as a hard cap.

6. Iowa: "The state with the most tile drained croplands is Iowa (5.7 Mha), where we have identified 5253 ground truth points, and the AgTile-US showed 91.1% accuracy." Midwest overall 82.7%-93.6%. Iowa/IL/IN/MN/OH are indeed absent from the problem-state list. CONFIRMED.

PROTOCOL: not applicable in the ML sense — this is a validation-against-ground-truth-points exercise (n~16,000 points, 5,253 in Iowa), not a train/test split. No leakage concern, but also no held-out-basin evidence.

ERRORS IN THE CLAIM (why a correction is needed rather than acceptance as written):
(a) NUMBER CONFLATION. The claim presents NM -79.06%, WV -42.38%, MS -15.90%, OK -14.06%, TX -11.53% as "state-level underestimates" of the NLCD cropland deficit. They are not — they are AgTile-US TILE AREA underestimates. The corresponding NLCD CROPLAND deficits for those two states are WV -92.00% and NM -27.45%, i.e. the claim has the two quantities swapped in magnitude and mislabeled. The reported effect-size line is therefore internally mixed.
(b) THE COUNTY-CALIBRATION ARGUMENT UNDERCUTS "BASIN TILE FRACTION IS BIASED LOW" FOR IOWA. The algorithm allocates cells iteratively "until the estimated tile drainage area exceeded the USDA census," then backs off in 0.1% slope increments. County totals are therefore approximately CONSERVED by construction wherever the mask is large enough to absorb them. In Iowa — 91.1% accuracy, no listed shortfall — the dominant error is spatial PLACEMENT of tile within a county, not county-aggregate under-allocation. For a multi-county Iowa basin the aggregate fraction is close to unbiased; the error behaves as within-county placement noise, worst for small single-county basins.
(c) THE MULTI-STATE TAIL ARGUMENT IS NON-SEQUITUR. Iowa basins extend into Minnesota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Missouri, Illinois, Wisconsin. Not one of those is a listed problem state. New Mexico, West Virginia, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Texas are geographically irrelevant to any Iowa drainage basin. The paper also notes the problem states' "total tile drained area of these states is less than 0.11 Mha" — trivial. So "bias larger for multi-state basin tails" has no support.
(d) "WORST IN INTERMEDIATE DRAINAGE CLASS" IS UNQUANTIFIED. The paper says most omissions fall in categories 3-5 but reports NO category-stratified error rate. There is no number to propagate into a bias model. Iowa tile is concentrated on poorly/very-poorly drained soils (Des Moines Lobe, categories 1-2), so the cat 3-5 penalty applies to a minority of Iowa tile — and the 91.1% Iowa figure already includes it.
(e) UNMENTIONED, LARGER CAVEAT. The paper states "The average error in tile drainage estimates based on the Census of Agriculture 2017 is 19.8%." This census-input error applies to Iowa too and likely dominates the mask-induced bias for our basins. The claim omits it.

TRANSFERABILITY TO THIS PROJECT: The claim is being used to argue AgTile-US is too biased to serve as the missing static between-site feature. That conclusion does not follow. AgTile-US is 30 m, CONUS-wide, covers every state an Iowa basin reaches, and validates at 91.1% in Iowa — the best-validated state in the product. Deployment target is fine: it is a static raster, requires no local nitrate history and no gauge, so it works at an arbitrary map pin. The n=19-families constraint is the real limiter here and it cuts AGAINST the claim's usefulness in both directions: with ~19 independent units, a basin tile-fraction covariate would have to carry a large, monotone between-site signal to be detectable at all, and a 5-15% multiplicative bias that is roughly common-mode across Iowa basins is largely absorbed by the model's own scaling. Heteroscedastic placement noise in small basins is the more relevant risk, and that is not what the claim argues.

claim: The 2012 Midwest SPARROW total-nitrogen model (Robertson & Saad 2019, SIR 2019-5114, Table 5) was calibrated on TN loads from 1,334 monitoring sites (1,344 considered, 1,335 in Table 1) and reports R2 = 0.950, Yield R2 = 0.913, conditioned RMSE = 0.487 natural-log units (51.8% in real space) and unconditioned RMSE = 0.555 log units (60.0% in real space). The 'Yield R2 = 0.913' is therefore NOT comparable to our between_r2 = 0.21 under LOFO — it is the in-sample cross-sectional fit of a 16-parameter regression to 1,334 sites, and the honest expectation for a truly unseen basin is materially worse. The 'conditioned' RMSE (0.487) is additionally optimistic because it resets predicted accumulated loads to MEASURED loads at upstream calibration sites — that is a gauged-upstream-neighbor protocol that DOES NOT WORK for our arbitrary-map-pin deployment target. Only the unconditioned RMSE (0.555 log units / 60%) reflects prediction with no upstream measurements, which is our situation.

1. NUMBERS — ALL EXACT. The RMSE obtained during model calibration (conditioned RMSE) was 0.487 and when the model was used for full prediction (unconditioned RMSE) was 0.555 (both in natural logarithmic units). These values equate to an RMSE of 51.8 percent for conditioned predictions and an RMSE of 60.0 percent for unconditioned predictions." No exaggeration, no garbled paraphrase.

2. SITE COUNTS — CORRECT INCLUDING THE INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY. Table 1 columns are "Sites considered for use in SPARROW models" and "Sites used in final SPARROW models": Streamflow 2,057 considered / 2,012 final; Total nitrogen 1,344 / 1,335; Total phosphorus 1,346 / 1,273; Suspended sediment 177 / 107; (also Suspended solids 1,085 / 1,082, which the claim omits but does not misstate). Table 5 and the body both say 1,334 for TN, disagreeing with Table 1's 1,335. The claim correctly flags all three figures (1,344 / 1,335 / 1,334) rather than papering over the report's own 1-site discrepancy. Streamflow 2,012, TP 1,273, sediment 107 all confirmed.

3. THE CRITICAL CAVEAT — NO VALIDATION — CONFIRMED. Case-insensitive grep for "cross-validation"/"cross validation" returns ZERO hits in the 13,723-line extraction. No hits for holdout, hold-out, leave-one-out, jackknife, validation set, independent validation, or split-sample. The only resampling anywhere is a parametric bootstrap (200 iterations) used in the LOAD-ESTIMATION step to put uncertainty on measured loads — not a spatial holdout of the SPARROW model. The reported statistics come from weighted nonlinear least-squares regression fit to the same sites they are scored on. The claim's characterization "in-sample calibration statistics... no cross-validation, no leave-one-basin-out, and no spatial holdout anywhere" is accurate.

4. THE CONDITIONED-RMSE CAVEAT — CONFIRMED VERBATIM, AND THE AUTHORS AGREE. Table 5 footnote b: "Conditioned RMSE is the root mean square error of the difference between the natural logarithm of measured calibration loads and the natural logarithm of predicted accumulated loads that were reset to the measured loads at the calibration sites upstream in the basin." Footnote d confirms unconditioned is the same "except the predicted accumulated loads were not reset." This is exactly the gauged-upstream-neighbor protocol the claim describes. The report's Methods section goes further and makes the claim's argument for it: "This replacement can result in an underestimation of the model error compared to when the model is used to simulate loads throughout the basin, using the unconditioned predictions (Qian and others, 2005; Wellen and others, 2014). Therefore, an unconditioned RMSE also is reported... The unconditioned RMSE provides the best representation of the predictive skill of a calibrated SPARROW model." The claim's insistence that only 0.555 / 60.0% is relevant to us is the authors' own stated position, not an adversarial reinterpretation.

5. INDEPENDENT SUPPORT THAT UNSEEN-BASIN PERFORMANCE WOULD BE WORSE. The report's spatial diagnostics — the closest thing to a transferability check, and they are residual diagnostics rather than holdout — FAIL for TN: loose-cluster Moran's I = 0.199, p = 0.0005 (n=1,334), and nested-share weighting coefficient 0.204, p = 3.3e-6. The report interprets significant Moran's I as meaning "the model might be improved by adding additional explanatory variables (beyond those tested in our study)... where the model consistently overpredicts or underpredicts." Body text admits "patterns of overpredictions and underpredictions in the western parts of the watershed" and that "the model did not predict the loads and yields as well for sites with relatively small loads," with unconditioned RMSE degrading to 0.65 for smaller loads. Spatially clustered residuals are precisely the condition under which in-sample cross-sectional R2 overstates performance at a spatially held-out basin. This strengthens the claim.

6. TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR SETTING — the claim's non-comparability argument holds, and there are two further reasons it under-states the gap. (a) TARGET MISMATCH: SPARROW's response is mean-annual TN LOAD (kg/yr) aggregated over 2012 conditions — a long-term cross-sectional average with the entire temporal axis integrated out. Our between_r2 = 0.21 is a between-site term for DAILY-MAX CONCENTRATION (mg/L) exceedance. R2 on log mean-annual load is inflated by several orders of magnitude of basin-area variation across 1,334 sites; load scales almost mechanically with area and runoff. Yield R2 = 0.913 is the area-normalized version and is the fairer of the two, but it is still an in-sample fit to a long-term mean, not daily concentration. These are different quantities and no rescaling makes 0.913 and 0.21 commensurable — a point the claim makes but could make more forcefully. (b) n=19 CONSTRAINT: SPARROW estimates ~14 coefficients from 1,334 sites (~95 sites per parameter). At our 19 independent basin families, fitting even SPARROW's structure is infeasible — a 14-parameter cross-sectional regression on 19 units is not estimable in any trustworthy way. SPARROW is not a method we can port; it is at best a source of PRIOR STRUCTURE (which source and land-to-water terms matter) or of PREDICTIONS-AS-FEATURES.

7. WHAT IS ACTUALLY USABLE, judged against the arbitrary-map-pin target. SPARROW predictions are published on the NHDPlusV2 catchment network, and the project already stores an NHDPlus comid per basin, so pre-computed SPARROW incremental TN yield for a target catchment is a static between-site covariate obtainable with NO local nitrate history and NO gauged upstream neighbor. That is deployment-legal, and it attacks exactly the between-site term where all our headroom is. Caveats: it is a 2012 static snapshot (no temporal variation — consistent with our finding that only static geography has helped); and its inputs partly overlap features we already have (fertilizer, manure, runoff, land use), so it may be redundant rather than additive. Worth an ablation, not a guaranteed win.

The brief says tile drainage density is "the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet." In the TP model the same variable is significant with the opposite sign (-0.091, p=0.0221). Source, per the report's reference list: Nakagaki, N., and Wieczorek, M.E., 2016, "Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for 12 Midwest states, 2012," USGS data release, http://dx.doi.org/10.5066/F7W37TDP — 12 Midwest states (so it covers Iowa AND the multi-state portions of our largest basins, which is where our inner-join under-counting is worst), 2012 snapshot, extrapolated to NHDPlusV2 catchments following Wieczorek and others (2019); supplemented for ND/SD from Finocchiaro (2014, 2016) tile-permit polygons. USGS data releases are free, public, no authentication, public-domain. I verified this citation as printed in the report but did NOT fetch the data release itself, so resolution/format/exact access mechanism are unconfirmed — treat coverage-years and delivery details as needing one confirmation fetch. Note the same 2012-static-snapshot risk that killed the 2017 N-surplus broadcast (-0.166): use it as a TIME-INVARIANT basin attribute, never broadcast as a time-varying feature.

Absence of such evidence here is not evidence it does not exist; the claim's assertion is scoped to "in the entire 60-page report," and that scoping I did verify directly.

The claim implies picking among proximity, attributes, and volume/signature is a free choice that is "nearly a wash." It is a wash in score, but not in data requirements. Table 2 defines Vol verbatim as "The three catchments with the smallest volume error for the (hypothetically) ungauged catchment are used as donors" — i.e. the volume error is computed against the receiver's measured discharge. Section 2.3.1 category D states these methods assume "it is possible to estimate hydrological signatures for the ungauged catchment... or to directly conduct a number of discharge measurements," and category E (Dist & Vol) states outright: "These approaches also require either estimates of hydrological signatures or a small number of local point observations." So Vol (0.80) and the Dist&Vol category (0.82) are partial-oracle methods, and Best (0.87) is a full oracle (three best donors "defined by RNP," which needs the receiver's full observed hydrograph).

For OUR deployment target — an arbitrary map pin with zero local observations — the realizable menu is only: spatial proximity 0.79, catchment attributes 0.78, fixed classification 0.76, against random 0.69. The zero-observation spread over random is therefore ~0.10 R_NP, not 0.13, and the spread between the two usable single-information families (Dist 0.79 vs Attr 0.78) is 0.01, not 0.02. The claim's headline conclusion actually gets STRONGER for us: among methods we can actually deploy, proximity and attribute similarity are within 0.01 of each other and both are worth ~0.10 over random. The "0.82 best realizable" figure should not be quoted in our context without the local-observation caveat.

(2) TRANSFERABILITY TO SUSTAG IS WEAK ON FOUR AXES, AND THE n=19 CONSTRAINT BITES HARD AND ASYMMETRICALLY.
- Donor-pool size is the mechanism, and we do not have it. The paper's central Lesson (b) is that "almost perfect donors exist for most catchments" — that is a direct function of choosing the 3 best from a pool of 670. Our pool is ~18 other independent basin families. Both the oracle ceiling (0.87) and the realizable gain over random shrink monotonically with pool size, and the paper offers no evidence at small n. This is a 671-basin result and must be flagged as likely infeasible at n=19: with 18 candidate donors, the nearest neighbor in attribute space is often not near at all. The paper's own Random baseline (3 of 670) is also a much stronger baseline than 3-of-18 would be, so even the direction of the gap is not safely portable.
- Wrong physical system. CAMELS is explicitly screened for minimally-impacted, near-natural catchments. Iowa row-crop basins are artificially drained; the attribute vector Pool et al. use for similarity (area, aridity, precipitation seasonality, snowfall fraction, wetland fraction, clay fraction, forest fraction) contains nothing resembling tile-drainage density, the control our own notes flag as dominant.
- Wrong target. This is calibrated-parameter transfer for streamflow — a mass-conserving water-balance quantity — evaluated by NSE-type efficiency. It is not evidence about transferring the ABSOLUTE LEVEL of a nitrate exceedance rate, which is our actual between-site deficit (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24). Nothing in this paper speaks to concentration or exceedance regionalization.
- Wrong model class. The finding concerns donor selection for parameter transfer in a conceptual bucket model (HBV). It does not translate into a feature for a gradient-boosted classifier. The legitimate reading for us is narrow and methodological: it is evidence that ATTRIBUTE-SIMILARITY-BASED transfer is not meaningfully worse than SPATIAL-PROXIMITY-BASED transfer, which mildly discourages spending effort on elaborate similarity metrics and mildly supports the observation that our lat/lon features already capture much of what attribute similarity would. It is NOT evidence that improving static between-site descriptors (e.g. acquiring tile-drainage data) is futile — Pool et al. hold the attribute set fixed and vary only the donor-selection rule, so the study says nothing about the value of a BETTER attribute, only about the value of a better rule for using a fixed attribute set.

PRIMARY-SOURCE CHECK — the quoted sentences are genuine and near-verbatim.

Paper confirmed: Marinos, R., Van Meter, K. J., & Basu, N. B. (2020). "Is the River a Chemostat?: Scale Versus Land Use Controls on Nitrate Concentration-Discharge Dynamics in the Upper Mississippi River Basin." Geophysical Research Letters. DOI 10.1029/2020GL087051. Retrieved via Semantic Scholar Graph API (paperId 252ca9192fcd9eefc16382599e3ab833d8e1853a, CorpusId 216193772, 39 citations as of retrieval).

Abstract text (verbatim, relevant clauses): "...we show, using high-resolution nitrate concentration data, that tile drainage is a dominant control on C-Q dynamics, with increasing drainage density contributing to more chemostatic C-Q behavior. We further find that concentration variability increases, relative to discharge variability, with increasing basin size across six orders of magnitude, and this pattern is attributed to different spatial correlation structures for C and Q."

The claim's first quoted clause is an exact match, word for word. The second is an accurate paraphrase. So there is NO misattribution, no exaggeration, no garbling of the cited sentences. On the primary-source lens the claim survives.

WHAT COULD NOT BE VERIFIED (and why this matters):
- Publisher full text: HTTP 402 at agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2020GL087051.
- Unpaywall (api.unpaywall.org, 10.1029/2020gl087051): "oa_status": "closed", "is_oa": false, "best_oa_location": null, "oa_locations": [], "has_repository_copy": false. There is no green/preprint copy anywhere in the Unpaywall index.
- Semantic Scholar has no openAccessPdf. Citation contexts from 4 citing papers (2025-2026) reference it only for generic C-Q framing ("linear, break-point, and power-law relationships"; "piecewise power law ... with threshold discharge as fitted parameter"; "temporal variability of NO3- ... depending on catchment characteristics and spatial scale") and quote none of its numbers.
- Therefore: number of sites, drainage-area range, power-law b values, and actual CVc/CVq magnitudes are STILL unknown. Web search budget for this session was exhausted (200/200), so no further hunt was possible.

Consequence: the project cannot cite a threshold from this paper, only a direction. Any statement of the form "Marinos et al. found median CVc/CVq = X" would be fabrication. Note also one citing paper (Ma et al. 2023 lineage, "Coupled Hydrologic and Biogeochemical Responses of Nitrate Export in a Tile-Drained Agricultural Watershed", 2025) attributes to Marinos a PIECEWISE power law with a fitted discharge threshold — i.e., the paper apparently did not fit a single global b, which further undercuts reading a single "chemostatic/non-chemostatic" label off it.

METHODOLOGY / INDEPENDENCE CAVEAT: "high-resolution nitrate concentration data" in the UMRB in 2020 almost certainly means the IIHR/IWQIS and USGS super-gauge sensor networks — plausibly overlapping the very 85 sites this project trains on. If so this is not independent external evidence about our data; it is a prior analysis OF our data. Unverified but should be assumed until the full text is obtained.

THE FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION IS THE PART THAT FAILS — four defects:

1. SELF-CONTRADICTORY USE OF THE TWO FINDINGS. The abstract's second finding says CVc/CVq INCREASES with basin size over six orders of magnitude — i.e., larger basins are LESS chemostatic. The project's inference assumes "Iowa nitrate is largely chemostatic" as a blanket property. The paper explicitly denies scale-invariance; its title is a question, and its answer is "it depends on scale and on tile density." You cannot license a blanket chemostasis premise from a paper whose headline result is that chemostasis erodes with scale.

2. THE 22-GAUGED-SITE TEST IS BIASED IN EXACTLY THE WRONG DIRECTION. All 22 discharge-bearing sites are USGS, which skews to larger drainage areas. Per the paper's own scaling result, that is the regime with the HIGHEST CVc/CVq. So a median computed on those 22 sites is an upper bound, not a representative value, and it says nothing about the small headwater basins an arbitrary map pin will frequently delineate. The test as designed would systematically fail to detect chemostasis where chemostasis is actually strongest. Additionally CVc is sensitive to record length and to 15-min vs daily aggregation, and CVc/CVq requires the site's own C and Q — a within-site, gauged-site statistic that is structurally uninformative about ungauged transfer, the deployment target.

3. "CHEMOSTATIC ⇒ Q CARRIES LITTLE INFORMATION ABOUT C" IS A NON-SEQUITUR. Chemostasis (Godsey/Thompson) bounds a VARIANCE RATIO, not a CORRELATION. A predictor with small amplitude can still be decisive, and here the target is a THRESHOLD, not a level: base rate 0.263 at 10 mg/L means many site-days sit near the boundary. For a site with mean C near 9-11 mg/L, even a low-amplitude, highly-correlated Q signal flips exceedance. Chemostasis therefore predicts Q adds little to R2 on concentration while remaining potentially useful for the binary violation target — close to the opposite of the stated implication. The implication also conflates b≈0 with zero residual structure; hysteresis and spring-flush seasonality persist under b≈0.

4. IT POINTS AT THE WRONG TERM AND MISREADS WHICH FINDING IS ACTIONABLE. Chemostasis means C ≈ a, a site-level near-constant. That is precisely the project's diagnosed deficit (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24). So the paper's first finding is not a reason to drop the discharge angle; it is direct evidence that TILE DRAINAGE DENSITY is a first-order control on the site-level regime — the one static attribute the project has already identified as missing with no data source found. Read correctly, this paper is an argument for prioritizing tile-drainage density as a STATIC between-site feature (which survives the n=19-families constraint far better than any temporal method, since it adds one static covariate rather than a learned per-site level), not an argument about Q.

n=19 CONSTRAINT: the paper's scale finding is a cross-basin regression whose effective n is unknown but, spanning six orders of magnitude of area, is likely well above 19 and certainly not restricted to independent basin families. Fitting a CVc/CVq-vs-area relation on this project's 22 gauged sites collapsing to a handful of independent families would be badly underpowered; do not expect to reproduce the scaling result locally, and do not treat failure to reproduce it as refutation.

DEPLOYMENT VERDICT: nothing in this paper requires or endorses target-site observations, so it is compatible with the ungauged-pin product — but the CVc/CVq diagnostic the project proposes is a gauged-site-only statistic and cannot be computed at the deployment target.

The quoted sentence is verbatim-accurate from the abstract of Marinos, Van Meter & Basu (2020) GRL 10.1029/2020GL087051 ("Is the River a Chemostat?..."), so the citation itself stands. Three corrections to how it is being used:

1. SCALE FINDING IS BEING READ BACKWARDS. The paper says CVc/CVq INCREASES with basin size across SIX orders of magnitude — i.e. larger basins are MORE chemodynamic. Iowa's ~85 monitored sites sit at the larger end of that gradient, so the paper predicts nitrate at our sites is chemoDYNAMIC, not chemostatic. The "more chemostatic" phrase is a relative, comparative statement about high-tile-density vs low-tile-density catchments, not an absolute b≈0 claim, and no CVc/CVq or b value is retrievable from any accessible source (paper is closed-access, Unpaywall oa_locations empty, no repository copy, no preprint). The claim's threshold rule ("median well below 1") is invented, not sourced.

2. THE PAPER FIT THRESHOLD C-Q MODELS, NOT FLAT ONES. Citing papers state Marinos et al. used a piecewise power law with fitted breakpoint Qt (b1, b2, Qt), and the paper is routinely cited as a canonical source for BREAKPOINTS and nonlinearity in nitrate C-Q. A separate UMRB study cites it as evidence that "nitrate exhibited consistently chemodynamic behavior." So the paper cannot be used to predict that discharge carries little information about concentration; if anything it implies a threshold/mobilization response that a monotone linear Q feature would miss but a tree model like XGBoost is well suited to capture.

3. THE INFERENCE "CHEMOSTASIS => Q USELESS FOR CONCENTRATION" IS A CATEGORY ERROR FOR THIS PROJECT. Chemostasis is a within-site C-Q slope statement; our headroom is between-site (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21). Under chemostasis a site's absolute concentration level is set by static source strength — which makes the paper's FIRST finding (tile drainage density is a dominant control) the actionable one: it is a static, between-site, ungauged-transferable covariate, exactly the class of feature that has worked on this project (lat/lon/geometry) while every temporal-hydrology feature has failed. Marinos et al. is therefore evidence FOR prioritizing a tile-drainage-density layer over NWM discharge ingestion, but NOT evidence that discharge will fail.

METHODOLOGICAL LIMITS TO STATE WHENEVER THIS IS CITED: n=33 watersheds (per citing papers; not verifiable in the closed full text), UMRB, >1 year of high-frequency (5-15 min to daily-mean) nitrate sensor data. Purely descriptive/correlative — NO split protocol, no held-out prediction, so it is not comparable to and says nothing directly about our LOFO 0.820. n=33 is in the same order as our 19 families, so it is not a 500-basin result that cannot transfer; but its site set spans six orders of magnitude in area within one basin, so nested-catchment pseudoreplication in the CVc/CVq-vs-area regression is plausible and undetermined. Every C-Q metric it reports requires the site's OWN nitrate AND discharge record, so nothing in this paper is directly computable at an arbitrary ungauged map pin — its only deployable output for us is the qualitative ranking of tile density as a between-site control.

The proposed diagnostic (compute CVc/CVq on the 22 USGS-gauged sites before any NWM ingestion) is still worth running — it is cheap and it is the right descriptive statistic — but the decision rule attached to it is wrong on two counts: (a) the paper predicts CVc/CVq > 1 (chemodynamic) at our basin sizes, so a low median would CONTRADICT rather than confirm the paper; and (b) whatever CVc/CVq comes out, it is a within-site statistic and cannot adjudicate the between-site deficit that holds essentially all remaining headroom. Do not use it to kill the discharge feature; use it to decide whether Q enters as a threshold/percentile-of-local-flow-regime feature rather than a raw magnitude.

The claim is factually exact on inputs, algorithm, and the -0.35% / 22.34 vs 22.42 Mha figures, and its collinearity warning is operationally sound. Two corrections:

(1) "Not an independent observation of tile drainage" is too strong on both ends. The county input IS an observation — USDA Census of Agriculture farmer-reported tile acreage — and the paper reports genuine INDEPENDENT validation the claim omits entirely: 16,000 tile-drainage ground-truth points manually identified from ESRI multi-resolution aerial imagery (15 m / 1 m / 0.6 m / 0.3 m) across ten states, giving 86.03% overall accuracy for CONUS (13.97% omission), 82.7-93.6% across the tile-drained Midwest, and 91.1% for IOWA specifically on 5,253 ground-truth points, with >98% accuracy in poorly drained soils and errors concentrated in marginal drainage categories 3-5. For this project's Iowa-basin use case that is the number that matters, and it is good. AgTile-US should be described as a census-constrained downscaling that has been independently validated at 91.1% in Iowa, not as an unvalidated composite.

(2) The redundancy is exact WITHIN a county but not ACROSS counties. Because the county census acreage enters as a per-county calibration constant, two counties with identical SSURGO drainage-class and slope distributions and identical cropland fraction receive DIFFERENT tile fractions whenever their census acreages differ. So basin-aggregated AgTile fraction carries county-scale information that is not recoverable from SSURGO + slope + NLCD alone; it is not a pure function of them. Practical consequence, which strengthens rather than weakens the claim's advice: add AgTile fraction as a single static per-bucket feature and do NOT also add the SSURGO drainage-class histogram or mean slope as separate features — they are the ingredients, not independent evidence. Also note the product is BINARY extent (drained yes/no, "does not distinguish drainage intensity/spacing"), so it proxies drained AREA, not the drainage DENSITY the project brief names as the dominant Iowa hydrologic control.

(1) THE CENTRAL MECHANISTIC ERROR. AgTile-US is NOT a deterministic function of SSURGO drainage class + slope + cropland alone, so the strong-collinearity prediction is overstated. The paper states: "thresholds of slope and soil drainage properties were estimated separately for each county." Paper's stated sequence: start at D=7 with slope S=0; increment S by 1% while accumulated area is below the county census target; on reaching S=20%, reset S=0 and decrement to D=6; repeat until accumulated area exceeds the census target; then fine-tune with 0.1% slope increments to minimize error. The claim's "iterated D=7 down to D=1" is the correct direction (the loop terminates when the county target is met, so D=1 is the floor, not necessarily reached in every county — a trivial imprecision).

No independent tile-location observation (permit records, field surveys, LiDAR/imagery tile-line detection) enters the pixel allocation. Therefore a basin-aggregated AgTile fraction cannot be statistically independent of basin-aggregated drainage class, mean slope, and cropland fraction. Feeding AgTile fraction AND SSURGO drainage class/HSG AND mean slope as three separate features would be near-collinear, and attributing a measured gain to "three independent attributes" would be wrong. The claim's prescription — attribute any gain to the composite — is correct.

Using the extracted slope values, we have identified the upper limit of slope (=20%)." There is no stated held-out split. The claim is directionally correct and its quoted numbers are exact, but it overstates redundancy in two specific ways that change what you should do with it.

(1) "NOT AN INDEPENDENT OBSERVATION" IS TOO ABSOLUTE. The pixel ALLOCATION is pure downscaling, as claimed. But one genuinely exogenous observation does enter: the USDA county-level tile acreage itself is farmer-reported survey data, not derived from soil or terrain. AgTile encodes, per county, WHERE ON THE (drainage-class, slope) ORDERING THE CUTOFF FALLS — and that cutoff is set by real reported acreage that cannot be recovered from gSSURGO + NLCD + SRTM alone. So AgTile fraction is not a deterministic function of the other three candidate features; it is those three features PLUS a county-resolution intensity signal. Practical consequence for this project: WITHIN a county, AgTile variation is pure soil+slope and is fully redundant. BETWEEN counties, AgTile carries real information. Since Iowa basins typically span many counties, the between-county component is where any genuine gain would come from — and that is exactly the between-site term where the project's headroom lies. Do not dismiss the feature; dismiss the triple-counting.

(2) The paper DID conduct an accuracy assessment against non-census data — 16,000 manually interpreted aerial-imagery points, 86.03% overall CONUS accuracy, 13.97% omission error — which the claim omits entirely. However, this assessment is compromised rather than absent: the same points calibrated the 20% slope threshold, and no held-out split is described, so treat 86.03% as an optimistic in-sample figure. State-level breakdowns (an Iowa-specific figure near 91% on roughly 5,000 points) came back inconsistent across two extraction passes and should be read directly from the paper's tables before being cited.

(3) Minor precision fixes: the soil input is GRIDDED SSURGO (gSSURGO) v2.0, native 10-m resampled to 30-m, not vector SSURGO; and the D-loop terminates when the county census target is exceeded, so D=1 is the floor of the search rather than a step every county reaches.

RECOMMENDED ACTION: add AgTile-US basin fraction as a single static feature; do NOT simultaneously add SSURGO drainage-class and mean-slope basin summaries as if they were independent attributes. If you want to test whether AgTile adds anything beyond terrain and soil, the clean ablation is AgTile-fraction versus (drainage-class + slope + cropland-fraction) as competing feature sets under the same LOFO protocol, not both together — and expect the discriminating signal to be between-county, so check whether it survives at n=19 families before believing it.

votes.correction:
Three detail corrections, none of which overturn the claim.

(a) "n basins: 74" should read "74 streamgages within TWO river basins" — nested, spatially dependent sites, not 74 independent catchments. This matters for the n=19 constraint: the study's evidence base is weaker than "74" implies, which cuts both ways (it is not a 500-basin CAMELS result that we must discount, but it also cannot support strong generalization).

(b) The claim's inference that "the binding constraint is the accuracy of the regionalized duration curve itself, not the dependence model" is NOT established by the abstract. Finding (4) introduces realistic error into "the estimation of FDCs AND correlations across the gaging network" — both components are degraded simultaneously, and the abstract does not decompose which one drives the loss of dominance. The dependence model at an ungaged site must itself be regionalized (the companion data release's kriged site-to-site correlations are precisely that), so correlation-estimation error is equally implicated. The defensible version: under realistic estimation error in BOTH the regionalized FDC and the regionalized rank-correlation structure, the copula advantage disappears; the abstract does not identify which of the two is binding.

(c) "Nondominating" is weaker than the claim's gloss "merely ties simpler methods." Nondominating means not uniformly best (e.g. not best across all sites, flow quantiles, or metrics); it is compatible with a modest average edge. Use the authors' word.

Operational bottom line for this project: the citation is legitimate and correctly quoted, but it is a streamflow paper whose ungaged result is qualitative, protocol-unstated, and drawn from nested gages in two humid southeastern river basins. It is adequate as a reason NOT to invest in copula/QPPQ machinery for the Iowa nitrate map-pin product; it is NOT adequate as evidence about what would fix the between-site term.

The claim stands as written; four precision fixes and three usage caveats.

PRECISION FIXES
(a) The server does NOT honor HTTP Range. There is no accept-ranges header, and a request with `-r 400000000-400002000` returned HTTP 200 with content-length 493183556 and the file from byte 0 (I got the header back, not the middle). Header verification works only because curl truncates a streamed full GET. Practical consequence: you cannot cheaply sample the middle of these files — plan on streaming and filtering (`curl ... | awk`) or a full 493 MB download.
(b) "1 row per NHDPlusV2 COMID" is right but not exactly — the file also carries a small number of negative synthetic reach ids (e.g. -92000151, -91074001) that are not NHDPlusV2 COMIDs. 18 of the first 167,893 rows. Filter comid > 0 before joining.
(c) The record lists 8 files, not 7: the seven data files plus an FGDC XML metadata file (listed with size 0 in JSON but fetchable). The XML is where the units live and should be read before deriving anything.
(d) Item-level `rights` is null. USGS data releases are public domain / CC0 by agency policy, but the release itself does not state a license string.

USAGE CAVEATS FOR THIS PROJECT
(1) The concentration derivation is NOT unit-safe as stated. al_tn is a long-term mean annual load and wbm_meanq is a mean flow whose units (kg/yr and ft3/s, most likely) are defined only in the FGDC XML — do not compute al_tn/(annual volume) until you have read the XML. Get the units right or the derived "concentration" will be off by a constant factor per reach, which is harmless for a tree split but not for interpretation.
(2) CIRCULARITY RISK, and it is the real one. SPARROW is a calibrated model, not an observation. Robertson & Saad (2019, SIR 2019-5114) calibrated the Midwest TN model against monitored load estimates at stream sites — and Iowa's monitoring network is exactly where this project's ~85 sites live. If any of the 85 sites (or their reaches) were SPARROW calibration sites, then al_tn/il_tn at those reaches encodes the observed nitrate level at the site, and a LOFO fold that holds out a basin family will still see a feature that was fit to that family's own loads. That is leakage that LOFO does not catch, because the leak is baked into the covariate rather than into the split. Before using this, pull the calibration-site list from SIR 2019-5114 and check overlap with the 85 sites; if there is overlap, report both "with SPARROW" and "with SPARROW, calibration-overlapping families dropped".
(3) It is a static 2012 base-year mean-annual product, so it can only move the between-site term. That is the correct place to aim — the project's own diagnostic (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24, seven failed temporal ablations, wins only from static geography) says the deficit is between-site static information. il_tn/IncAreaKm2 (incremental TN yield), the fert/man/nfix source shares, and DEL_FRAC are per-reach static scalars that describe exactly the "how loaded is this basin" quantity the model is missing, and they can be aggregated over an arbitrary NLDI-delineated basin at prediction time with no local history and no gauge — so it IS compatible with the arbitrary-map-pin deployment target. But note that with n=19 independent basin families you are adding correlated static columns to a between-site regression with ~19 effective units; expect the honest test to be whether between_rate_r2 moves at all under LOFO, and expect wide error bars on any gain. Add a small number of SPARROW-derived columns (yield, dominant source share, DEL_FRAC), not all 40.

(c) MATERIAL OMISSION FOR OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET: a large share of the 19 approaches CANNOT be applied at an ungauged map pin. The methods genuinely available with no local observations are the distance-only and attribute-only families at median R_NP 0.79 and 0.78, versus 0.70 for random donors. The usable no-local-data margin over random is therefore roughly 0.08-0.09 R_NP, not the 0.12 implied by the top-ranked method.

The mechanism transferred is a calibrated conceptual-model parameter vector, which has no analogue in a feature-based XGBoost classifier - so this paper does not supply a method we can implement, only a protocol design and a set of donor-selection heuristics. The flexible region-of-influence approaches select the 3 most similar donors from 670; at n=19 families a 3-donor region of influence draws from 18, so the donor pool is thin enough that the paper's central comparison (flexible RoI beating fixed classification) is untestable here. Target variable also differs fundamentally: daily streamflow evaluated with KGE variants, median catchment area 341 km2, versus our binary daily nitrate exceedance in tile-drained Iowa agricultural basins. Cite this paper for PUB protocol design and for the negative-ish result that attribute-based donor selection lands mid-rank (0.78) and barely beats spatial proximity (0.79), which is consistent with our own finding that static geography carries the between-site signal. Do not cite it as evidence that any regionalization method will deliver gains at n=19.

The claim is accurate as stated; only two refinements and a set of usage caveats are needed.

REFINEMENT 1 (internal inconsistency in the source, not in the claim): the paper's running text and abstract say 19 regionalization approaches and state "a total of 23 methods," but the caption of Table 2 reads "Description of the 18 Regionalization and 4 Benchmark Approaches Tested in This Study" (18+4=22). The claim reproduces the paper's own dominant wording (19+4=23); the discrepancy is the authors', not the claimant's. Cite it as "19 approaches (Table 2 caption says 18) plus 4 benchmarks."

REFINEMENT 2 (protocol, important for our rules): the holdout is SPATIAL ONLY. Donor parameter sets were calibrated on the same window they were evaluated on — "Calibration and evaluation were conducted during the simulation period from October 1, 1989 to September 30, 1999." There is no temporal holdout, and no nesting or region blocking, so this protocol is WEAKER than our leave-one-basin-family-out. Numbers from this study must not be treated as an upper bound comparable to LOFO transfer, and none of its metrics (R_NP/R_KG on daily hydrographs) are comparable to our AUC/PR-AUC on a binary exceedance target in any case.

USAGE CAVEATS FOR OUR PROJECT (the claim is true but should not be used to motivate donor-based regionalization here):

(a) The n=19-families constraint is fatal for the method family this paper evaluates, and the paper's own Figure 1 analysis quantifies why. With 670 candidate donors: "for a relative performance value of 0.7, half of the hypothetically ungauged catchments have at most 23 suitable donor catchments" — i.e. the median catchment has roughly 3.4% of the pool as usable donors. Scaled to our 18 available donor families, the expected number of suitable donors is well under one. The paper also reports that for the median catchment MOST donors are worse than random parameter sets ("For the other 60% of the donor catchments, one would be better off using random parameter sets"). Donor-transfer regionalization derives essentially all its power from a large, hydroclimatically diverse donor pool; at n=19 the pool is too small for the selection step to find anything.

(b) The two best-performing approach families are unavailable at our deployment target. The paper's own conclusion is that approaches combining spatial proximity with VOLUME information (streamflow-derived signatures) rank highest — and it concedes "volume information is per definition missing in ungauged catchments," recoverable only "from a small number of field measurements" or regionalized signatures. Our product pin has no discharge, and only 22 of 85 training sites have streamflow at all (zero of the 61 IWQIS sites), so we cannot even build the donor-side signature library statewide.

(c) Two of the four benchmarks are oracles, not deployable methods. UB requires calibrating on the target's own observations; Best requires knowing the target's observed hydrograph to rank donors by R_NP. The impressive "median 0.87, close to local calibration" number is an oracle ceiling, not an achievable ungauged result. The achievable numbers are the 0.76 (classification-based) to ~0.8x range against a 0.69–0.70 random-donor floor.

(d) Domain mismatch is large: HBV rainfall-runoff parameter transfer for daily streamflow in largely undisturbed CAMELS reference catchments, versus nitrate exceedance classification in tile-drained Iowa row-crop basins. CAMELS gauges are selected for minimal human disturbance, which excludes precisely the artificially drained, fertilized agricultural systems we model; tile drainage is not represented in HBV at all. The transferable insight is conceptual, not numerical: it corroborates our own finding that the hard part is the between-site absolute level, and that similarity must be defined on the right attributes — but it offers no evidence that donor-based transfer will work at n=19 with no volume information.

Two refinements, neither of which overturns the claim.

(1) "Validation is point-based AND county-based" overstates the county part. The county comparison is NOT independent validation - it is circular. The paper says the map is "consistent with USDA 2017 county-level census BECAUSE the geospatial model was constrained by county-level census estimates," and the only number given is a -0.35% CONUS-total area difference, with state-level totals in Table 1. No county-by-county R2 or correlation is reported. The map is a downscaling of the county census, not an independent measurement of it. The only genuine validation is the 16,000-point photo-interpretation (Iowa 91.1%, n=5,253 points). Describe it as point-validated with a county-total mass-balance constraint.

(2) The claim omits a real risk to its own falsifiable test: COLLINEARITY WITH EXISTING FEATURES. AgTile-US is masked to NLCD-2016 cropland and driven by slope + SSURGO drainage class, so basin tile fraction is close to a "flat, poorly drained cropland fraction." The model already carries 8 CDL crop classes x 3 distance buckets plus lat/lon, and in Iowa the corn/soy fraction on low-slope poorly drained ground is nearly the same quantity. The new column may therefore be substantially spanned by features already present - which would explain a null result without meaning tile drainage is unimportant. Before running the ablation, check the correlation of basin tile fraction against the existing per-bucket corn/soy fractions and against lat/lon across the 19 families; if |r| is high, the honest test is a partial/orthogonalized contribution, not a raw add-one-column comparison.

(3) Minor: the product is a STATIC 2017 snapshot (single reference year, USDA 2017 census). The claim's framing already wants exactly one static column, so this is compatible - but it must not be broadcast as a time-varying feature, which is precisely the failure mode that sank the 2017 N-surplus broadcast (-0.166). Use it as a time-invariant per-basin attribute only.

The claim's prediction - that a static basin attribute should move between_r2 (0.21) and between_rate_r2 (0.24) rather than within_r2 (0.42) - is a project design statement, not a source claim, and is not testable against this paper. votes.correction:
Claim is accurate as written; adopt it, but state these five caveats explicitly when using the layer.

(a) "86.03% accuracy" is RECALL ON POSITIVES ONLY — there is no false-positive assessment. All 16,000 points were manually digitized from ESRI aerial imagery at locations "when a tile drainage signature is detected," i.e. all are tile-present positives. The paper's own arithmetic confirms this: 86.03% accuracy + "13.97% omission error" = 100%. There is no confusion matrix, no true negatives, no commission error, no kappa. A map that over-painted tile everywhere would score ~100% under this validation. This matters directly for us: we intend a basin-MEAN fraction, and mean fraction is biased precisely by commission error, which is the one error mode never measured. Do not describe this as "86% classification accuracy" in project docs; describe it as "86.03% of known tile-drained ground-truth points correctly captured (omission error only; commission error unquantified)."

(b) Validation is not fully independent of model fitting. The paper extracts the slope thresholds that constrain the decision tree from the same ground-truth point set later used for validation. Treat 86.03%/91.1% as optimistic in-sample-flavored numbers.

(c) The map is CENSUS-CONSTRAINED BY COUNTY by construction — cells are accumulated until the county total matches the 2017 USDA census. So county aggregates reproduce the census almost exactly, and the map's genuine added value is sub-county ALLOCATION. For a basin spanning several counties, basin-mean tile fraction is close to an area-weighted county-census average. Effective independent information is ~county-scale (99 counties in Iowa), not 30 m. Still fine at n=19 families, but do not claim 30 m of real signal.

(d) Known systematic low bias, stated by the authors: NLCD-2016 underrepresents cropland by "18.15% underrepresentation for the CONUS," and average USDA census error is "19.8%." Tile fraction is therefore biased low, unevenly.

(e) Denominator ambiguity — a practical implementation note. Because non-cropland cells are 0, a naive basin-mean conflates "not tiled" with "not cropland." Compute BOTH tile_area/basin_area and tile_area/cropland_area per distance bucket; the latter is the actual management-intensity signal and the former is the loading-relevant one.

Finally, one risk to the falsifiable prediction that the claim should have flagged: tile-drained fraction is spatially very smooth across Iowa (Des Moines Lobe vs. Loess Hills / driftless SE), and lon and lat are already the #2 and #3 permutation-importance features. There is a real chance XGBoost has already absorbed most of this signal through lat/lon and the new columns add little. That does not argue against trying it — it is cheap, static, and of the exact class that has produced this project's only wins — but the ablation should be run against a lat/lon-included baseline (not a stripped one), and a null result should be interpreted as "already captured by coordinates," not as "tile drainage does not matter."

The claim is substantively correct and operationally usable; three corrections and one caution.

(1) MISQUOTE. The sentence attributed verbatim to the authors ("does not represent spatial or temporal changes in drainage installation") is not in the paper. Replace with the actual text: "The data deliver a static representation of U.S. tile drainage for the year 2017." The claim's conclusion - static snapshot, cannot supply any time-varying tile signal - is nonetheless correct.

(2) IT IS A MODELED PRODUCT, NOT AN OBSERVATION, AND THIS IS THE MAIN THREAT TO THE CLAIM'S CENTRAL ARGUMENT. AgTile-US is a deterministic decision tree over SSURGO soil drainage category and SRTM slope, thresholded until accumulated area matches USDA COUNTY-level census tile acreage. The per-basin tile fraction is therefore a smooth function of soil drainage class and slope, constrained only at county granularity. The claim asserts this is "exactly the between-site static information the LOFO gap needs." At n=19 independent basin families in Iowa, that new attribute may be substantially collinear with lat/lon - already the #2 and #3 features by permutation importance - and with the CDL crop fractions. It is not guaranteed to be independent information. Before assuming lift, compute the correlation of basin tile-fraction against lat, lon, log_basin_area and the CDL bucket features; if R^2 against existing statics is high, expected gain is small.

(3) DENOMINATOR AMBIGUITY - the claim says "one number per basin" but there are two distinct features. Non-agricultural land is MASKED OUT, not coded 0, so (a) tile cells / total basin cells and (b) tile cells / agricultural cells are different quantities. (b) is drainage intensity, the physically meaningful control; (a) conflates drainage with crop cover already captured by the 8 CDL classes x 3 buckets. Build both; they are not interchangeable. Also note the mask is NLCD-2016 cropland, a different land-cover product from the CDL currently used, so cell-level agreement with existing crop features is imperfect.

(4) CAUTION, NOT A BLOCKER, ON THE 2017 DATE. This is superficially the same 2017 endpoint as the N-surplus product whose forward-broadcast failed badly (-0.166). The failure modes differ: that was a TIME-VARYING feature held constant, whereas this is used as a static basin attribute where no temporal claim is made. Tile installation is also far more inertial than annual nitrogen application, so a 2017 snapshot is a defensible constant across 2008-2026. Do not treat the prior negative result as predicting failure here, but do enter it as a static attribute only - never as a per-day feature.

FIT TO THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: clean. It is a raster, so it is computable for an arbitrary map pin's NLDI-delineated basin with no local nitrate history, no discharge gauge, and no monitored upstream neighbor. It requires nothing from the target site's own observations. FIT TO n=19: unusually good - one additional static scalar is affordable at 19 effective units in a way a large catchment-attribute set is not. Iowa mapping accuracy (91.1%) is above the CONUS average.

(2) CLASS DEFINITION. The claim says 0 = undrained cropland / 1 = tile-drained cropland. The paper's classes are defined over an NLCD-2016 agricultural-land mask, not a CDL cropland mask, and the paper flags 18.15% under-representation of CONUS croplands in NLCD-2016. Operationally this matters: AgTile-US's denominator is NOT the same cropland footprint as our CDL-derived crop-class features, so a basin tile fraction computed as (tile cells / CDL crop cells) mixes two incompatible masks. Compute tile fraction against basin AREA, or against AgTile-US's own 0+1 domain, not against CDL.

METHODOLOGY CAVEAT NOT IN THE CLAIM, and this is the one that should temper expectations. AgTile-US is not an independent observation of tile. It is a top-down disaggregation: county-level USDA 2017 Census of Agriculture drained-acreage totals are allocated within each county by a decision tree over SSURGO drainage class (D=1-7) and SRTM slope (0-20%), poorly-drained/low-slope cells taken first, until the county total is matched. Consequences:
- Within a county, the layer is a deterministic function of soils + slope. A basin-aggregated tile fraction is therefore close to a smooth reparameterization of "fraction of basin that is poorly-drained, low-slope agricultural land," modulated only by the county-total scaling. It is NOT information orthogonal to soils/topography; if you also add SSURGO drainage class or basin slope as features you will be adding a near-collinear copy.
- Its true independent resolution is the COUNTY, not 30 m. Iowa has 99 counties; an Iowa basin of typical size spans a handful of them. So the effective independent variation available to distinguish our 19 basin families is on the order of tens of county values, not millions of pixels. The 30 m number is a rendering resolution, not an information resolution.
- Inherited error: the paper states USDA census dependence carries approximately +/-19.8% average error.

An arbitrary map pin, once NLDI returns the upstream basin polygon, yields a tile fraction with no nitrate history, no discharge gauge, and no monitored neighbor required. Train-time and deploy-time feature construction are identical, so there is no gauged-site dependence and no leakage pathway. CONUS coverage does resolve the stated multi-state under-count problem for the large basins (Iowa basins extending into MN/SD/NE/MO), unlike the Iowa-only joins.

n=19 CONSTRAINT: flagged, and it is the binding limit. This adds ONE static scalar per basin against ~19 independent units. It is the correct KIND of information given the diagnosis (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21; headroom is between-site), and it is cheap and low-risk because static geography is the only feature class that has previously won on this project. The file also contains the model's own calibration/monitoring quantities: flux_530_final, flux_154_final, flux_600_final, flux_665_final (monitored/detrended load estimates at calibration sites), mean_dflow_predpd, and the weighting terms TNAllSN_inv_resid2_hat, TPAllN_inv_resid2_hat, sedN_inv_resid2_hat, flowDN_inv_resid2_hat. Ingesting these would inject observed nitrogen load into the feature set at exactly the monitored locations, and they are unavailable in the ungauged-pin sense. The claim's named subset is safe; a blanket "ingest the file" is not.

3. VALUES ARE INCREMENTAL PER CATCHMENT, NOT BASIN-CUMULATIVE. ManN2012, fert_sw_N_kg, cmaq_TN_12_kg, sum_ptsrc_kgn_wwtp are per-catchment kilogram totals paired with IncAreaKm2. For an arbitrary map pin you must sum over the NLDI-returned upstream COMID set and then divide by CumAreaKm2 to get kg/km2 — raw sums would largely re-encode basin area, which the model already has as log_basin_area. This is mechanically compatible with the existing NLDI delineation step, so it works for the deployment target, but it is an extra accumulation stage, not a lookup.

4. TWO OF THE LISTED COLUMNS ARE NEARLY DEGENERATE IN IOWA. Measured on the downloaded file: `aridity` is exactly 0 for 99.71% of Iowa catchments (it is a western-region delivery term) and `sum_ptsrc_kgn_wwtp` is 0 for 99.10% (nonzero only where a WWTP exists — meaningful only after upstream accumulation). Also `tiles13_perc2`/`ltiles13_perc2` are 0 for 58.68% of Iowa catchments, so this tile variable is far coarser and sparser than the Iowa tile-drainage literature would imply; do not treat it as a resolved tile-drainage layer.

They cannot restore the time-varying dimension the gTREND surplus product had before 2017; they replace a 68%-NaN time series with a complete constant. That is a genuine fix for the missingness and for the between-site term, but it must not be described as recovering temporal N-input variation — it removes it.

These are static per-site features: under LOFO they take at most 19 distinct effective values, so adding ~20 of them is a ~20-parameter regression on 19 independent units. Combined with the report's county-apportionment caveat (fertilizer, manure, no-till, CRP all derive from county averages downscaled by land use), the realized between-site resolution is county-scale, which within a single Iowa basin family is close to constant. Expect this to be a high-variance addition prone to memorizing family identity; it should be added as a small, pre-selected subset (e.g. accumulated fert+manure+deposition per km2, ldrainden, lcat_KFCTUP, lcat_STCLAY) with the LOFO protocol enforced, not as a 20-column block. 3. "Substituted or supplemented" for the 2017-ending N surplus overstates the substitution half. These are 2012 single-year static snapshots with zero temporal dimension. They cannot replace a time-varying surplus; they can only inform the between-site term. This matters because the project already has a directly analogous negative result: broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward in time scored -0.166. Recommend ADD as static between-site features, never SUBSTITUTE into the existing time-varying slot, or that failure is likely to reproduce.

4. n=19 CONSTRAINT — unaddressed by the claim and binding here. The project's diagnosis is that essentially all headroom is in the between-site term, which has ~19 effective independent units. Adding ~20 new static per-basin predictors to a 19-unit between-site regression is a p>n overfitting setup; LOFO will not reliably distinguish real transfer from noise. Recommend a hand-picked subset of 3-5 area-weighted aggregates (e.g. tiles13_perc2, ManN2012+fert_sw_N_kg combined, ldrainden, CAT_STCLAY) rather than the full block, with the count fixed a priori rather than selected on LOFO score.

5. The claim UNDERSELLS on tile drainage. It says "beyond tile drains," but tiles13_perc2 / ltiles13_perc2 are in this very file at 0.00% missing — directly addressing the project's stated gap that tile drainage density is the dominant Iowa hydrologic control with "NO data source identified yet." Caveat: in Iowa 58.7% of catchments are zero with median 0 and p90 60.9%, a strongly bimodal pattern consistent with real tiling concentrated in the Des Moines Lobe rather than with missingness. It needs area-weighted aggregation to basin scale to be informative; per-catchment it looks sparse.

6. Minor: the same SIR passage the claim quotes describes the catchments as "about 2 km2" while the abstract says a 2.7 km2 mean — a small internal inconsistency in the source, not in the claim.

Basu et al. (2010) separately used the r-squared of the linear regression between ANNUAL load and ANNUAL discharge as a chemostasis measure, implying linearity in the load-Q relation; chemostatic responses in agricultural catchments are attributed to a large legacy soil/groundwater N store buffering concentration, and homogeneously distributed sources produce chemostatic export while heterogeneously distributed sources produce chemodynamic export.
