votes.evidence:
CITATION IS REAL AND CORRECTLY ATTRIBUTED. Thompson, S. E., Basu, N. B., Lascurain, J., Aubeneau, A., Rao, P. S. C. (2011), "Relative dominance of hydrologic versus biogeochemical factors on solute export across impact gradients," Water Resources Research, DOI 10.1029/2010WR009605, 334 citations (OpenAlex). Its abstract does concern the concentration/discharge variability ratio and does attribute chemostasis to spatially homogeneous mass stores. So the qualitative core is sound and the DOI is right.

THE NUMBER 0.3 IS WRONG. I found no source using 0.3. The two conventions actually in the literature are 0.5 and 1.0. Frietsch & Schuetz (2026), Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci. 30, 2059-2077, DOI 10.5194/hess-30-2059-2026 (gold OA, read in full), Section 2.3.3: "Solutes with CVC/CVQ > 0.5 were classified as chemodynamic ... whereas CVC/CVQ <= 0.5 indicated chemostatic behaviour. The threshold of 0.5 ... was chosen following Thompson et al. (2011), who showed that conservative tracers typically yielded values around this level. This benchmark has been adopted in subsequent studies (Ebeling et al., 2021; Musolff et al., 2017) ... Although alternative thresholds (e.g. 1) exist in the literature (Musolff et al., 2015), 0.5 was deemed most appropriate." Independently, the HyGCS toolbox documentation (hygcs.readthedocs.io) uses "CVc/CVq > 1 = chemodynamic, < 1 = chemostatic," citing Musolff et al. 2015, Adv. Water Resour. 86, 133-146. The Speir/Rose et al. 2023 WIREs Water C-Q review (read in full) gives NO numeric threshold at all and attributes the classification scheme to Musolff et al. 2015, citing Thompson et al. 2011 only for the concept. Note also that per Frietsch & Schuetz, Thompson et al. 2011 did not set a hard cutoff; 0.5 is a value later readers inferred from Thompson's conservative-tracer results. So "0.3 conventionally taken as the chemostatic threshold" is unsupported and off by a factor of ~1.7-3.3 from the real conventions.

BASU ET AL. 2010 IS CHARACTERIZED CORRECTLY, BUT ITS OWN TEXT DESTROYS THE PROJECT-LEVEL INFERENCE. Basu et al. (2010), GRL, DOI 10.1029/2010GL045168 (author copy read in full). Sample: 21 MARB catchments (10^4-10^6 km2) + 14 Baltic Sea Drainage Basin catchments (10^2-10^5 km2) + Hubbard Brook/Loch Vale forested reference sites + 3 Lake Okeechobee + 2 Swan River, 10-30 yr records. They do use zero-intercept linear regression of annual load LT on annual discharge QT with R2 as the criterion ("consistent linear relationships (R2 = 0.7 +/- 0.2) between annual exported nutrient loads, LT, and annual discharge, QT"), and a separate model-adequacy criterion "linear fits to the LT-QT relationship are judged adequate (R2 > 0.8) for a range of b values (-0.4 < b < 1.4)". So that part of the claim checks out. BUT the same paper states verbatim: "non-chemostatic responses are typical of nutrient (TN and TP) export from managed catchments in the MARB and BSDB (Figures S1 and S2). Notwithstanding non-chemostatic response at the daily or monthly time scales, we find consistent linear relationships ... between annual exported nutrient loads and annual discharge." Basu's chemostasis is an ANNUAL-scale, flow-weighted-concentration claim about basins of 10^4-10^6 km2. This project predicts DAILY MAX nitrate and daily 10 mg/L exceedance in Iowa, which is inside the MARB. The cited source explicitly says N is NOT chemostatic at that timescale in that region. Basu et al. also pre-empt a statistical objection that applies directly to the proposed decision rule: the LT-QT correlation is partly "spurious ... since discharge is a component of load calculation."

THE METRIC IS SCALE-DEPENDENT IN EXACTLY THIS REGION. Marinos, Van Meter & Basu (2020), "Is the River a Chemostat?: Scale Versus Land Use Controls on Nitrate Concentration-Discharge Dynamics in the Upper Mississippi River Basin," GRL, DOI 10.1029/2020GL087051 (abstract via OpenAlex; paper is closed access): "tile drainage is a dominant control on C-Q dynamics, with increasing drainage density contributing to more chemostatic C-Q behavior. We further find that concentration variability increases, relative to discharge variability, with increasing basin size across six orders of magnitude." So CVc/CVq in the UMRB is a strong function of basin area and tile density, not a stable solute property. Computing it across the project's 22 gauged sites (which span a wide area range) would mostly recover basin area — a feature the model already has as log_basin_area.

BROADER NEGATIVE EVIDENCE ON THE LINEARITY IMPLICATION. Moatar et al. (2017), WRR, DOI 10.1002/2016WR019635, 293 French monitoring stations, 40 years: "84% of all catchment-element combinations were chemodynamic for at least half of hydrograph" and "60% showed nonlinear C-Q curves." Diamond & Cohen (2017), DOI 10.1002/hyp.11424, 44 Florida rivers, found significant C-Q slope breaks near median flow and concluded "generic power-law characterization" is inadequate. Universal chemostasis + load-Q linearity is not a safe default.

METHODOLOGICAL WARNING AGAINST THE PROPOSED USE, FROM THE FIELD'S OWN REVIEW. Speir/Rose et al. (2023), WIREs Water: "C-Q metrics are interrelated and may not be independent of each other ... the range of concentration variability is inherently linked to the quantitative estimation of both b and CVC/CVQ (Jawitz & Mitchell, 2011; Musolff et al., 2015; Thompson et al., 2011) ... caution and correction procedures should be applied when conducting statistical analyses on derived metrics (e.g., regressing metrics against each other) because this can involve testing multiple hypotheses on the same dataset and thereby inflating Type I error." The proposed decision rule is precisely "regress a derived C-Q metric against catchment attributes." The same review's methods table lists CVC/CVQ as needing ">1 year of 5-15 min frequency sensor data," so grab-sample sites and sensor sites are not comparable on this metric.

THE LOAD-BEARING INFERENCE IS A NON-SEQUITUR AND IS PARTLY BACKWARDS. The claim asserts chemostasis "predicts ... the site-mean concentration should track the N-source term ... rather than the hydrologic term." Neither source says this, and it does not follow. Basu's own definition is Cf = LT/QT: under chemostasis the site-mean concentration IS mass flux divided by water flux, so long-term mean runoff sits in the denominator and is a first-order BETWEEN-site control, not an eliminated one. Chemostasis implies that SAME-DAY discharge is uninformative about concentration while LONG-TERM CLIMATOLOGICAL water yield is highly informative. The project's seven failed ablations were all short-window/event-scale temporal features; none of them tested a static long-term runoff or precipitation climatology term. So the theory, read correctly, does not "explain" the failures and does not endorse dropping hydrology — if anything it argues for adding a static climatological water-yield normalizer that the current 68-feature set lacks.

DEPLOYMENT-TARGET AND SAMPLE-SIZE VERDICT. CVc/CVq requires paired C and Q at the site. Discharge exists at 22 of 85 sites and zero of 61 IWQIS sites; the shipped product is an arbitrary map pin with no gauge at all, so this can never be a feature at prediction time. As a diagnostic it is computable, but on 22 sites that collapse to well under the project's 19 independent basin families, and any between-site regression of the resulting metric on N surplus / row-crop fraction / tile density would have effective n around 10, with the metric itself confounded by basin area (Marinos et al. 2020) and by sampling frequency. That is not a "cheap decision rule"; it is an underpowered correlation on derived quantities that the field's own review warns against computing this way.

Water Resour. 86, 133-146). (2) The threshold is NOT 0.3. (2) CVc/CVq << 1 AS CHEMOSTATIC — TRUE, verbatim. Para [20]: "Godsey et al. [2009] proposed a simple null hypothesis that in-stream concentrations should reflect dilution of a fixed mass available for export (i.e., C = aQ^-1). A propagation of variance analysis... implies that for this null hypothesis, CVC/CVQ = 1. Chemostatic behavior could then be considered a case where the variability in concentration was highly buffered compared to this null hypothesis, i.e., CVC/CVQ << 1. Note that if C = aQ^0 (the Godsey et al. [2009] criterion), then CVC/CVQ = 0."

(3) THE 0.3 THRESHOLD — TRUE and exact, but "conventionally taken" is an overstatement. Para [28]: "For the geogenic species... the mean CVC/CVQ was 0.17 (range 0.15–0.19) with standard deviation 0.06 (range 0.04–0.07), i.e., uniformly well below 1... We define a chemostatic CV ratio as being within two standard deviations of the mean geogenic CVC/CVQ, that is ~0.3." So 0.3 = 0.17 + 2(0.06), an internal empirical calibration to the geogenic reference solutes measured at THIS paper's own 31 subwatersheds. It is not a community convention and the paper does not present it as one.

(4) "CHEMODYNAMIC" TERMINOLOGY — the word "chemodynamic" appears ZERO times in the paper (grep count 0). CVc/CVq = 1 is the DILUTION null hypothesis (C proportional to 1/Q), not "chemodynamic". Numerically harmless, terminologically drifted.

(5) BASU ET AL. 2010 ANNUAL LOAD–Q r-squared — TRUE, verbatim. Para [19]: "Basu et al. [2010a] argued that chemostatic behavior implied near linearity in the annual load (LT)–discharge (QT) relationship (LT = Cf QT), as measured by the correlation coefficient (r^2)." Basu et al. 2010a = GRL 37, L23404, doi:10.1029/2010GL045168, "Nutrient loads exported from managed catchments reveal emergent biogeochemical stationarity" (MARB + Baltic Sea Drainage Basin, TN and TP, annual aggregates). Thompson himself flags a circularity the claim omits: "the definition of load as LT = Cf QT complicates the interpretation of the LT-QT r^2 value as a measure of linearity, due to the construction of LT as a linear function of QT."

(6) LEGACY-STORE BUFFERING — TRUE, abstract verbatim: "These 'chemostatic' responses are hypothesized to arise when a large mass store, the parent material for geogenics or chemically recalcitrant legacies of fertilization in agricultural catchments, buffers concentration variability."

(7) HOMOGENEOUS vs HETEROGENEOUS SOURCES — PARTIALLY TRUE, and materially garbled. Abstract: "the decline in CVC/CVQ arises if the internal mass store is distributed homogeneously in space AND there is sufficient time for mass transfer to reach steady state between runoff events." The claim drops the second, co-necessary timescale condition. Further, the "homogeneity" is a parameter xi in a single-reactor model denoting UNIFORM VERTICAL mass distribution in the soil profile: para [26] region, "repeating the analysis with xi != 0 (not shown) showed that chemostatic behavior couldn't be recovered unless xi ~ 0, recapitulating the Seibert et al. [2009] requirement of spatial homogeneity." This is a modeled inference, never an empirical test of landscape source heterogeneity across catchments.

METHODOLOGY / SAMPLE SIZE. Para [12]-[13]: "data from 31 small intensively studied watersheds (0.1–22 km2)" drawn from only NINE experimental watersheds (LTERs/experimental forests) — i.e. 31 nested subwatersheds within 9 independent sites, the exact pseudoreplication structure this project already corrected for with its 85 sites -> 19 families. Sites were deliberately chosen small "thus minimizing the effects of spatial averaging on the hydrochemistry" — the opposite regime from Iowa's large, partly multi-state basins. Only TWO of the nine are agricultural (Little Vermillion River, IL — tile-drained; McDonogh, MD). Sampling: daily flow, "daily to monthly sampling of nitrate over at least a 3 year period"; CVs computed on the full record, no spatial holdout of any kind (protocol: not applicable, this is a descriptive synthesis, not a predictive study). Para [23] documents that CV is unstable when the mean is low or near detection limit.

THE NITRATE RESULT IS THE WEAKEST PART OF THE PAPER, AND IT IS THE PART THE CLAIM LEANS ON. Abstract: "Nitrate showed a suggestive pattern in CVC/CVQ with export, but further data are needed to confirm its generality." Para [30]: nitrate CVc/CVq had "mean 0.70, standard deviation 0.49" across sites, decreasing with export "albeit less abruptly than in the case of the exogenous salts"; "The lowest values of CVC/CVQ for NO3- were in the range of 0.2–0.4, comparable to the geogenic species. Although suggestive, the data at high export levels remain scarce." So on the paper's own ~0.3 criterion, MOST of its nitrate sites are NOT chemostatic; only the sparse high-export tail approaches it. Same paragraph warns the metrics disagree for N specifically: "Numerous sites displayed b ~ 0, but nonetheless exhibited a wide range of variability as measured by CVC/CVQ."

AUTHOR'S OWN CAVEAT AGAINST THE CLAIM'S USE, para [20]: "Describing a condition of low CVC/CVQ as chemostatic behavior, however, should not be overinterpreted. This use of the term chemostatic does not imply that concentrations are truly invariant, or uncorrelated with variations in flow."
votes.correction:
The citation checks out and the numbers are exact — keep it — but three things must be fixed before this is used to justify anything.

1. PROVENANCE OF THE 0.3. It is not a "conventional" threshold. It is 0.17 + 2 x 0.06, two SDs above the mean CVc/CVq of GEOGENIC solutes measured at Thompson's own 31 subwatersheds (nested in 9 experimental sites, 0.1-22 km2). It is a relative reference calibrated on that dataset, in a paper with only 2 agricultural catchments. Do not cite it as a community standard, and do not treat crossing 0.3 as a physical fact about an Iowa basin. Also fix the title ("across impact gradients") and drop "chemodynamic" — the word never appears; CVc/CVq = 1 is Godsey et al. 2009's pure-DILUTION null (C ~ 1/Q), not a chemodynamic label.

2. THE PAPER DOES NOT ESTABLISH THAT AGRICULTURAL NITRATE IS CHEMOSTATIC. Its nitrate result is mean CVc/CVq = 0.70 (SD 0.49) — above the 0.3 line for most sites — with only the sparse high-export tail reaching 0.2-0.4, and the abstract explicitly says "further data are needed to confirm its generality." The agricultural-legacy-N story rests on Basu et al. 2010 GRL (doi:10.1029/2010GL045168), which is ANNUAL total-N load vs ANNUAL discharge over MARB and Baltic basins, not daily concentration. Cite Basu for the legacy-N mechanism, not Thompson.

3. THE FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION AS STATED IS NOT WHAT CHEMOSTASIS PREDICTS. Chemostasis constrains WITHIN-site variance of C relative to Q. It does not say the between-site mean concentration tracks the source term alone. Under Basu's own formulation the invariant quantity is the flow-weighted concentration Cf = LT/QT — a RATIO. So chemostasis predicts site-mean concentration ~ (delivered N load per unit area) / (mean annual runoff depth), which means the hydrologic term does not drop out, it moves into the DENOMINATOR as a long-term water-yield normalizer. That is a genuinely different and more useful engineering prescription than "use surplus and row-crop fraction": build a static per-basin feature of the form (N surplus or row-crop fraction) / (long-term mean annual runoff or precipitation), i.e. a normalized source-loading intensity, rather than the raw source terms currently in the model. This is a static, climatological feature computable at an arbitrary ungauged pin from PRISM/Daymet normals plus a runoff-coefficient raster — it does not need the target's discharge. That is the actionable, deployment-compatible reading, and it is not what the claim states.

Two further constraints to attach. (a) DIAGNOSTIC ONLY, NEVER A FEATURE: CVc/CVq needs paired C and Q at the site. That exists at 22 of 85 sites (26%, all USGS, zero IWQIS) and at ZERO arbitrary map pins. It can characterize the training sites; it can never be an input at deployment. (b) THE n CONSTRAINT BITES TWICE: those 22 gauged sites collapse to well under 19 independent basin families, so any regression of site-mean level on chemostasis-derived predictors has single-digit effective units — smaller than Thompson's own 9 independent sites, and with the same nesting problem. Additionally the timescale is wrong for the product: CVc/CVq is a whole-distribution variance statistic computed on daily-to-monthly grab samples (Basu's on annual aggregates), while the target is DAILY-MAX nitrate crossing 10 mg/L. A basin can be perfectly chemostatic at CVc/CVq = 0.3 and still swing across 10 mg/L constantly if its mean sits near 8. Chemostasis says nothing about the upper tail, which is the entire classification problem.

Finally, "consistent with our observed pattern that static geography wins and temporal features fail" is post-hoc, not diagnostic. A chemodynamic system with uninformative same-day weather features would produce the identical symptom, and the failed features were precipitation and fuel moisture, not discharge — the C-Q relation was never actually tested here. If you want a real test, compute CVc/CVq on the 22 gauged sites (checking, as Thompson does in para [23], that the flow range during concentration sampling spans the full flow-duration curve, and noting the 0.66-0.97 discharge density gaps), and separately regress site-mean nitrate on surplus/runoff. The CV ratio itself decides nothing about the model.

claim: Four SPARROW limitations bear directly on using its output as a feature for an arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin. (1) TEMPORAL RESOLUTION MISMATCH: the released TN/TP/SS predictions are LONG-TERM MEAN-ANNUAL loads with base year 2012 (detrended over 2000-2014); there is no daily, seasonal, or event-scale output, so SPARROW can only supply a static per-basin LEVEL term and can contribute nothing to the WHEN question — which matches this project's diagnosis that the deficit is in the between-site term (between_r2 0.21) and not the within-site term (within_r2 0.42). (2) SMALL-BASIN EXTRAPOLATION: the report states 'The uncertainty associated with SPARROW predictions is expected to increase for drainage basin sizes smaller than those of stream monitoring sites used to calibrate the model', and that 'most of the sites used to calibrate the SPARROW models were located on medium to large streams and may not represent the smallest streams in the Midwest' — for the TP model only 5 percent of calibration sites were on streams draining less than about 31 km2. (3) SPATIALLY CONSTANT COEFFICIENTS: source and land-to-water coefficients are constant across the whole Midwest, and the authors report that 'relatively large residuals were still identified in the western part of the study area', suggesting systematic regional bias that would propagate into any feature built from SPARROW output. (4) The report notes a Bayesian hierarchical regionally-varying-coefficient SPARROW (Alexander 2015; Strickling & Obenour 2018) was NOT used here and 'could improve their predictability'. No published evaluation of SPARROW output used as an INPUT FEATURE to an ML model appears in this data release or its parent report — that experiment is untested here and would have to be run.
effectSize: TP model: only 5% of calibration sites on drainage areas < ~31 km2; 14/15/28% of TN/TP/SS lost in delivery to the Great Lakes and 19/23/52% to the Gulf of Mexico

votes.correction:
The claim is substantively accurate and quotes the primary source almost verbatim; keep it, with five precise fixes.

1. ATTRIBUTION FIX (the only real error). The sentence "The uncertainty associated with SPARROW predictions is expected to increase for drainage basin sizes smaller than those of stream monitoring sites used to calibrate the model" is NOT in SIR 2019-5114 — the word "uncertainty" appears exactly once in the report, inside a reference title. Do not attribute it to the report. Replace it with the report's actual wording: "it is difficult to know how well the model predicted loads in drainages smaller than this... caution should be taken when interpreting the finest scale model results (for example, predictions for the individual incremental drainages of the reaches)." The quoted sentence appears to be USGS data-release/DSS boilerplate; I could not retrieve the FGDC XML for data release https://doi.org/10.5066/P93QMXC9 to confirm, so cite it as unverified or drop it.

2. THE 5 PERCENT / 31 km2 FIGURE IS TP-ONLY, AND OUR TARGET IS NITRATE. The report gives this calibration-size statistic only for the TP model. It gives no equivalent number for the TN model, whose calibration n (1,334) is close to TP's, so a similar small-basin gap is plausible but is NOT documented. Since our target is nitrate, state that the TN-model small-basin coverage is unquantified in the source rather than importing the TP number.

3. SITE-COUNT LABEL. "1,334 TN ... sites considered" is wrong; 1,334 is the TN model's final calibration n (report text and TN summary table; Table 1 says 1,335 — an internal inconsistency in the report). "Sites considered" were 1,346 TN / 1,344 TP / 1,262 SS / 2,057 streamflow; "used in final models" were 1,335 TN / 1,273 TP / 1,082 suspended solids + 107 suspended sediment / 2,012 streamflow.

4. THE SMALL-BASIN CAVEAT IS ABOUT ACCURACY, NOT AVAILABILITY — which strengthens the operational case rather than killing it. The Midwest SPARROW network has a mean catchment size of 2.7 km2 (vs 480 km2 in the 2002 models), and output is keyed to NHDPlusV2 comid, which this project already stores per basin. So a SPARROW-derived level term IS obtainable for an arbitrary NLDI-delineated map pin with no local history — it is a legitimate deployment-compatible static feature. The correct framing is: cheap to attach, but expect the feature to be least trustworthy exactly where NLDI pins land on small headwater catchments, which is likely a large share of arbitrary map pins in Iowa.

5. POINT (3) OVERREACHES SLIGHTLY. "Systematic regional bias that would propagate into any feature built from SPARROW output" is stronger than the source supports for Iowa. The report locates the large residuals in the "western part of the study area" (elsewhere identified with the Missouri and Arkansas River Basins); it does not document bias in Iowa specifically. Also, a smooth regional bias in a SPARROW feature is partly absorbable by an XGBoost model that already has lat/lon as its 2nd and 3rd most important features — so residual regional bias is a reason to expect diminished marginal value, not a reason to expect harm.

FLAGGING THE n=19 CONSTRAINT (the claim does not do this and should). Adding SPARROW yield as a static per-basin covariate is a between-site term, and between-site signal is precisely what our 19 independent basin families have to estimate. One or two extra static columns is a modest, low-risk ask at n=19 — far safer than any method whose evidence base is 300+ catchments — but LOFO over 19 folds will give a very noisy estimate of its benefit; a gain smaller than roughly 0.03-0.05 PR-AUC will not be distinguishable from fold noise. Pre-register the ablation and report per-fold spread, not just the mean. Note also that SPARROW's own calibration is on 1,334 sites with nested/clustered geometry and in-sample fit statistics; its published R2 0.950 is not evidence of transfer and must not be cited alongside our LOFO 0.820.

A. The first quoted sentence in point (2) -- "The uncertainty associated with SPARROW predictions is expected to increase for drainage basin sizes smaller than those of stream monitoring sites used to calibrate the model" -- DOES NOT APPEAR in SIR 2019-5114. Zero hits for "uncertainty associated", "expected to increase", "smaller than those", "calibrate the model" in that construction. It is USGS SPARROW data-release FGDC metadata boilerplate, not report text; the FGDC XML attached to doi:10.5066/P93QMXC9 could not be retrieved (ScienceBase file endpoint returned a 1,205-byte stub), so it is unverified in either location. Attributing it to "the report" is a misattribution.
B. Point (3) overstates. Report: "In SPARROW models, it is typically assumed that the sources and land-to-water delivery variables interact in the same manner throughout the modeled area, based on the use of spatially constant source and land-to-water delivery model coefficients. However ... In this study, spatially varying land-to-water delivery variables WERE included in the models to better describe these differences; however, relatively large residuals were still identified in the western part of the study area." So land-to-water delivery is NOT spatially constant in this model; only source coefficients are.

The claim's "1,334 TN ... considered" conflates the calibration count with the considered count.

TRANSFERABILITY TO THIS PROJECT:
- Point (1) transfers cleanly and is the most decisive: SPARROW can only ever be a static per-basin level covariate. That is precisely the term this project needs (between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42), so the limitation is real but does not disqualify the feature -- it scopes it. A static covariate also carries essentially no n=19 penalty at feature-construction time (it is computed from the published model, not learned from our 19 families); the n=19 constraint applies only to whether XGBoost can learn a useful response to it, which is the untested experiment.
- Point (2) transfers with a caveat the claim does not state: the ~31 km2 threshold bites only for map pins on very small headwater catchments. It is a real risk for the arbitrary-map-pin product specifically because NLDI will happily delineate a tiny headwater basin, but it is not a general disqualifier.
- Point (3) transfers WEAKLY to Iowa and the claim's framing is misleading on geography. The flagged bias region is the arid western Missouri/Plains portion of the study area; the report separately states "Site density, for all models, was generally lower in the west and higher in the eastern parts of the Midwest area." Iowa sits in the high-density Corn Belt core, so the systematic-regional-bias concern is materially weaker here than the claim implies.
- Point (4) transfers as stated; Alexander (2015) and Strickling & Obenour (2018) are correctly cited by the report as unused alternatives.

MATERIAL OMISSION THAT CUTS THE OTHER WAY: the Midwest SPARROW models already include tile drainage as a land-to-water delivery variable -- "Ln (tile drains, percentage of catchment)", input variable LTILES13_PERC2, sourced from Nakagaki and Wieczorek's subsurface tile drainage extent for 12 Midwest states (2016) -- with coefficient +0.101 (95% CI 0.064-0.139, p<0.0001) in the TN model and -0.091 (CI -0.156 to -0.026, p=0.0221) in the TP model. This project lists tile drainage density as the dominant Iowa hydrologic control with "NO data source identified yet." The SPARROW data release therefore supplies both the raw tile-drainage covariate and a calibrated level model that uses it, at mean catchment size 2.7 km2, keyed by NHDPlus comid (already stored per basin in this project), across the full multi-state Midwest.

ALSO RELEVANT AND UNSTATED: the report recommends "use measured loads (conditioned model predictions) for monitored reaches, and ... unconditioned model predictions or simulated loads only for unmonitored reaches." The unconditioned branch is the only one available at an ungauged map pin, and is the acknowledged lower-accuracy branch. This strengthens the claim's direction.

NO HOLDOUT EVALUATION: correct as reported. SPARROW is calibrated NLLS/weighted regression on all retained sites; the report evaluates by comparing measured vs predicted at calibration stations (figs. 6, 10, 14, 18) -- in-sample fit, not spatial holdout. It also documents nested-site pseudoreplication explicitly and corrects for it by weighting residuals by nested basin-area share (p=3.3e-6 for unequal nested-site effect). Its reported R2/RMSE values are therefore NOT comparable to this project's LOFO 0.820 and must never be cited alongside it.

VERBATIM ABSTRACT, FIRST SENTENCE: "Flow-duration curve (FDC) based streamflow estimation methods involve estimating an FDC at an ungaged or partially gaged location and using the time series of nonexceedance probabilities estimated from donor streamgage sites to generate estimates of streamflow." This is essentially word-for-word the claim's decomposition into (a) FDC at the target = marginal/site level and (b) nonexceedance-probability time series from donors = timing/rank dynamics. The claim's characterization of the framework is NOT a garbled paraphrase; it is accurate.

CONTRIBUTION SENTENCE: "We develop a mathematical framework to illustrate the connection between copulas and prior FDC-based approaches." The claim's phrasing — "showing that prior FDC-based methods are special cases" — is a strengthening of "illustrate the connection." It is the standard and almost certainly correct reading (Sklar's theorem separates marginals from the dependence structure; single-donor QPPQ with rank preservation is the comonotonic-copula corner case), but I could NOT confirm the paper uses "special case" language because the full text is inaccessible. Treat "special cases" as an inference, not a quote.

n IS MISSTATED IN THE CLAIM METADATA. Abstract: "a decade of daily streamflow data from 74 sites located within two river basins in the southeast United States." The claim's "n basins 74" is a conflation. It is 74 GAGES inside 2 BASINS — a dense, nested, heavily cross-correlated donor network in a single humid region, not 74 independent catchments. This matters directly for rule 5: the donor-network richness that makes the copula rank structure estimable in this paper does not exist for Iowa nitrate at n=19 independent basin families.

THE OMISSION THAT MATTERS MOST. The claim quotes the framework but drops the paper's own verdict on the regime the Iowa product actually operates in. Abstract findings (3) and (4), verbatim: copulas "(3) outperform other methods when used for partially gaged sites with several years of available data; and (4) remain a competitive albeit nondominating method for ungaged sites and partially gaged sites with limited data when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network." The demonstrated PERFORMANCE WIN is confined to partially gaged targets — sites with years of their own observations, which the Iowa deployment target by definition does not have. In the truly ungaged case with realistic FDC/correlation estimation error, the paper's own conclusion is explicitly NON-DOMINANCE. The paper is therefore legitimate evidence that the decomposition is the right FORMALISM, and simultaneously evidence that the decomposition does NOT by itself buy accuracy once the marginal must be regionalized with error. The claim presents only the first half.

In Iowa this is precisely the existing bottleneck: between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24. Domain shift is substantial and unaddressed: streamflow is mass-conserving with drainage-area-ratio scaling and strong regional rank coherence; nitrate concentration in tile-drained Iowa is closer to chemostatic, controlled by tile density and N application, with no conservation law linking a donor to a target. CORRECTED USABLE STATEMENT: Worland et al. It provides NO empirical evidence that this architecture improves ungaged-site accuracy — its own ungaged-case result under realistic marginal-estimation error is explicit non-dominance — and no evidence at all for water-quality concentrations, tile-drained agricultural systems, exceedance classification, or n≈19 donor networks. Use it to justify an EXPERIMENT, never to predict a gain. And note the paper's implied warning: the architecture's accuracy is capped by how well the target's marginal can be regionalized, which is already the measured Iowa bottleneck (between_rate_r2 0.24), so the expected value of this refactor is low unless it is paired with genuinely new static predictors (tile-drainage density being the obvious missing one).

Abstract sentence 1, near-verbatim: "FDC-based streamflow estimation methods involve estimating an FDC at an ungaged or partially gaged location and using the time series of nonexceedance probabilities estimated from donor streamgage sites to generate estimates of streamflow." ACCURATE.

2. "Stated contribution is a copula-based mathematical framework showing prior FDC-based methods are special cases... rank-correlation structure modeled separately from the marginals." Abstract: "We develop a mathematical framework to illustrate the connection between copulas and prior FDC-based approaches." Title says "Generalized Framework." The marginals/dependence separation is Sklar's theorem, which is what a copula generalization means. "special cases" is a mild strengthening of "illustrate the connection," but it is the standard and fair reading. SUBSTANTIALLY ACCURATE.

3. "n basins 74." Abstract: "a decade of daily streamflow data from 74 sites located within two river basins in the southeast United States." The number 74 is exact — but they are 74 GAGES NESTED INSIDE TWO BASINS, not 74 independent regions. The claim's "n basins 74" mislabels sites as basins.

5. The claim's own deployment warning (component b needs a concurrently observed donor with estimable rank correlation) is correct and consistent with the paper.

MATERIAL OMISSION — the paper's ungaged-case finding is the weak one. The abstract enumerates four results. Copulas (1) outperform others "in the limiting case of perfect information with regard to the rank-based correlation structure and FDCs across the gaging network"; (2) hedge against poor performance as donors get sparser; (3) outperform "for partially gaged sites with several years of available data"; and (4) "remain a COMPETITIVE ALBEIT NONDOMINATING method for ungaged sites and partially gaged sites with limited data WHEN REALISTIC ERROR IS INTRODUCED in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network." Result (4) is exactly the Iowa deployment regime — an arbitrary map pin, zero local history, FDC and correlations both estimated with error. In that regime the paper reports NO dominance. The claim cites the paper as architectural endorsement while silently dropping the one result that governs our use case. The gains live in regimes (1) and (3), both of which require target-site observations or a dense well-characterized gage network that we do not have.

METHODOLOGY — could not verify the split protocol. The claim reports "not-applicable," which is defensible for a structural assertion, but the paper does run comparative ungaged/partially-gaged experiments whose protocol (presumably leave-one-site-out over the 74 gages) I could not confirm from the paywalled text. Per the rules I state this rather than guess. Note a pseudoreplication concern that would need the full text to settle: 74 gages inside only two river basins are heavily nested and hydrologically shared, so a leave-one-gage-out protocol over them is much closer to interpolation within a dense network than to our LOFO-over-19-families transfer test. None of this paper's numbers are comparable to our LOFO 0.820 under rule 1.

TRANSFERABILITY — three specific mismatches, even granting the claim is true as written:

(a) THE DECOMPOSITION ISOLATES OUR PROBLEM, IT DOES NOT SOLVE IT. Under QPPQ, once timing is handed to donors, ALL remaining error is in the target's marginal. That marginal is precisely what the Iowa model already fails at (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24, "a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker"). The paper offers no method for estimating the marginal from static attributes — it assumes an FDC is supplied by some external regionalization, and result (4) shows performance degrades once that supply is realistically noisy. So this is a diagnostic reframing, not evidence of an accuracy gain.

(b) n=19 CONSTRAINT BITES THE DEPENDENCE STRUCTURE, NOT JUST THE MARGINAL. The copula's value comes from modeling a pairwise, spatially structured rank-correlation matrix across the gaging network. Estimating that surface is what 74 densely nested gages buy you. With 19 independent basin families the pairwise correlation surface is barely estimable, which pushes us toward exactly the "sparser and less informative donor" regime where the abstract claims only a hedge, not a win.

(c) THE ANALOGY TO rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1 IS THE DEGENERATE CASE, AND ARGUING FROM THIS PAPER CUTS AGAINST KEEPING IT AS-IS. Our cross-site lags are a SINGLE STATEWIDE SCALAR mean, identical for every target pin. A copula donor channel is by construction site-specific and distance/attribute-weighted. So this paper does not validate the current feature; if anything it implies the current feature is the collapsed, information-poorest version of the donor channel, and that the upgrade would be donor weighting by basin similarity. Separately, streamflow rank co-movement between gages in one basin is driven by shared storms and routing; nitrate exceedance in tile-drained Iowa is driven by drainage flushing and fertilizer timing, and the project has already recorded that essentially every hydrologically motivated temporal feature failed — so the assumption that a strong transferable rank-correlation structure exists for nitrate is unvalidated here.

GENUINE MERIT WORTH KEEPING: the binary target maps onto this framework cleanly and non-trivially. A site's violation base rate IS the exceedance probability of its concentration-duration curve evaluated at 10 mg/L. That makes "predict the site's CDC exceedance level from static attributes as a separate head, keep a donor-driven timing channel" a coherent architecture to try, and it matches the project's own diagnosis that the headroom is entirely between-site. The paper is legitimate conceptual support for that decomposition. It is not evidence that the decomposition will raise AUC at an ungauged pin.

A copula donor channel is site-specific and similarity-weighted; a single statewide scalar mean identical for every target pin is its degenerate collapse. Read properly, the paper suggests REPLACING the statewide mean with distance/attribute-weighted donor selection, not preserving it. Also note the decomposition ISOLATES rather than solves the project's deficit: it moves 100% of the residual error into the site marginal (the concentration-duration curve), which is exactly the between-site term the model already fails at (between_r2 0.21) and for which this paper supplies no estimation method. - QPPQ = (a) target-site FDC + (b) nonexceedance-probability time series from donor gages: this is the standard definition in the QPPQ literature the paper builds on (Fennessey 1994; Hughes & Smakhtin 1996; Archfield & Vogel 2010, doi:10.1029/2009WR008481). Consistent, though not directly read in this paper's text.

METHODOLOGY — the claim's "split protocol: not-applicable" understates the paper. Per the abstract the paper DOES report comparative performance under distinct scenarios: perfect-information, sparse-donor, partially-gaged (several years of record), and ungaged/data-limited with measurement uncertainty. So there is an ungaged-site evaluation; it is not protocol-free. Two structural caveats: (i) 74 sites inside only TWO river basins means heavy nesting and strong spatial pseudoreplication — the effective number of independent hydrologic units is far below 74, which is worth noting since the Iowa project has the same pathology (85 sites -> 19 families); (ii) the result ordering matters and the claim omits it: the copula advantage is reported as largest when rank-correlation structure is known and for PARTIALLY GAGED sites, and merely "competitive" for fully ungaged sites. The Iowa deployment target is the fully-ungaged regime — precisely where the paper reports the weakest advantage.

TRANSFERABILITY — the second half of the claim is where it breaks down.
1. The paper is about STREAMFLOW only. It contains nothing about nitrate, water quality, or concentration-duration curves. Extending it to nitrate exceedance is analogy, not evidence.
2. The donor mapping is wrong. QPPQ's channel (b) is a PAIRWISE transfer from specific donor gages weighted by an estimated rank correlation that decays with separation distance. Iowa's rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1/2/3/5 is a single STATEWIDE SCALAR MEAN with no donor identity and no distance-dependent correlation model. It is a common-mode seasonal/hydroclimatic index, not a copula donor term. Calling it "the analogous donor signal" is a garbled correspondence.
3. The paper does not solve the marginal-regionalization step. In QPPQ practice the ungaged FDC comes from a separate regional regression on static attributes (e.g., Archfield et al. 2013; Worland et al. 2018 ML for FDC quantiles), and that step is the dominant error source at ungaged sites. That step is exactly the Iowa deficit (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24). The paper supplies a decomposition, not a remedy.
4. The paper runs no comparison of decomposed-vs-monolithic ML architectures, so it cannot be "evidence that the correct architecture is" a two-headed model.
5. n=19 constraint: fitting a rank-correlation-vs-distance function uses site PAIRS and might survive at 19 families; regionalizing a concentration-duration curve from static attributes is a ~19-effective-unit regression and hits the project's existing ceiling head-on. The paper offers zero evidence at that sample size.

Also relevant to the project's negative-result pattern: this is a rank/marginal decomposition, not another temporal feature, so it does not fall under the seven failed temporal ablations — but note the Iowa model already scores macro_auc 0.90 (good within-site timing) and 0.24 between-site, i.e., the timing channel is ALREADY near-saturated. A framework that formalizes the split does not add skill to the channel that is already weak.

The claim is correct as stated. Four refinements, none fatal, plus one interpretive overreach to guard against.

(a) VINTAGE IS 2012, NOT 2013. The claim says "circa-2013 snapshot." The underlying Nakagaki & Wieczorek layer is the 2012 vintage, built from the 2012 Census of Agriculture state-level tile acreage + NLCD 2011 cultivated cropland + STATSGO2 drainage class. The "13" in TILES13_PERC2 is not the data year. ND/SD permit polygons are 2016 (ND) and 2012 (SD). Say "circa-2012."

(b) THE BOUNDING BOX IS NOT EVIDENCE OF TILE COVERAGE. The -114.85/-72.51, 27.66/50.15 box and the 30 place tags describe the SPARROW model domain, not the tile layer's footprint. The tile layer covers 12 states only: SD, NE, KS, MN, IA, MO, WI, IL, MI, IN, OH, KY (plus ND/SD permit polygons). The operative conclusion still holds — all of Iowa and every upstream state Iowa basins reach are inside those 12 — but the claim reaches the right answer via the wrong evidence.

(c) THE FIELD IS INCREMENTAL, NOT ACCUMULATED. Appendix 2 defines it as "percent of catchment" — the local NHDPlusV2 catchment (mean 2.7 km2), not upstream-accumulated. To get a basin-level tile fraction the project must area-weight tiles13_perc2 across all catchments in the delineated basin itself. Do NOT feed ltiles13_perc2 (a log of a 2.7 km2 local value) directly as a basin feature. Also note the access route is clumsy: extracting 2 columns requires streaming a 740 MB text file. The Wieczorek et al. (2019) "Select Attributes for NHDPlus Version 2.1 Reach Catchments" series publishes NHDPlus attributes in CAT/ACC/TOT form (pre-accumulated upstream), which would be the better route if a tile-drainage member of that series exists — I could not confirm one within budget (my ScienceBase keyword search returned 0 hits, likely a query-syntax issue, not proof of absence). Worth 10 minutes to check before committing to the 740 MB parse.

(d) EFFECT SIZE IS MODEST — AND CONTRADICTS THE PROJECT'S PRIOR. In a ln-ln land-to-water term, coefficient 0.101 means doubling tile percentage raises TN delivery by only 7.3% (2^0.101 = 1.0725); a 10x increase gives +26%. Compare the other land-to-water terms in the same Table 5: Ln(runoff) 0.673, Ln(soil clay) 0.292, Ln(no-till) 0.124, tile 0.101. Tile drains are the WEAKEST significant land-to-water delivery term in SPARROW's own TN fit. The project's stated prior that "tile drainage density is the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa" is NOT supported by this model — runoff dominates by ~7x in log-space elasticity. Expect a real but small between-site contribution, not a fix for the between_r2 0.21 problem. (Note also Table 7: the TP model gives tile drains a NEGATIVE coefficient, -0.091, 90% CI [-0.156, -0.026] — hydrologically sensible, tiles bypass overland P transport. Sign is nutrient-specific; only the TN sign is relevant here.)

(e) n=19 CONSTRAINT. SPARROW's 0.101 rests on 1,334 calibration sites; that is 70x this project's 19 independent basin families. The coefficient's significance says nothing about whether XGBoost can learn a tile effect from 19 effective units. Worse, tile drainage in Iowa is strongly spatially structured (Des Moines Lobe vs driftless/loess regions), so it will correlate with lat/lon — already the #2 and #3 permutation-importance features. Marginal gain over existing geography may be near zero even though the underlying physics is real. Test it as a single scalar basin-mean tile fraction under LOFO, and pre-register that a <0.01 PR-AUC gain is a null. Do not add both linear and log forms and all three distance buckets — that is 6 spatially-smooth columns against 19 units.

(f) ADJACENT LEAKAGE HAZARD NOT IN THE CLAIM. Using the tile INPUT layer is clean. Using the SPARROW OUTPUT files (mw_sparrow_model_output_TN.txt predicted loads) as features would NOT be — SPARROW was calibrated on 1,334 monitoring sites that plausibly include this project's Iowa sensor sites, so predicted TN load at a target comid is partly a function of observed nitrate at that same location. That would leak under LOFO and inflate the between-site term specifically. Take the input column; leave the output files alone.

(g) DOMAIN MISMATCH TO STATE PLAINLY. SPARROW models long-term MEAN-ANNUAL TN LOAD in log space; this project predicts DAILY-MAX CONCENTRATION exceedance of 10 mg/L. The 0.101 coefficient is in-sample with no holdout, and the R2 0.950 is on loads (dominated by basin area and flow) and is not comparable to anything in this project. The coefficient is legitimate evidence that tile extent carries between-catchment TN information; it is not evidence about daily exceedance skill at an ungauged pin.

The claim stands; four refinements, one of which materially changes how much to expect.

(a) DATE: not "circa-2013". The source product is Nakagaki & Wieczorek (2016), "Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for 12 Midwest states, 2012" (doi 10.5066/F7W37TDP), and the release is a "2012 Base Year" model. The "13" in tiles13_perc2 is a misleading variable-name artifact — treat it as circa-2012. ND permit polygons are as of 2016, SD as of 2012.

(b) COVERAGE ARGUMENT IS RIGHT BY THE WRONG EVIDENCE. The bounding box and place tags prove nothing — the bbox extends to -72.51 lon (US East Coast) and the place tags list 32 states including Virginia, New Mexico and Texas; these are metadata artifacts of the NHDPlusV2 network extent, not the model domain. The actual coverage guarantee is that Nakagaki & Wieczorek covers the 12 Midwest states (incl. MN, SD, NE, MO), which does encompass every multi-state upstream portion of an Iowa basin. Conclusion holds; cite the tile product's 12-state extent, not the bbox.

(c) EFFECT SIZE IS STATISTICALLY STRONG BUT A MODEST ELASTICITY — this tempers the project's "dominant hydrologic control" framing. 0.101 is an exponent on ln(tile %), so land-to-water delivery scales as tile%^0.101: doubling tile percentage raises the delivery factor only ~7.3% (2^0.101). Compare the same table's Ln(runoff) at 0.673. Also, in the TP model in the same report the identical variable takes a NEGATIVE coefficient (−0.091, 90% CI [−0.156, −0.026], SE 0.040, p=0.0221, t=−2.3, VIF 2.0), so the sign is constituent-specific and this is a fitted mass-balance term, not a universal driver. Expect a useful but not transformative between-site feature.

(d) CONSTRUCT MISMATCH TO STATE EXPLICITLY: the 0.101 is evidence that tile% carries between-site signal for LONG-TERM MEAN ANNUAL TN LOAD at 1,334 sites. It is NOT evidence of predictive lift for our target (daily-max nitrate CONCENTRATION exceedance of 10 mg/L). Load vs. concentration and annual vs. daily are different constructs; the feature must still earn its place under our LOFO protocol.

OPERATIONAL NOTES FOR USE (all verified by me): file is comma-delimited .txt, 739,943,566 bytes, 89 cols, public-domain USGS, no authentication, direct HTTP GET (browser UA required; ScienceBase 403s some clients). Values are per INCREMENTAL NHDPlusV2 catchment, so a basin-level feature requires area-weighted aggregation over upstream ComIDs using IncAreaKm2 (column 4) as the weight. This fits the deployment target cleanly: arbitrary map pin -> NLDI upstream ComID list -> join tiles13_perc2 -> area-weighted mean. No local nitrate history, no gauge, no upstream monitor required. The project already stores NHDPlus comid per basin, so the join is direct.

n=19 CAVEAT: this is a static feature, not a method whose evidence base needs 300+ basins, so the n=19 constraint does not disqualify it. But it cuts the other way — a single static column that correlates with a site's absolute level is exactly the kind of feature that can look good spuriously across only 19 independent families. Evaluate strictly under LOFO and judge against the between_rate_r2 0.24 / between_r2 0.21 baselines, not overall AUC. The claim itself is accurate and should stand. Two corrections to how it is being used, plus one actionable finding.

1. The FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION overstates what the paper supports. The paper's own headline result — the TD scheme "enhanced the UNCALIBRATED NWM performance by about 20-50% of the fully calibrated NWM" — means calibration alone already recovers roughly half to four-fifths of what the missing tile-drainage process costs. The operational NWM v2.1/v3.0 retrospectives are calibrated products with regionalized parameters, i.e. the Calib/CalibTD arm of the paper, not the Uncalib arm. The paper shows CalibTD beats Calib, so residual structural error exists, but its magnitude in the calibrated configuration is not the 14%/11%/2.3% numbers — those are TD-on-vs-TD-off simulation deltas, and the volume delta is only 2.3%. 2. The sign is not established as a uniform "low bias." Adding TD increased peaks and baseflow but DECREASED surface runoff (−7 to −29%) and recharge (−43 to −50%); the redistribution is between flow pathways, with net volume changing only 2.3%. The no-TD NWM is therefore mis-partitioned rather than simply low. Since nitrate delivery in Iowa is dominated by the tile pathway specifically, a mis-partitioned NWM Q is arguably a worse feature than a uniformly biased one — the caution in the claim is directionally right, but the mechanism should be stated as pathway mis-partitioning, not low bias.

3. ACTIONABLE, AND MORE VALUABLE THAN THE CLAIM ITSELF: the same first author published the tile-drainage dataset this project lists as an unfilled gap ("NO data source has been identified yet"). Overall accuracy 86.03% against 16,000 ground-truth points; IOWA SPECIFICALLY 91.1% accuracy on 5,253 ground-truth points; heavily tile-drained Midwest states 82.7-93.6%. Access: figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742, no login, no authentication — verified via the figshare v2 API, license CC BY 4.0, files AgTile-US-TIFF.zip (125.8 MB), AgTile-US-NetCDF.zip (128.9 MB), AgTile-US.zip (185.2 MB), plus a metadata txt. Direct download e.g. https://ndownloader.figshare.com/files/23079140.

Fit to the deployment target: this is a STATIC RASTER, so tile-drained fraction can be computed for an arbitrary NLDI-delineated basin at a map pin with zero local history and zero gauge — it satisfies the deployment constraint completely, unlike modeled NWM discharge. It is exactly the class of feature that has historically worked on this project (static geography and geometry) and not the class that has failed seven times (temporal/hydrologic). Caveats to flag: (a) n=19 families still applies — tile fraction per basin is one number per site, so it adds at most a couple of degrees of freedom to the between-site term and cannot be validated as a "win" on 19 units without wide error bars; (b) it is static for 2017, so it carries no time variation and cannot be broadcast as a time-varying feature (recall the 2017 N-surplus broadcast failure — use it as a static basin attribute only, never expanded per-day as a pseudo-temporal variable); (c) it is a modeled product constrained to county census totals, so within-county spatial detail is a decision-tree allocation, not observation, and its errors are spatially structured by county boundary; (d) the crop mask is NLCD 2016, which the authors report has 18% less cropland than the USDA census, so tile area is under-allocated in some counties.

Bottom line on the original claim's practical advice: the caution against using NWM modeled discharge as a between-site feature is reasonable but rests on an over-strong reading of the abstract. The far stronger move implied by the same author's work is to skip modeled Q entirely and ingest AgTile-US tile fraction per distance bucket as a static basin attribute.

The cited source says exactly what the claim quotes — every quoted phrase and every percentage is verbatim-correct — so the attribution stands. Three corrections are required.

Spatial transfer appears only as Gower's-distance parameter regionalization from the 49 donors to 939 HUC10 receivers, which is itself never independently validated. The "20-50%" figure is a median-of-seasonal-distributions statement on the 49 calibration basins.

(2) The falsifiable implication is NOT supported by this source and is partly contradicted. The +14%/+2.3%/+11% numbers are a TD-on vs TD-off sensitivity **within a single calibrated parameter set** ("No tile drainage ... is not equal to Calib"), not a bias of any operational NWM run. Because the operational NWM is calibrated, the missing tile process is largely absorbed into compensated parameters — the paper says Calib's DKSAT is "an effective hydraulic conductivity for the combined subsurface material and tile drain system" and that Calib is "over-calibrated to accommodate the absence of TD". The residual bias is not a uniform low bias: against 139 gauges, Calib's median event peak-flow bias is **+5% (high)**, and low flows are **overestimated** (CalibTD still +50%). Most decisively, the paper **never regresses bias against tile-drainage percentage**, so "error magnitude scales with tile density" is an untested extrapolation, not a finding. Rewrite the claim as: NWM V2.0 omits tile drainage, and switching the process on changes simulated Midwest hydrology substantially; the resulting error in the *calibrated* operational product is seasonally and flow-regime dependent (high-flow peaks slightly over, low flows strongly over), and its correlation with tile density is unquantified in the literature.

(3) The practical consequence for this project is the opposite of the claim's framing. The paper is not a reason to avoid modeled Q; it is the origin of the tile-drainage dataset the project has been unable to find. **AgTile-US** — 30 m binary tile-drained cropland, CONUS coverage including the out-of-Iowa parts of multi-state basins, static single epoch, figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742, CC BY 4.0, unauthenticated bulk download (TIFF 126 MB / NetCDF 129 MB), described in Sci Data 7:257 DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x — is directly ingestible as percent-tile-drained per distance bucket. It is a static between-site geographic feature, the only feature family that has produced wins here, and it requires no discharge record at the target pin. Recommend it as a first-class action item; treat NWM retrospective Q as a separate, lower-priority and more error-prone proposition.

votes.correction:
Keep the source-level claim; discard or heavily qualify the derived implication. Four corrections, in order of importance to this project:

1. THE BIAS DIRECTION IS WRONG. The implication asserts NWM carries a "structural, spatially systematic LOW bias" in tile-drained Iowa. The paper's own bias statistics say the opposite for the operational (calibrated) configuration: median event PEAK-FLOW BIAS in Calib is +5% (over-prediction), reduced to +0.57% in CalibTD; the median low-flow bias in Calib is TWICE that of Default, and even CalibTD "still overestimated low flows by 50%." The paper attributes low-flow over-prediction to excessive groundwater recharge and the one-way NWM groundwater scheme (citing Jachens et al. 2021; Karki et al. 2021). Operational NWM in tile country reads as biased HIGH at low flow and mildly high at peaks, not low.

2. THE +14%/+2.3%/+11% ARE MODEL-MINUS-MODEL SENSITIVITIES, NOT MEASURED BIASES AGAINST OBSERVATIONS. They come from "comparing 'No tile drainage' with 'With tile drainage'" simulations (Sec. 3.4), i.e. CalibTD vs Calib. Critically, when TD is added WITHOUT recalibration the level does not move: "There are no considerable differences in the estimated Bias between Default and DefaultTD" and "There is no considerable difference between Default and DefaultTD in the estimated peak flow bias." What TD buys is DYNAMICS and TIMING — COR +0.15, NSE +0.16, KGE +0.22 for high flows (DefaultTD vs Default); event hit rate 44%→~65% (Default→DefaultTD), 78% in CalibTD vs 71% in Calib; false-alarm rate 22.5%→17.5%; peak timing error −3/0/4/2 h. The 20–50% figure is likewise an improvement in NSE/KGE-type skill (e.g. spring median NSE 0.22→0.33 for DefaultTD vs 0.22→0.55 for Calib), not a bias correction.

3. THE PAPER NEVER TESTS ERROR-VS-TILE-DENSITY SCALING, AND ITS DESIGN CANNOT. Both gauge sets are pre-screened to tile fraction ≥10% (49 calibration basins and the 188-gauge pool), truncating the range of the exact covariate the implication needs. No regression or stratification of NWM error against tile fraction appears anywhere in the paper. The paper's actual closing mechanism runs the other way for level: "the operational NWM parameters are over-calibrated to accommodate the absence of the TD process in the model during winter and spring" — i.e. operational calibration has already absorbed much of the missing-TD water-balance effect into parameter values, which makes residual level error idiosyncratic-per-donor-basin rather than a clean monotone function of tile density. That is a weaker and messier error structure than the claim asserts, but it is still bad for a between-site feature — just for a different reason (regionalization-donor artifacts, not tile-scaled low bias).

4. VERSION AND MAGNITUDE SCOPE. The study is NWM V2.0; it says nothing about v2.1 or v3.0 retrospective, so "v2.1/v3.0 carries this bias" is an extrapolation, not a finding (that these versions still lack a tile scheme is plausible but must be verified separately against NWM release documentation, not this DOI). And the alarming −43% to −50% figure is GROUNDWATER RECHARGE, an internal flux absent from the streamflow product; the streamflow-volume effect is 2.3% annually (seasonal 17% winter / 13% spring / 13% fall / 2.8% summer). The risk to a modeled-Q feature is real at event/peak scale, small at annual-volume scale.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT (deployment target: arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin). Do not use this paper to rule out NWM retrospective Q as a feature; it does not establish the tile-scaled low bias the argument needs. But also do not expect NWM Q to fix the between-site deficit: everything the paper demonstrates TD improves — timing, hit rate, event dynamics — is the axis on which this model is already strong ("a good timer"), and the paper shows the LEVEL effect gets absorbed by calibration. Prior expectation for NWM Q as a between-site level feature should therefore be LOW, on the paper's own evidence.

CHEAP DIRECT TEST THAT DOMINATES FURTHER LITERATURE SEARCH: the project already has observed discharge at 22 USGS sites. Pull NWM v3.0 retrospective Q (CONUS, hourly, 1979–2023, NHDPlusV2 comid-indexed — comids are already stored per basin; free, no auth, Zarr/NetCDF on the NOAA Open Data Dissemination AWS bucket noaa-nwm-retrospective-3-0-pds, s3://noaa-nwm-retrospective-3-0-pds, public domain) and regress NWM-vs-observed percent bias on AgTile-US tile fraction across those 22. That measures the error structure directly in Iowa instead of inferring it, and it needs no new data acquisition. AgTile-US itself (30 m binary tile-drained cropland, CONUS, one epoch ~2017, Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis, Franz 2020, Scientific Data, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x, free download) is separately the most concrete answer to the project's flagged "no tile-drainage data source identified" gap — note its CONUS extent covers the multi-state portions of the large basins, which is exactly where the current Iowa-only crop/N-surplus inner join under-counts.

n=19 CAVEAT: this source's n (49 calibration basins, 139 evaluation gauges, 939 HUC10s) is not a constraint on using its FINDING, since the finding is about a physical model's structure, not a learned mapping. The n=19 constraint bites only on the downstream test above, where 22 gauged sites give weak power to detect a bias-vs-tile-density slope — expect to be able to rule out only large effects.

(b) MECHANISM IS OVERSTATED. "SPARROW output at that reach partly encodes that site's own observed level" is not how the released product works. Load-substitution ("conditioning") is applied during calibration and to the calibration-RMSE, not to the distributed reach predictions; the public data release ships "simulated" = unconditioned loads. The actual leakage pathway is therefore diffuse: one Iowa site is one of 1,335 calibration targets influencing a ~10-20 parameter nonlinear regression fit over the whole Mississippi/Great Lakes/Red River domain, and it is further downweighted by the nested-share weighting scheme the report describes (p.9). That is closer to 1/1335 leverage on global coefficients than to memorization of a reach's level. Additional criteria the claim omits also shrink the contaminated set: the paired gauge must include 2012 with no gaps, be within 40 km, have a watershed-area ratio 0.75-1.33, and be on the same stream if the WQ basin exceeds 260 km2.

(c) TARGET MISMATCH. SPARROW TN is long-term (2000-14) MEAN-ANNUAL TOTAL NITROGEN LOAD, detrended to a 2012 base year. Our target is daily-max NITRATE CONCENTRATION exceedance of 10 mg/L. Even a fully contaminated reach leaks only a slow, basin-average level signal, not the daily label. That said, the between-site absolute-level term is precisely this project's stated deficit, so the leak, if present, would land exactly where it would most flatter a LOFO number.

NET RECOMMENDATION, revised: keep the audit, drop the alarm level. Before reporting any LOFO gain from a SPARROW-derived feature, join our ~85 sites (and the 19 families) against the SIR 2019-5069 / P93QMXC9 calibration-site table by NHDPlus comid or lat/lon, and report how many FAMILIES (not sites) contain at least one TN calibration site. At n=19 folds, even 3-4 contaminated families is worth a caveat, which is why the check is worth doing despite the diffuse mechanism. Report the gain with and without those families. The claim's inference that IWQIS sensors are cleaner is sound in its logic — a post-2015-only record cannot satisfy "period of record within 3 years of 2012" plus 24 samples — but note IA DNR is a listed provider and many IWQIS sensors sit at USGS gauges, so this must be checked per site rather than assumed by network.

votes.correction:
Claim stands as written; four precisions that sharpen it.

(a) SEVERITY DEPENDS ON WHICH SPARROW PRODUCT IS USED, and the claim does not distinguish. SIR 2019-5114 reports both "conditioned" predictions ("predicted accumulated loads that were reset to the measured loads at the calibration sites upstream in the basin") and "unconditioned" predictions (not reset). Using conditioned output as a feature is direct, severe leakage: the measured load at a monitored upstream site is injected into the prediction. Using unconditioned output leaks only through ~10-20 shared regression coefficients fit to 1,334 sites, where any single site carries roughly 0.07% of the calibration weight -- a weak leak, likely second-order relative to the nested-basin residual weighting. Check which product the extracted feature comes from before deciding how much to discount a LOFO gain.

(b) APPENDIX 3 ESTABLISHES EXPOSURE, NOT MEMBERSHIP. Table 3.1's caption is agencies whose data were "considered for use"; it rosters contributors to the ~94,000-site compilation, from which fewer than 2% (1,346 TN) survived screening and 1,334 were finally calibrated. Iowa-agency presence therefore does not imply any specific Iowa site is a calibration target. The claim already hedges correctly ("likely to BE"), but the site-by-site check it calls for is mandatory, not optional.

(c) THAT CHECK IS OPERATIONALLY POSSIBLE and should be named: the companion USGS data release Saad, D.A., and Robertson, D.M., 2019, "SPARROW model inputs and simulated streamflow, nutrient and suspended-sediment loads in streams of the Midwestern United States, 2012 base year," https://doi.org/10.5066/P93QMXC9 (free, public, ScienceBase bulk download, no authentication, USGS public domain). Match our 85 sites to it by NHDPlus comid plus a distance tolerance; the report allows a calibration WQ site to sit up to 40 km from its paired gauge, with watershed-area ratio 0.75-1.33, so comid-exact matching alone will under-detect overlap.

(d) THE LEAK IS EVALUATION-SIDE ONLY, NOT DEPLOYMENT-SIDE -- worth stating explicitly against this project's deployment target. SPARROW output is a static per-reach covariate defined at every NHDPlus comid in the Midwest, so it is fully available at an arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin with no local nitrate history; it does not require the target site's own observations or a gauged upstream neighbor. The consequence of the circularity is that a LOFO score computed with SPARROW as a feature would overstate what a genuinely unmonitored pin receives, not that the feature is unusable in the product. Mitigation: report LOFO twice, once on all 19 families and once restricted to families with zero SPARROW-calibration overlap, and treat the gap as the optimism bias.

(e) Minor wording: 1999-10-01 to 2014-09-30 is the report's water-quality/streamflow DATA COMPILATION window, not a "calibration window"; combined with the within-3-years-of-2012 rule the effective period of record for calibration sites is about 2009-2014, so the claim's "roughly 2009-2015" overshoots the late end by up to a year.

VERDICT: every citable fact in the claim is EXACT, but the headline conclusion ("CIRCULARITY WARNING, CONFIRMED") is refuted by direct inspection of the distributed SPARROW product. The leakage mechanism the claim asserts does not exist in the data a user would actually consume.

=== WHAT VERIFIED EXACTLY (primary source read in full) ===
Source confirmed: Robertson, D.M., and Saad, D.A., 2019, "Spatially Referenced Models of Streamflow and Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Suspended-Sediment Loads in Streams of the Midwestern United States," USGS SIR 2019-5114, doi:10.3133/sir20195114. PDF pulled (45.8 MB) and converted; page HTML 403s to WebFetch, so I used curl + pdftotext.

1. "71 agencies" — VERBATIM. p.9-10: "Water-quality data from 71 Federal, State, regional, local, Tribal, university, and private sampling agencies and organizations were used to estimate TN, TP, SS, and TSS loads throughout the Midwest area (appendix 3)." The claim's word order and list are exact.

2. Five Iowa providers in appendix 3 — VERBATIM, all five, matching codes and names, from Table 3.1 ("Sampling agencies that collected water-quality data used to calculate total nitrogen, total phosphorus, suspended-sediment, and suspended solid loads considered for use in the 2012 Midwest SPARROW models"), p.69: "IA DMWW / Des Moines Water Works, Iowa.", "IA DNR / Iowa Department of Natural Resources.", "IA GSWSP / Iowa Geological Survey Watershed Snapshots.", "IA ISUCOE / Des Moines River Water Quality Network.", "IA VWMP / Iowa Volunteer Water Monitoring Program."

3. Site-selection criteria — VERBATIM: water-quality site needed "a minimum record length of 3 years, have at least 24 samples, and have at least 3 samples in each of the four 3-month seasons"; "The water-quality period of record also had to be within 3 years of the 2012 base year"; streamgage needed "a minimum record length of 10 years of daily mean values (with no data gaps)" and the record "had to include 2012."

4. Window 1999-10-01 to 2014-09-30 — CONFIRMED twice: report text ("from October 1, 1999, to September 30, 2014") and the data release metadata (Start Date 1999-10-01, End Date 2014-09-30).

5. n=1,334 TN calibration sites — EXACT. Table 5: "Number of sites 1,334"; text: "the model was calibrated with TN loads from 1,334 monitoring sites." (Table 1 separately reports 1,346 TN sites *considered*; the claim correctly used the final figure.)

=== WHY THE CONCLUSION IS REFUTED ===
A. The distributed output is UNCONDITIONED, and the report defines the distinction itself. SIR 2019-5114 p.9: "the model-simulated load at each upstream calibration site is replaced with its measured load... The resulting downstream load that is simulated using the upstream measured load is referred to as the 'conditioned' predicted load used in model calibration, whereas the load exclusively predicted by the model is referred to as the 'unconditioned' predicted load or simply the 'simulated load.'" Conditioning exists ONLY inside calibration.

B. I checked what is actually published. Data release: Saad & Robertson, 2020, doi:10.5066/P93QMXC9 (ScienceBase item 5cbf5150e4b09b8c0b700df3), titled "...and SIMULATED streamflow, nutrient and suspended-sediment loads." Eight files; I range-fetched the header of mw_sparrow_model_output_TN.txt (493 MB). Full column set: comid, IncAreaKm2, CumAreaKm2, wbm_meanq, al_tn + 7 source-specific al_tn_* (accumulated load), alse_* (standard errors), il_tn + il_tn_* (incremental load), DEL_FRAC, SE_DEL_FRAC, res_decay, se_res_decay. There is NO station ID, NO observed/measured load, NO residual, and NO conditioned prediction anywhere in the file. Every reach value is a deterministic function of that catchment's attributes and the ~20 GLOBAL coefficients — computed identically at calibrated and uncalibrated reaches. There is no site-specific anchor to leak.

C. Magnitude. A single Iowa site's own observations influence the shipped number at its own reach only via its ~1/1,334 share of a globally shared coefficient vector, spread across the entire Mississippi/Great Lakes/Red River domain. That is not "SPARROW output at that reach partly encodes that site's own observed level" in any sense that biases a LOFO evaluation.

D. Target mismatch further attenuates it. SPARROW TN is long-term MEAN-ANNUAL TOTAL NITROGEN LOAD in kg/yr, detrended to 2012 — not daily nitrate concentration. The information path (site's 2009-2014 TN grab samples -> 1/1334 of a global coefficient -> mean-annual TN load at a comid -> our XGBoost's estimate of that site's violation rate) is far too attenuated to produce the optimistic bias asserted.

E. The claim's prescribed remedy is also not executable as written. It says to check overlap "site-by-site against the SPARROW calibration site list" — that list is NOT in the P93QMXC9 data release (no station field in any of the 8 files). Site-level loads and station lists live in the companion Saad, D.A., Schwarz, G.E., Argue, D.M., Anning, D.W., Ator, S.W., Hoos, A.B., Preston, S.D., Robertson, D.M., and Wise, D., 2019, SIR 2019-5069, doi:10.3133/sir20195069.

=== RULE-1 PROTOCOL FLAG (matters more than the leakage worry) ===
SPARROW TN reports R2 0.950 and Yield R2 0.913 — these are IN-SAMPLE calibration fits over 1,334 sites, NOT spatially held out. They are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 and must never be quoted as evidence of ungauged-reach skill. The honest transfer-relevant number the report gives is unconditioned RMSE = 0.555 natural-log units = 60.0 percent in real space for TN (vs conditioned 0.487 / 51.8 percent) — and even that is computed at calibration sites, so it is still not a true held-out figure. The report explicitly states unconditioned RMSE "provides the best representation of the predictive skill of a calibrated SPARROW model."

=== TRANSFERABILITY / DEPLOYMENT ASSESSMENT ===
SPARROW TN is a legitimate and well-targeted candidate static between-site feature, and this claim would wrongly discourage it. It is keyed by NHDPlusV2 comid (the project already stores comid per basin), covers the whole Mississippi/Great Lakes/Red River domain including every multi-state portion of Iowa basins, requires no local history and no gauge at the target, and supplies exactly the absolute-level between-site information the project's diagnosis says it lacks (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24). It is free, no authentication, public domain, bulk HTTP download. Caveat under the n=19-families constraint: it adds 1-2 static columns, not a method needing hundreds of basins to fit, so n=19 is not a barrier — but with only 19 independent units, a single strong static covariate can also be overfit at the fold level, so it should be added as one or two features (e.g. delivered TN yield = al_tn/CumAreaKm2) and evaluated under the existing LOFO, not as a large block.

=== HIGH-VALUE SIDE FINDING (directly answers an open project gap) ===
The project states tile drainage density is "the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet." SIR 2019-5114 uses it as a SIGNIFICANT land-to-water delivery variable in the TN model: "Ln (tile drains, percentage of catchment)", coefficient 0.101 (90% CI 0.064-0.139), p<0.0001, t=4.5, variable name LTILES13_PERC2. Source, fully operational: Nakagaki, N., and Wieczorek, M.E., 2016, "Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for 12 Midwest states, 2012," USGS data release, doi:10.5066/F7W37TDP (ScienceBase 55f6e42ae4b0477df11bff10). 30-meter raster; single time slice (2012, from the 2012 Census of Agriculture + NLCD 2011 cultivated cropland + STATSGO2 drainage class); per-cell value = estimated tile-drained area in square meters; covers SD, NE, KS, MN, IA, MO, WI, IL, MI, IN, OH, KY — which encompasses ALL upstream multi-state portions of Iowa basins; free bulk download, no authentication, USGS public domain. Note the metadata's Iowa-specific caveat: reported tile-drained area exceeded cropland on poorly drained soils, so the excess was assigned to cropland on moderately drained soils — Iowa is the one state given special treatment, so the product is smoothed from state-level totals and carries no within-state independent signal beyond the crop/soil mask. That is a real limitation: it may correlate strongly with CDL crop fractions already in the feature set. A catchment-attributed version already joined to NHDPlusV2 comid exists via Wieczorek and others, 2019 (USGS Select Attributes for NHDPlus v2.1 Reach Catchments, doi:10.5066/F7765D7V), which would avoid re-doing the raster aggregation.

=== WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY ===
I did not enumerate how many of the project's ~85 Iowa sites appear on the TN calibration list (would require pulling SIR 2019-5069's site tables). Given finding B, that check is no longer necessary to justify using SPARROW as a feature. Web search budget for this session was exhausted, so I could not survey independent literature on SPARROW-as-covariate; all findings above come from the primary source and the published data files themselves, which is the stronger evidence for this particular question.
