votes.correction:
The claim is correct on substance and on every quoted number; two refinements, neither of which changes its conclusion.

(1) "Reported split protocol: not-applicable" is the one imprecise field. The paper does have an explicit and consequential protocol: temporal holdout at the SAME basins the model was trained on. Main setup: "time periods for training (1 October 1999 through 30 September 2008), validation (1 October 1980 through 30 September 1989), and testing (1 October 1989 through 30 September 1999)." The Fig. 6 sample-size experiment uses "k-fold cross-validation so that all models were tested on the same basin(s) where they were trained (during different time periods)." So it is a GAUGED-basin, temporally-split protocol — the weakest possible protocol relative to our LOFO. Under rule 1 none of its NSE numbers are comparable to our LOFO 0.820, and this fact makes the claim's conclusion stronger, not weaker: the paper does not even measure spatial transfer, which is exactly the axis our project is stuck on. (Minor internal inconsistency worth noting: the Fig. 6 passage says training period "1999-2000" and test period "1980-1989", swapping the roles of the validation and test windows given in the main setup. Looks like an editing slip in the paper; immaterial here.)

(2) The paper contains one section that DOES bear on our situation, and it cuts against using this paper to justify anything at n=19 — worth surfacing rather than discarding. Section 4 "How many basins are necessary?" finds median NSE still rising monotonically at 531 basins: "even these 531 basins are most likely not to be enough to train optimal LSTM models for streamflow." Section 5 additionally trains on basins grouped by USGS HUC — "There are 18 HUCs represented in the CAMELS data set, with between 2 and 79 basins per HUC" — i.e. groupings of roughly the size of our 19 independent basin families, and the conclusion is that restricting to such groups is WORSE than pooling everything: "even if enough basins exist to divide your training data into hydrologically informed training sets, one is likely to be better off simply training a single model with all available data." So the paper's own evidence says an LSTM at our effective sample size sits far down the left tail of its learning curve. Anyone citing Kratzert et al. 2024 as support for switching this project from XGBoost to an LSTM is citing a paper that (a) never tested a GBDT, (b) never touched water quality, (c) never held out a basin spatially, and (d) whose sample-size analysis implies our n is well below where regional LSTMs start to pay off.

claim: The USGS data release (Wieczorek, Jackson, Schwarz, Sekellick & Staub, ver. 5.0, June 2025, DOI 10.5066/F7765D7V) provides 158 separate static/basin attribute tables joined to NHDPlusV2 by a single integer COMID key, in 13 themes (Best Management Practices, Chemical, Climate and Water Balance Model, Climate, Geology, Hydrologic, Hydrologic Modifications, Landscape, Population Infrastructure, Regions, Soils, Topographic, Water Use). Every table supplies three spatial aggregations per COMID — CAT_ (local reach catchment), ACC_ (divergence-routed upstream accumulation), TOT_ (total upstream watershed accumulation) — plus companion CAT_NODATA/ACC_NODATA/TOT_NODATA columns giving the percent of catchment area the source coverage does NOT cover. VERIFIED BY DIRECT DOWNLOAD: the tile-drainage table contains exactly 2,699,864 COMID rows covering CONUS, columns ['COMID','CAT_TILES_Early90s','CAT_NODATA','ACC_TILES_Early90s','ACC_NODATA','TOT_TILES_Early90s','TOT_NODATA'], -9999 as the NODATA sentinel. Access: unauthenticated HTTPS GET of per-item zipped CSV from sciencebase.gov/catalog/file/get/<itemid> (13 MB zipped, 154 MB CSV for the tile table); parquet copies are listed but their sciencebase.usgs.gov/manager/ URLs returned an HTML app shell rather than the file, so the CSV zip is the working access path. License: CC0 1.0 Universal (public domain), no authentication. Coverage is full CONUS, so it covers Iowa AND the multi-state portions of basins — directly addressing the project's known inner-join undercount for out-of-state basin area, because the NODATA column reports coverage explicitly instead of silently dropping cells. All attributes are STATIC single-epoch snapshots, so they are usable at an arbitrary ungauged map pin provided the pin's basin can be decomposed into NHDPlusV2 COMIDs.

The claim makes no performance promise, so it is not refuted by this, but any downstream recommendation must select a handful of a-priori-motivated attributes (tile drainage, base flow index, STATSGO hydrologic group, topographic wetness index) rather than bulk-joining the release.

(1) LICENSE: not CC0 1.0. The ScienceBase item carries no rights field; FGDC metadata states accconst = "None. Please see 'Distribution Info' for details." plus a use-limitation disclaimer. Describe it as USGS public-domain / unrestricted, no authentication — not as CC0.

(4) THE TILE TABLE IS TWO TABLES, AND THE NODATA STORY IS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT THE CLAIM IMPLIES. The verified 2,699,864-row / 154 MB / CAT_TILES_Early90s table is child item 58d9dec6e4b0543bf7fda70e (Nakagaki 2016, early 1990s). In it, CAT_NODATA == 100 for 87.96% of COMIDs and TOT_NODATA == 100 for 79.41%, with the tile VALUE written as 0.0000 in those rows — so a naive join silently yields zeros, exactly the undercount failure the claim says the dataset fixes. It fixes it only if you explicitly filter on the NODATA columns. The sibling child item 57067469e4b03f95a075ad3e (TILES92_CONUS, 1992 NRI practice 606, Wieczorek 2004) has the same 2,699,864 rows, columns COMID,CAT_TILES92,CAT_NODATA,ACC_TILES92,ACC_NODATA,TOT_TILES92,TOT_NODATA, 0.00% NODATA everywhere, and TOT_TILES92 > 0 for 2,488,931 COMIDs. RECOMMENDATION: use TILES92 as the primary tile covariate and Early90s only as a cross-check, always gating on the NODATA columns.

(5) -9999 SEMANTICS: in CAT_NODATA it means 100% NODATA; in ACC_*/TOT_* it means the flowline is disconnected from the routing network and cannot be accumulated. It is not a single uniform "NODATA sentinel".

Everything else in the claim verified exactly: DOI, 5-author ver. 5.0 citation, 158 children, 13 themes, COMID integer key, 2,699,864 rows, the exact column list, 13 MB zip / 154 MB CSV, unauthenticated sciencebase.gov/catalog/file/get access, and parquet manager URLs returning an HTML app shell (HTTP 200, text/html, 4,255 bytes).

votes.correction:
Six corrections. None overturn the core claim; two matter operationally.

1. COLUMN NAMES ARE WRONG. Actual header of TILES92_CONUS.txt: COMID,CAT_TILES92,CAT_NODATA,ACC_TILES92,ACC_NODATA,TOT_TILES92,TOT_NODATA. The claim's "CAT_TILES_Early90s" / "ACC_TILES_Early90s" / "TOT_TILES_Early90s" do not exist. Any ingest code written from the claim will KeyError. (TILES_Early90s is the SPARROW-model naming, not this release's.)

2. THE -9999 SENTINEL NEVER OCCURS IN THIS TABLE, AND NODATA IS INFORMATIONALLY EMPTY. grep -c -- "-9999" over all 2.7M rows returns 0. Computed column ranges: CAT_TILES92 [0.0, 100.0], ACC_TILES92 [0.0, 100.0], TOT_TILES92 [0.0, 100.0], and CAT_NODATA / ACC_NODATA / TOT_NODATA are all identically 0.0000 (min = max = 0.0, zero rows with NODATA > 0). This directly undercuts the claim's headline transferability argument. The claim says the NODATA column "directly addresses the project's known inner-join undercount for out-of-state basin area, because the NODATA column reports coverage explicitly instead of silently dropping cells." For the tile table that is vacuous — NODATA is a constant zero and carries no coverage diagnostic. The source raster was evidently zero-filled outside its footprint, so a catchment with no NRI drainage data and a catchment with genuinely 0% tile drainage are indistinguishable. The argument may hold for other tables in the release; it must be re-checked per table before being relied on.

3. FILE SIZES AND FORMAT. Zip is 12,107,588 bytes (11.5 MiB), not "13 MB". Uncompressed is 139,700,008 bytes (133 MiB), not "154 MB". The member file is TILES92_CONUS.txt (comma-delimited, .txt extension), not a .csv.

4. "EVERY TABLE SUPPLIES THREE SPATIAL AGGREGATIONS" IS FALSE AS A UNIVERSAL. The parent summary states FOUR spatial components, not three: reach catchments, riparian buffer zones, network-accumulated catchments, network-accumulated riparian buffers. Several child items ship only one aggregation: the ClimGRID water-balance items are split into separate items per routing type ("per Flowline Catchment" / "Using Divergence Routing" / "Using Total Upstream Routing"), and riparian items (e.g. "NLCD 2001 Percent Imperviousness in 100 Meter Riparian Buffer") are buffer-only. Others split CAT/ACC/TOT into separate zips within one item — e.g. "Select Topographic Attributes: Select Basin Attributes" ships BASIN_CHAR_CAT_CONUS.zip (50.4 MB), BASIN_CHAR_ACC_CONUS.zip (55.0 MB), BASIN_CHAR_TOT_CONUS.zip (57.2 MB) as three separate downloads. Budget for per-item schema discovery; do not assume one zip = one 7-column table.

5. CC0 IS NOT STATED ON THE RECORD. The ScienceBase JSON `rights` field is null for both the parent and the tile item; no occurrence of "CC0", "Creative Commons", "public domain", or "license" anywhere in either JSON or in the FGDC XML. The XML carries only a liability disclaimer and "Use of this data is considered acceptance of the limitations of this data." The data are almost certainly free to use (USGS-authored, 17 U.S.C. 105), but "License: CC0 1.0 Universal" is an inference the cited source does not support. Cite it as a USGS public-domain data release, not CC0.

6. "ALL ATTRIBUTES ARE STATIC SINGLE-EPOCH SNAPSHOTS" IS FALSE — and the truth is better for this project. Many child items are multi-epoch: NLCD 2019 version supplies 2001/2004/2006/2008/2011/2013/2016/2019; housing density 1940-2010; block-level population density 1990/2000/2010; CDL as separate 2012/2013/2014 items; monthly PRISM and ClimGRID series. That means some of these can be used as slowly-varying covariates, not only as static ones.

ADDITIONAL FINDINGS THE CLAIM OMITS, ALL MATERIAL TO THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET:

A. THE PIN LOOKUP IS SIMPLER THAN THE CLAIM SAYS. The claim hedges "provided the pin's basin can be decomposed into NHDPlusV2 COMIDs." Not needed. TOT_ and ACC_ are already the accumulated upstream value at that reach, so the deployment path is: NLDI resolves the pin to one outlet COMID (this repo already does exactly that — /Users/isaac/dev/sustag/deploy/build_virtual_basin.py and /Users/isaac/dev/sustag/src/build/_make_basins.py both already call NLDI for the enclosing COMID), then one hash lookup into the table. No basin decomposition, no zonal statistics, no local history. This is a genuinely deployment-compatible static feature source — the strongest part of the claim.

B. THE TILE LAYER IS 1992 AND COARSE — a serious caveat the claim does not mention. FGDC process step: source is "Downloaded the source data from http://water.usgs.gov/GIS/metadata/usgswrd/XML/nri92_cp606.xml", i.e. Wieczorek (2004) "Estimated area of artificial drainage for the year 1992", derived from the 1992 National Resources Inventory Conservation Practice 606 — an expanded statistical sample, not a mapped drainage network. The metadata's own use constraint, verbatim: "One should use caution and read this document before using these data to estimate smaller areas. These data should not be used for site-specific evaluation, surveying, or engineering purposes. They should also not be used beyond the limits of the source data's scale." Iowa tile drainage has expanded materially since 1992. Validation was only a spot check: "Basin metrics were spot checked by randomly creating a set of basins across the country... Results demonstrated the process performed correctly" — no quantitative accuracy statistic, and "No formal positional accuracy tests were conducted." So this resolves the project's "no tile drainage data source identified" gap only partially: it gives a plausible relative ranking of basins by drainage intensity, not a defensible absolute percentage.

C. n=19 CONSTRAINT. This release has no effect size and no split protocol — it is a data source, not a study, so rules 1/2/5 apply to how it is used, not to the claim. Judged against n=19 independent basin families: adding one TOT_TILES92 scalar is a single between-site covariate against ~19 effective units. That is the right shape for the diagnosed between-site deficit (between_r2 0.21) and is affordable. The danger is the obvious next move — this release offers 158 tables and easily thousands of TOT_ columns. Bulk-joining them and letting XGBoost pick creates a p >> 19 selection problem where LOFO will select on noise across folds. Recommend a pre-registered handful (tile drainage, STATSGO hydrologic group / soil restrictive layer, base flow index, topographic wetness index, basin slope, N from fertilizer+manure) chosen on hydrologic reasoning before seeing LOFO scores, not a wide sweep.

D. STRUCTURAL CHURN RISK. Parent provenance, verbatim: "2026-03-26: The structure of this data release has been updated to support migration to a new USGS data system." The broken parquet URLs are almost certainly collateral from that migration. Pin the downloaded files locally; do not build a live-fetch dependency on the ?f=__disk__<sha> URLs, which are content-addressed and can change.

E. FGDC METADATA BUG. In the tile table's entity-attribute list, the third variable is labeled "ACC_TILES92" a second time where the actual header says TOT_TILES92. Anyone auto-generating a schema from the XML will produce a duplicate key. Parse the CSV header, not the XML.

The claim is factually exact on every number (74 gages, 37 Mobile-Tombigbee HUC4 0316, 37 Trinity HUC4 1201-1204, daily 2000-2009, 16 methods, QPPQ/regionalization framing). Two characterizations need fixing, both of which strengthen rather than weaken the skepticism:

Iowa's 19 is a POST-COLLAPSE, leak-safe count derived from 85 raw sites (basins that nest and overlap in time are grouped). Worland's 74 is a RAW gage count with no equivalent deduplication. The correct raw-to-raw comparison is 74 vs 85 - Iowa is the LARGER network. Measured pairwise Spearman correlations (all 666 pairs per basin) show Mobile-Tombigbee median rho 0.774 with 42% of pairs above 0.8 and a max of 0.984, plus nested mainstem/tributary gage structure; applying Iowa's own nesting rule would collapse 74 to well below 19. Moreover the study fits and evaluates each basin SEPARATELY (model_e, model_w in sb_main.R), so the effective number of independent regionalization units is closer to 2, not 74. This paper is therefore NOT a demonstration that QPPQ-family regionalization works at small n; it is a two-basin study on dense, highly correlated networks.

CORRECTION 2 - the "spatial-holdout" protocol label is too generous, and the distinction is fatal for the Iowa deployment target. 7 of the 16 methods (QPPQ_nearest_neighbor, QPPQ_highest_rho, QPPQ_IDW, QPPQ_mu, bivar_cop_nn, bivar_cop_rho, multivar_norm_cop) use quantile(R[,i],...), i.e. the TARGET SITE'S OWN 10-year observed record, to build its flow-duration curve. That is the "partially gaged" half of the paper's title, not the ungaged half. In a genuinely ungaged application the FDC must be regionalized by a separate regression step that this data release does not perform - and that step is where most ungaged-basin error originates. Additionally, the default donor-selection step picks the highest-correlation donor using observed target correlations (leakage); the leak-safe variant requires the optional loo_krige_cor() kriging step that sb_main.R explicitly marks as not needed to run anything else.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PROJECT: only 9 of 16 methods (DAR, IDW, correlation-weighted, and averaging variants) are genuinely ungaged-capable, and all 9 still require a gauged donor with a CONCURRENT time series. The Iowa product predicts at an arbitrary map pin with zero local history, has discharge at only 22 of 85 sites, ZERO of the 61 IWQIS sites, and no guaranteed monitored neighbor - so even the ungaged-capable subset has no donor to draw from at a typical pin. The target is also daily streamflow, not a water-quality exceedance probability. The claim's own closing caveat (dense contiguous networks, a condition Iowa does not satisfy) is correct and if anything understated. Treat this source as evidence about QPPQ's data requirements, not as a small-n existence proof.

votes.correction:
The claim is factually exact but contains one framing error and one critical omission, both of which matter for how the Iowa project should use this source.

1. FRAMING ERROR — "74 independent units" is not apples-to-apples with Iowa's n=19, and overstates the donor network. The claim compares 74 raw gages against Iowa's 19 *leak-safe basin families* (85 raw sites collapsed by nesting + temporal overlap). Applying Iowa's own grouping rule to this network would collapse it far below 74: basin_area in coord_input.csv spans 15.72 to 47,698 (units per metadata: the abstract says squared meters but values are clearly km2), a ~3,000x range inside only two HUC4s. That range is the signature of heavy nesting — the large-area gages' basins physically contain most of the small ones. So "~4x more independent units than n=19" is an upper bound and probably a substantial overstatement; the effective independent count may be closer to Iowa's 19, or below it. This cuts IN FAVOR of the claim's own skeptical thrust: the source is even more sample-size-comparable to Iowa than stated, and correspondingly its results are even less able to certify a method at scale. It also means this study is itself vulnerable to pseudoreplication — 74 leave-one-out folds drawn from 2 contiguous basins are not 74 independent tests.

2. CRITICAL OMISSION — this is NOT an ungauged-prediction result in the sense the Iowa deployment requires. The paper title says "Ungaged and Partially Gaged," and the archived implementation is the partially-gaged case. In sb_functions.R the QPPQ variants are computed as `QPPQ_IDW <- quantile(R[,i], (U[,-i]%*%w)/sum(w))*area[i]` and `QPPQ_mu <- quantile(R[,i], apply(U[,-i],1,mean))*area[i]` — the `quantile(R[,i], ...)` term maps estimated non-exceedance probabilities back through THE TARGET SITE'S OWN OBSERVED runoff distribution, i.e. its own flow-duration curve. Likewise the rho-weighted and copula methods use `sigma[i,-i]`, the OBSERVED target-to-donor correlations. sb_main.R confirms this is the default and that removing the leak requires the separately-provided `loo_krige_cor` ("needed to use 'est cor' rather than observed"). Consequence for the deployment target: these 16 methods, as archived, require the target site's own observation record. Per the project's non-negotiable rule, that DOES NOT WORK for an arbitrary Iowa map pin with no local history. The claim should state this prominently rather than only noting the "no guaranteed monitored neighbor" issue — the deeper blocker is that QPPQ needs the target's own FDC, not just a nearby donor.

3. Minor corrections: the data file labels the second basin "Galveston-Trinity", not "Trinity" (metadata title uses "Trinity"). The archive's own sb_main.R carries a stale comment "estimate DVs using 11 models" while the output has 16 method columns — the metadata's 16, and the claim's 16, are correct. The claim should cite the paper DOI 10.1029/2019WR025138 alongside the data release. Finally, the target variable is daily streamflow, not a water-quality exceedance, so even the sample-size comparability does not make its effect sizes transferable to nitrate violation classification.

"The performance of copula methods is compared to several other streamflow estimation methods using a decade of daily streamflow data from 74 sites located within two river basins in the southeast United States with different climate characteristics and physiographic properties. Result (4) bundles error-in-FDC-estimation together with the site condition ("ungaged sites and partially gaged sites with limited data"). The claim is directionally correct and its quotations are exact, but three refinements are needed.

(1) "RANKING REVERSES" IS AN OVERSTATEMENT — use "loses dominance." The abstract supports copulas moving from "outperform other methods" (perfect information) to "competitive albeit nondominating" (realistic error). That is a demotion from the top rank, not an inversion of the method ordering. Whether any competitor overtakes copulas, and by how much, is in the paywalled full text and was not verifiable. Restate as: "the paper reports that copulas' advantage is contingent on the information regime — dominant under perfect information about FDCs and rank correlations, non-dominant once realistic estimation error is introduced." This is the weaker claim, and it is fully supported.

(2) THE FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION IS AN ANALOGY THE PAPER NEVER MAKES, though it is a sound one. Worland et al. studied STREAMFLOW estimation via FDCs and the QPPQ family. They say nothing about nitrate, concentration-duration curves, exceedance classification, or level/shape decomposition for water quality. The extension from FDC to CDC is inference by structural analogy, not transferred evidence. It should be cited as methodological precedent for the general principle — that plugging in a quantity the deployed system would have to estimate creates an optimistic-bias regime — not as evidence that a CDC decomposition will behave the same way for nitrate. Notably, the project does not need this paper to justify the protocol rule: it follows directly from the project's own rule 1. The paper's value is that it is an empirical demonstration, in a neighboring domain, that the perfect-information regime does not merely inflate a number but changes which method appears best — which is a stronger and more useful point than "it overstates the gain."

Every method compared in the paper — copula and QPPQ alike — maps a time series of nonexceedance probabilities FROM DONOR STREAMGAGE SITES onto the target. The shipped product is an arbitrary Iowa map pin with no nitrate history and NO GUARANTEE OF A MONITORED NEIGHBOR, so the donor-transfer machinery does not apply. Further, abstract points (2) and (3) — the copulas' strongest results — concern PARTIALLY GAGED sites with several years of the target's own data. WHAT THE PAPER ACTUALLY SAYS (Towler, Foks, Dugger, Dickinson, Essaid, Gochis, Viger, Zhang 2023, HESS 27:1809-1825, DOI 10.5194/hess-27-1809-2023):

CONFIRMED EXACTLY:
- "The evaluation is performed on daily streamflow for 5390 streamflow gages from 1983 to 2016 (~33 years)"; precisely "1 October 1983 to 31 December 2016, or just over 33 years (~12 100 d)". Claim's n and period are exact.
- Models: National Water Model v2.1 (WRF-Hydro) vs National Hydrologic Model v1.0 (PRMS). Correct.
- Central is among the two worst regions; NWMv2.1 > NHMv1.0 there. Correct.
- Quote 1 is verbatim: "for both models in the Central region, relatively poor performance is concentrated along the plains areas that span from the high plains (i.e., North Dakota) vertically down through the center of the CONUS (i.e., South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, and Texas)."
- Regions are ecoregion aggregations from Falcone (2011), not HUC2. Claim correctly notes this, and the caveat that an Iowa/HUC-07-specific figure is NOT obtainable is honest and correct.

FOUR ERRORS IN THE CLAIM:
1. NUMBERS WRONG. Table 4 ("Median values for each region") prints, for Central: NHMv1.0 KGE 0.33, NWMv2.1 KGE 0.45. Not 0.40 and 0.29. Both understated (~0.05 and ~0.04). Full Table 4 KGE, NHM/NWM: West 0.29/0.32; Central 0.33/0.45; Southeast 0.48/0.56; Northeast 0.63/0.65. Also printed for Central NWMv2.1: r 0.71, rSD 0.87, PBIAS +4.4%.
2. QUOTE 2 MISQUOTED. Paper says "Performance is MORE mixed as one moves further east in the Central region (e.g., around the Great Lakes)." Claim says "most mixed".
3. "Central region subset size not stated" IS FALSE. The paper states it explicitly in the Fig. 3 caption: Central n = 1450 (Central Plains + Western Plains + Mixed Wood Shield). Other regions: West 1510, Northeast 1218, Southeast 1212.
4. SPLIT PROTOCOL MISLABELED. The claim reports "temporal-holdout". It is NOT. The authors' own limitation: "the calibration periods of the models differed, and both overlapped with the evaluation period used in this study. While this overlap can introduce biases into the evaluation process, it allowed us to evaluate long-term performance for the same sites and time periods for both models." NWMv2.1 calibrated on WY2008-2013 (validated 2014-2016); NHMv1.0 calibrated on odd water years 1981-2010. Both sit inside the 1983-2016 evaluation window. This is a calibration-overlapping evaluation, which makes 0.45 OPTIMISTIC — which strengthens rather than weakens the claim's conclusion.

ONE SUBSTANTIVE CORRECTION TO THE CLAIM'S REASONING (matters for the project): the claim argues 0.40 "is the performance at GAUGED locations where NWM parameters were regionalized with gauge information available" and that ungauged performance "is bounded above by this." That framing is loose. NWMv2.1 calibrated 14 soil/vegetation/baseflow parameters at only 1,378 predominantly-natural gaged basins, then used a hydrologic-similarity strategy to REGIONALIZE parameters to the remaining basins. So roughly 74% of the 5,390 evaluation gauges (~4,000) never had their own observations fit — they received transferred parameters, which IS the ungauged-transfer case. The 0.45 median is therefore already largely a regionalized-parameter number, not a strict upper bound reachable only at calibrated sites. The calibration-period overlap still inflates it somewhat. Net: the practical conclusion survives intact, and arguably on firmer ground than the claim's own argument.

TRANSFERABILITY TO THIS PROJECT (the lens I was assigned):
- The plains quote does NOT describe Iowa. The named poor-performance corridor is North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, Texas. Iowa sits in the EASTERN part of Central, exactly where the paper says performance is "more mixed" and gives the Great Lakes as the example. Using the plains sentence to characterize expected NWM fidelity in Iowa is a stretch; the honest statement is that the paper supports "Central regional median KGE 0.45, no Iowa-specific number obtainable, Iowa is in the better-performing eastern portion of that region."
- Metric mismatch is real and under-stated: this is KGE on DAILY STREAMFLOW. The project needs a between-site LEVEL term for nitrate exceedance. KGE rewards correlation, variability ratio, and bias jointly; a KGE of 0.45 is compatible with decent timing and poor absolute volume. Note Central NWMv2.1 PBIAS is only +4.4% (median), so volume bias is actually modest in Central — the KGE penalty there comes mostly from r 0.71 and rSD 0.87. That is a timing/variability deficit, and this project already has a timing-adequate model (within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90). So NWM's strongest axis in Central is the axis the project needs LEAST.
- n=19 FAMILIES CONSTRAINT: this paper is a benchmark of a physically-based model, not an ML method with a learned-from-basins parameter budget, so the n=19 objection does not bite in the usual way — NWM output is a pre-computed covariate, available at any NHDPlus reach regardless of how many training basins exist. Adding 1-2 NWM-derived features costs ~1-2 degrees of freedom against 19 independent units, which is affordable. That is a genuine point in favor of trying it, independent of whether this specific claim's numbers were right.
- TILE DRAINAGE: NWM/WRF-Hydro has no explicit tile-drainage representation, which the project itself identifies as the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa. This is a strong a priori reason to expect NWM discharge to mis-rank Iowa basins specifically, but it is NOT supported by this paper — the paper never mentions tile drainage. Anyone citing Towler for that point is over-reading it.
- DEPLOYMENT TARGET: NWM retrospective output is keyed to NHDPlus comid, which the project already stores per basin, and requires no local nitrate history or local gauge. So it IS compatible with the arbitrary-map-pin product, unlike most gauge-dependent methods. That compatibility is the main reason to care.
- The project's own prior negative results are the stronger caution: seven hydrologically-motivated TEMPORAL features have already failed, and NWM discharge is another temporal hydrologic covariate. A long-term-mean or flow-regime-summary NWM statistic (a static between-site descriptor) is far better aligned with the diagnosed deficit than a daily NWM discharge series would be.

BOTTOM LINE: directionally correct, materially wrong in four specifics. Corrected numbers still support the claim's falsifiable implication — NWM Central fidelity is mediocre and is a weak instrument for a between-site level term — but the argument should be made with 0.45/0.33, with the calibration-overlap caveat, and WITHOUT implying the plains sentence describes Iowa.

Towler et al. 2023 (HESS 27:1809, DOI 10.5194/hess-27-1809-2023) benchmarked NWMv2.1 and NHMv1.0 daily streamflow against 5,390 USGS gauges, 1 Oct 1983 - 31 Dec 2016 (~33 yr, ~12,100 d). Table 4 median KGE for the Central region (n = 1,450, an aggregation of Falcone 2011 ecoregions: Central Plains + Western Plains + Mixed Wood Shield, NOT HUC2) is NWMv2.1 = 0.45 and NHMv1.0 = 0.33 — not 0.40 and 0.29 as claimed. Central NWMv2.1 also shows r = 0.71, rSD = 0.87, PBIAS = +4.4%. Regional medians (NHM/NWM): West 0.29/0.32, Central 0.33/0.45, Southeast 0.48/0.56, Northeast 0.63/0.65.

The protocol is NOT temporal-holdout. Both models' calibration periods overlap the evaluation window (NWMv2.1 calibrated WY2008-2013; NHMv1.0 on odd water years 1981-2010), and the authors flag this: "both overlapped with the evaluation period used in this study. While this overlap can introduce biases into the evaluation process, it allowed us to evaluate long-term performance for the same sites and time periods for both models." So 0.45 is an optimistic figure.

The second quotation is misquoted: the paper says performance is "more mixed" (not "most mixed") as one moves further east in the Central region. The Central subset size IS stated (n = 1,450); the claim wrongly says it was not.

The claim's inference that 0.45 is an upper bound only achievable where gauge information was available is loose: NWMv2.1 calibrated parameters at just 1,378 predominantly-natural gaged basins and regionalized to the rest by hydrologic similarity, so roughly 74% of the 5,390 evaluation gauges are already effectively ungauged-transfer cases. The practical conclusion nonetheless holds.

Critically for Iowa: the "plains" sentence names North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, and Texas. Iowa lies in the eastern portion of the Central region, which the paper describes as "more mixed," not as the poor-performing plains corridor. No Iowa/HUC-07-specific figure is obtainable from this paper — that caveat in the original claim is correct and should be retained. Also note the Central KGE shortfall is driven mainly by correlation (r 0.71) and variability ratio (rSD 0.87) rather than volume bias (PBIAS +4.4%), i.e. a timing/variability deficit — the axis on which this project's model is already adequate, not the between-site level term where the headroom lies.

votes.correction:
The claim is accurate on every identifier and should be acted on, but four corrections matter, one of them material.

1. MATERIAL — the "no authentication / free for commercial use / shippable" chain is valid for Figshare and INVALID for the GEE path. The claim correctly establishes CC-BY 4.0 on the data, then attaches that to the Earth Engine delivery mechanism. Earth Engine is a separate licensing regime from the dataset: it requires a Google account and a registered Google Cloud project (authentication, contradicting "NO authentication" for that path), and Google's Earth Engine FAQ states it "is free for noncommercial use" while directing "commercial or operational applications" to paid Cloud pricing. A deployed public-facing product is an operational application. So AgTile-US-via-GEE is NOT free-and-unauthenticated for the shipped product; AgTile-US-via-Figshare is.

2. The GEE asset is an ee.Image (the catalog loads it as a single Image), not an ImageCollection — the claim's hedge resolves to Image. It is also a community mirror maintained under samapriya's sat-io project, not an official NCAR or Google-curated asset, so its persistence is not guaranteed by the data producer.

3. The "no local raster storage" framing is backwards for this deployment target. The CONUS GeoTIFF is 126 MB zipped — trivial to vendor. Local storage is strictly superior here: no auth, no EE quota, no per-request latency, no third-party runtime dependency, and it dodges correction (1) entirely. A 30 m reduceRegion over a large multi-state NLDI basin is a seconds-to-minutes call subject to EE timeouts, on the critical path of every map-pin request. RECOMMENDATION: bulk-download the GeoTIFF from Figshare and compute basin tile fraction locally with the existing basin-cell machinery. Reserve GEE for prototyping only.

4. Fitness for this project (the claim does not overstate, but the ceiling should be stated). Genuine strengths: it is CONUS-wide, so unlike the Iowa-truncated CDL/N-surplus inner join it correctly covers the multi-state portions of the largest basins — it fixes that known under-counting bug for this one variable. It is binary at 30 m, so "mean over basin cells" is a clean, well-defined tile fraction. And it is a purely STATIC between-site covariate, which is precisely the class that has worked on this project (geometry + static geography) rather than the temporal class that has failed seven times. Iowa validation accuracy is 91.1%.

Caveats to carry: (a) n=19 FAMILIES — this variable moves only between sites, so it is evaluated against ~19 effective independent units. Add ONE basin-wide tile fraction first, not three distance-bucketed copies; the bucketed version spends three degrees of freedom on a between-site term that has ~19 points, and the riparian-bucket result (CLF +0.039 PR-AUC, REG worse) shows bucketing static geography is not reliably free. (b) It is a MODELED product that downscales county-level Ag Census totals using NLCD cropland + slope + SSURGO drainage class, not observed tile locations. It is therefore a soils-plus-cropland-plus-census composite and may be partly collinear with existing CDL crop-fraction features — expect a smaller incremental gain than "the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa" suggests. (c) It is single-year 2017 held constant across 2008-2026. This superficially resembles the known failure "broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward (-0.166)", but differs in kind: N surplus is a genuinely time-varying flux, whereas tile infrastructure is near-static on decadal timescales, so a constant value is defensible. That prior failure is still a reason to test rather than assume.

Directionally correct; three corrections, one of which invalidates the recommended deployment path.

(A) THE GEE PATH IS NOT AUTH-FREE AND IS NOT FREE FOR A COMMERCIAL PRODUCT. This is the claim's one real error. "No authentication required" and "free for commercial use, so shippable in a deployed product" are true of the Figshare download, but the claim chains them onto the GEE reduceRegion deployment story. Google's own docs: "To use Earth Engine you'll need access to a Cloud project that: has the Earth Engine API enabled, is registered for commercial or noncommercial use" (developers.google.com/earth-engine/guides/access), and the FAQ states "Earth Engine is free for noncommercial use" with commercial/operational applications directed to paid Google Cloud pricing. Projects registered before 2025-04-15 must verify noncommercial eligibility. So a shipped product doing per-pin reduceRegion calls needs a Google account, a registered Cloud project, and a PAID Earth Engine plan if the product is commercial. The CC-BY 4.0 data license governs the raster, not the platform serving it; it does not make the GEE route free.

(B) ASSET TYPE. It is an ee.Image, not an ImageCollection — catalog snippet is exactly `var tile30m = ee.Image("projects/sat-io/open-datasets/agtile/AgTile-US");`. Related: the dataset is a SINGLE STATIC 2017 SNAPSHOT (tied to the 2017 Census of Agriculture), with no time dimension. Also note the GEE copy is a third-party community mirror maintained by the awesome-gee-community-catalog project (sat-io), not an official NCAR or Google-curated asset — no persistence guarantee. The authoritative artifact is the Figshare DOI.

(C) SOURCE ATTRIBUTION. The cited page (gee-community-catalog.org/projects/tile/) does NOT contain the Figshare DOI and does NOT mention CC0 metadata; it cites only the Sci Data paper DOI. Those two specifics are substantiated, but by the Figshare API and the paper, not by the cited source. Cite them accordingly.

RECOMMENDED DEPLOYMENT PATH INSTEAD OF GEE: bulk-download AgTile-US-TIFF.zip (126 MB compressed) once from Figshare, no auth, CC-BY 4.0, clip to the Upper Mississippi/Missouri region, and compute per-basin tile fraction locally. Caution on the "no local raster storage" selling point: uncompressed CONUS is 153810 x 96815 uint8 ~= 14.9 GB, so clip before storing. This route has zero licensing or authentication ambiguity for a commercial product; the GEE route does not.

FIT TO THIS PROJECT (n=19 constraint). Favorable relative to most candidates: it adds 1-3 STATIC BETWEEN-SITE scalars (basin tile fraction, optionally per distance bucket), which is exactly the term where the project's remaining headroom sits, and matches the established pattern that only geometry/static-geography features have won here. It is CONUS-wide, so it also covers the multi-state portions of the largest basins — directly addressing the documented Iowa-only inner-join undercount. Iowa validation is genuinely strong (91.1%, n=5,253). Cost is 1-3 features, not a 300-basin architecture, so the n=19-families constraint is survivable, though any between-site coefficient is still estimated from ~19 effective units and must be tested under LOFO, not a random split.
MAIN RISK TO STATE UP FRONT: AgTile-US is DERIVED from county census totals + SSURGO drainage class + slope. Per-basin tile fraction is therefore substantially a smooth function of soils, slope and county location, and lat/lon are already the #2 and #3 permutation-importance features. Expect meaningful collinearity with existing static geography and a real chance of low marginal LOFO gain. This is a cheap test, not a guaranteed win.

The unconditioned RMSE of ~60% in real space is the closest thing to a transfer-relevant error and implies roughly a factor-of-1.6 typical error on predicted mean-annual load. Source: Robertson & Saad 2019, USGS SIR 2019-5114, table 5.

TABLE 5 (caption: "Summary of calibration results for the 2012 Midwest SPARROW total nitrogen model") — every quoted number matches verbatim:
- Conditioned RMSE, natural log units: 0.487
- Conditioned RMSE, percentage in real space: 51.8
- Unconditioned RMSE, natural log units: 0.555
- Unconditioned RMSE, percentage in real space: 60.0
- Mean exponentiated weighted error: 1.129
- R2: 0.950
- Yield R2: 0.913
- Number of sites: 1,334
Body text (p. 29) corroborates: "The model explained 95 percent of the variance in TN loads and 91 percent of the variances in yields... conditioned RMSE was 0.487 and... unconditioned RMSE was 0.555 (both in natural logarithmic units). These values equate to an RMSE of 51.8 percent for conditioned predictions and an RMSE of 60.0 percent for unconditioned predictions in real (kilograms per year) space."

TARGET VARIABLE: confirmed "long-term mean-annual TN loads," detrended to the 2012 base year; water-quality record within 3 years of 2012, min 3 yr record, >=24 samples, >=3 samples per season, paired streamgage within 40 km.

SPLIT PROTOCOL — the load-bearing part of the claim, CONFIRMED: grep of the full text for "cross-valid", "holdout", "hold-out", "independent test", "validation dataset", "withheld", "jackknife", "leave-one", "split sample", "out-of-sample" returns ZERO hits. The only "bootstrap" hit (p.~11) is parametric bootstrap for load-estimation uncertainty at the calibration sites, not model validation. All reported fit statistics are in-sample calibration fit on the same 1,334 sites used to estimate the 17 coefficients. There is no spatial holdout of any kind.

DEFINITIONS confirming the conditioned/unconditioned distinction the claim relies on (Table 5 footnotes b and d): conditioned RMSE resets predicted accumulated loads to MEASURED loads at upstream calibration sites; unconditioned does not. So the claim is right that unconditioned (0.555 / 60.0%) is the closer analogue to true prediction, and right that even that is still in-sample. Footnote c gives the real-space conversion: 100 x (exp[RMSE^2]-1)^0.5 — i.e. 60.0% is a coefficient of variation, not a percent bias.

ADDITIONAL EVIDENCE STRENGTHENING THE CLAIM (report's own limitations, p. 29): "the model did not predict the loads and yields as well for sites with relatively small loads. The unconditioned RMSE was 0.65 for TN loads less than 14 logarithmic units compared to 0.39 for loads greater than 14 logarithmic units." Also: residuals have significant regional structure (Moran's I = 0.199, p = 0.0005) with systematic over/underprediction in the western study area — i.e. the model has exactly the between-site level bias that is our project's central problem, even in-sample.

TWO FACTUAL ERRORS IN THE CLAIM (detail only, do not change the conclusion):
1. Site-count provenance is garbled. Table 1 gives, for TN: 1,344 sites CONSIDERED and 1,335 used in the final SPARROW model, out of 93,994 original water-quality sites. The 1,346 figure in the claim is the TOTAL PHOSPHORUS "considered" count, not TN. (The report is itself internally inconsistent by one site: Table 1 says 1,335 final TN sites, Table 5 and p. 28 text say 1,334.)
2. "Factor-of-1.6 typical error" is a loose reading. 60.0% is a real-space CV derived from exp(RMSE^2); the one-sigma multiplicative error implied by 0.555 log units is exp(0.555) = 1.74x, not 1.6x.

ONE FRAMING OVERSTATEMENT: the claim says R2 0.950 "is on accumulated load, a quantity dominated by drainage area." True and standard, but the report also publishes Yield R2 = 0.913, which is area-normalized and still high, so area dominance alone does not explain the number away. The decisive objection is the absence of any holdout, not the area effect.

TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET — the claim's non-comparability conclusion holds for a reason stronger than it states: SPARROW's target is a LONG-TERM MEAN-ANNUAL LOAD (kg/yr) at a reach, a single number per site. Our target is a DAILY binary exceedance of 10 mg/L concentration. These differ in temporal resolution (decadal mean vs daily), in units (mass flux vs concentration), and in the discharge dependence (SPARROW load requires a modeled streamflow; our product has no gauge). No mapping exists between AUC 0.820 / R2 0.328 on daily site-days and R2 0.950 on log mean-annual load, under ANY split protocol. Note however that SPARROW is a genuinely ungauged-capable paradigm — it predicts on every NHDPlus reach in the network, so it is architecturally the right shape for an arbitrary map pin; it is only the reported statistics that are in-sample.

HIGHLY ACTIONABLE SIDE FINDING for the parent agent: the Midwest 2012 SPARROW TN model includes "Ln (tile drains, percentage of catchment)" as a calibrated land-to-water delivery variable, coefficient 0.101 (90% CI 0.064-0.139), SE 0.023, p<0.0001, t=4.5, VIF 2.3, over 1,334 Midwest sites. This is exactly the tile-drainage covariate our project lists as missing with "NO data source identified," it is significant across the Midwest including all of Iowa, and the underlying tile-drainage layer is a public USGS/SPARROW model input. This is a concrete lead worth a separate acquisition task. Other calibrated delivery terms: ln(runoff) 0.673 (t=18.5, the strongest), detrended air temperature -0.048, ln(soil clay %) 0.292, CRP/farm-acre ratio -4.758, ln(% no-till) 0.124.

N-CONSTRAINT NOTE: n=1,334 calibration sites vs our 19 independent basin families. SPARROW's coefficient estimates are a ~70x larger spatial sample, so its per-coefficient standard errors are not achievable by refitting anything comparable on our data. The usable transfer is to INGEST SPARROW's already-fitted covariates and, potentially, its per-reach predicted TN yield as a static between-site feature — not to reproduce its calibration.

(3) "R2 0.950 IS DOMINATED BY DRAINAGE AREA" — DIRECTIONALLY RIGHT, OVERSTATED AS PHRASED. Log-accumulated-load R2 across basins spanning many orders of magnitude in area is indeed inflated by the area-load relationship. However, the same table reports Yield R2 = 0.913, which IS area-normalized (kg/km2/yr) and still high, so drainage area cannot be the whole story. Ours is DAILY-MAX CONCENTRATION exceeding 10 mg/L. A static long-term-mean model has no temporal dynamics and cannot emit a daily violation probability. The two numbers are not on the same axis in any sense — target, units, and time scale all differ — so no rescaling of SPARROW's RMSE makes it a benchmark for LOFO AUC 0.820. The n=19-families constraint is NOT the operative objection here (SPARROW used 1,334 sites); target mismatch plus zero spatial holdout are.

CONTEXT NOT IN THE CLAIM, RELEVANT TO THE PARENT PROJECT: the TN model includes ln(tile drains, percentage of catchment) as a land-to-water delivery variable, coefficient 0.101 (SE range 0.064-0.139), p<0.0001, t=4.5 - significant in a 1,334-site nitrogen model covering Iowa. SPARROW variable name LTILES13_PERC2. Underlying data: Nakagaki, N., and Wieczorek, M.E., 2016, "Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for 12 Midwest states, 2012," USGS data release, doi:10.5066/F7W37TDP - 12 Midwest states (covers Iowa and multi-state basin portions), free, no authentication, USGS public domain.

TRANSFERABILITY: the claim's non-comparability argument is sound and in fact understated. Beyond the protocol issue, SPARROW predicts a long-term MEAN-ANNUAL load (kg/yr) detrended to one base year from a 17-variable mechanistic mass balance (7 sources, 4 aquatic decay terms); the project predicts DAILY exceedance of 10 mg/L. Mean-annual aggregation removes essentially all the temporal variance the project's model is scored on, so there is no arithmetic path from a 60% error on a multi-year mean load to a daily AUC or daily-max R2. "0.950 vs 0.820" is a category error independent of the holdout question. On n: 1,334 sites vs 19 independent basin families is a ~70x gap, but it cuts oddly here - SPARROW's large n comes with NO holdout, so its n buys no evidence about spatial transfer.

(1) "1,346 TN sites considered out of 93,994" is wrong per the report's Table 1, which assigns 1,344 considered / 1,335 used to TOTAL NITROGEN and 1,346 to TOTAL PHOSPHORUS. The report's own p.12 text contradicts its Table 1 ("Less than 2 percent (1,346 and 1,344 of 93,994) of original water-quality sites with TN and TP data, respectively"), so the claim faithfully reproduces a source-internal inconsistency. Cite it as "1,344 TN sites considered per Table 1 (the report's text says 1,346; the two disagree)". (2) Table 1 lists 1,335 TN "sites used in final SPARROW models" against Table 5's 1,334 - another off-by-one source inconsistency; 1,334 is the operative calibration n stated in both Table 5 and the narrative. (3) "roughly a factor-of-1.6 typical error" is loose: 60.0% is computed as 100*(exp(RMSE^2)-1)^0.5, a coefficient of variation, whereas the one-sigma MULTIPLICATIVE factor is exp(0.555) = 1.74x. State "a factor of roughly 1.6-1.75 depending on convention." Additionally, soften "the R2 of 0.950 is on accumulated load, a quantity dominated by drainage area, so it is not comparable" - the premise is right and is why SPARROW reports a yield R2 at all, but Yield R2 = 0.913 IS area-normalized and still high, so drainage-area dominance alone does not carry the argument. The sufficient and stronger grounds for non-comparability are (a) all four statistics are in-sample at calibration sites with confirmed residual spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I 0.199, p=0.0005), and (b) the target quantity is a multi-year mean-annual load, not a daily exceedance, so the metrics are not on the same axis at all.

Both quoted fragments in the claim are word-for-word correct. "74 sites" is correct and is stated as "74 sites located within two river basins in the southeast United States with different climate characteristics and physiographic properties," using "a decade of daily streamflow data."

Every competing partially-gaged method in that framework also consumes target-site observations. So the abstract says only that the copula's RELATIVE edge over its rivals emerges with several years; it says nothing about when target-site observations start paying off at all. The claim's central sentence — "implies a data threshold on the order of years, not days, before target-site observations pay off" — is a misreading of a method-ranking result as a data-quantity threshold. The source does not support it.
(b) The claim calls this "a direct negative." The paper's ungaged finding is mildly POSITIVE: copulas "remain a competitive albeit nondominating method for ungaged sites." The paper is an endorsement of FDC-based transfer including the fully ungaged case, not a negative result about it.
(c) "Several years" is never quantified in the abstract and I could not reach the full text, so the exact withheld record lengths, the CV protocol, and the metrics are UNVERIFIED. The claim itself concedes protocol "unknown" — under rule 1 that makes this number non-comparable to our LOFO 0.820 in either direction.

TRANSFERABILITY.
(d) The FDC/QPPQ framework REQUIRES a network of concurrent donor gages supplying the daily nonexceedance-probability time series mapped onto the target's estimated FDC; abstract point (2), "hedge against poor performance when donor information becomes sparser," is about DONOR density, not target record. The Iowa analogue of that donor index already exists and is already the top permutation feature (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1). The project has therefore already implemented the timing half of QPPQ and it works (within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90); what is missing is the FDC half, the site's absolute level. Streamflow FDCs in humid southeastern basins are dominated by drainage area and are close to log-linear in it, making the ungaged FDC regression well-conditioned. Three corrections to how the claim uses it:
1. Do not cite this paper for "a data threshold on the order of years, not days." It does not measure the marginal value of a short target record. If that threshold matters to the project, it needs a different source (short-record augmentation / record-extension literature, e.g. MOVE and Farmer-Vogel style estimators, which report useful gains from far shorter records) or an internal experiment: hold out a site, feed back k days of its own nitrate observations, and sweep k. That experiment is cheap here and would answer the question directly for nitrate rather than by analogy from streamflow.
2. The paper's ungaged result is mildly POSITIVE, not a negative. Framing it as "a direct negative" inverts it. The correct negative for the arbitrary-pin product is definitional, not empirical: zero observations means there is no site-level offset to estimate, so quantile mapping and a site random intercept are unidentifiable at the pin. State that as a structural fact, with the paper cited only as the standard reference for the ungaged-FDC-from-basin-attributes alternative.
3. The paper's structure actually ARGUES FOR the project's remaining path rather than against it. Its ungaged case regresses FDC parameters on basin characteristics, then maps a donor-derived nonexceedance time series through that curve. The Iowa model already has the donor index (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1, top permutation feature) and already performs well on timing (within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90); the deficit is the level, i.e. the FDC. Estimating a per-site nitrate duration curve from static attributes and composing it with the existing cross-site index is a coherent restructuring of the current model, not a new dependency on target-site data.

Two caveats to attach whenever this is cited: (i) it is a STREAMFLOW result, and streamflow FDCs are dominated by drainage area in a way nitrate concentration duration curves in tile-drained Iowa are not — the dominant control here (tile-drainage density) is missing from the features entirely; (ii) headline n=74 overstates independence, since the sites nest within two basins, so its effective spatial replication is small — which means it is not disqualified by the n=19 constraint, but also that it is thin evidence.

votes.evidence:
SOURCE IDENTIFIED AND CITATION IS ACCURATE. https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70215879 = Worland, S.C., Steinschneider, S., Farmer, W.H., Asquith, W.H., and Knight, R., 2019, "Copula theory as a generalized framework for flow-duration curve-based streamflow estimates in ungaged and partially gaged catchments," Water Resources Research 55(11):9378-9397, DOI 10.1029/2019WR025138, CC-BY. Retrieved via the USGS pubs-services JSON API (https://pubs.usgs.gov/pubs-services/publication/70215879) and cross-checked against the Semantic Scholar record; the two abstracts match character-for-character.

QUOTES ARE EXACT. Abstract verbatim: "...copula approaches: (1) outperform other methods in the limiting case of perfect information with regard to the rank-based correlation structure and FDCs across the gaging network; (2) provide a hedge against poor performance when donor information becomes sparser and less informative; (3) outperform other methods when used for partially gaged sites with several years of available data; and (4) remain a competitive albeit nondominating method for ungaged sites and partially gaged sites with limited data when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network." Study design per abstract: "a decade of daily streamflow data from 74 sites located within two river basins in the southeast United States." So n=74 and the phrasing in the claim are both correct.

THE CLAIM IS NEVERTHELESS REFUTED, ON FOUR GROUNDS.

(1) THE PAPER DOES NOT STUDY WHETHER TARGET-SITE OBSERVATIONS "PAY OFF." Points (3) and (4) are a ranking of copulas AGAINST OTHER FDC-BASED METHODS (QPPQ-family, nonlinear spatial interpolation of FDCs, etc.), all of which also consume whatever target-site record exists. The statement "copulas dominate at several years, only tie at limited data" is a statement about when the copula's RELATIVE edge over its competitors emerges. It is logically consistent with all methods gaining large absolute skill from a few weeks of target data. The claim converts a method-ranking result into a data-sufficiency threshold ("years, not days, before target-site observations pay off"). That inference is not supported by the abstract, and I could not obtain the body to check whether the paper reports absolute skill-vs-record-length curves.

(2) THE ZERO-OBSERVATION CASE IS NOT "BELOW EVEN THE LIMITED DATA REGIME" — IT IS ONE OF THE PAPER'S TWO HEADLINE REGIMES. Point (4) reads "for ungaged sites AND partially gaged sites with limited data." Fully ungaged (zero target observations) is explicitly inside the studied range, not outside it. The claim's central rhetorical move — that the Iowa deployment sits off the bottom of the paper's tested range — is contradicted by the sentence it quotes.

(3) "COMPETITIVE ALBEIT NONDOMINATING" IS NOT "NO ADVANTAGE," AND NOT A NEGATIVE RESULT. The paper's finding for ungaged sites is that the method performs on par with the best available alternatives under realistic FDC/correlation estimation error. That is a neutral-to-mildly-positive result for zero-observation regionalization, not "a direct negative." The claim upgrades "does not dominate" into "finds no advantage," which reverses the sign of the reported conclusion.

(4) THE PAPER IS ARGUABLY EVIDENCE FOR, NOT AGAINST, THE PATH THE CLAIM CALLS THE ONLY REMAINING OPTION. In the fully ungaged configuration, FDC-based estimation works exactly the way the claim's own final sentence describes: regionalize the FDC (the marginal, i.e. the absolute LEVEL) from static basin attributes, and borrow the nonexceedance-probability time series (the TIMING) from donor gauges. The abstract reports that configuration as competitive. So the source supports, rather than refutes, the static-attribute FDC-regionalization route for an ungaged pin. The claim's last clause is therefore right, but it is presented as a grudging residual when it is in fact the paper's own ungaged method.

FURTHER METHODOLOGY AND TRANSFERABILITY CAVEATS (these weaken the claim's evidentiary base rather than rescuing it):
- SPLIT PROTOCOL UNDETERMINED. The claim says "unknown"; I could not determine it either. Wiley returns HTTP 402/403 on the pdfdirect and landing URLs despite a CC-BY license; no repository copy exists (Unpaywall lists only the publisher location; EuropePMC hitCount 0; CORE has no match). Per rule 1, this must be stated as undetermined, and no number here is comparable to the project's LOFO 0.820.
- "SEVERAL YEARS" AND "LIMITED DATA" ARE NEVER QUANTIFIED IN ANY TEXT I COULD REACH. The claim's paraphrase "on the order of years, not days" is an unverifiable interpolation of an unquantified qualitative phrase.
- PSEUDOREPLICATION IN THE SOURCE'S OWN n. 74 sites inside only TWO river basins means heavy nesting and spatial dependence; the effective number of independent units is far below 74, likely closer to the project's own 19-family scale than the headline suggests. This cuts both ways: it makes the source less authoritative than n=74 implies, and it removes the usual "their n is huge, ours is 19" objection.
- DOMAIN MISMATCH. Daily STREAMFLOW in two humid southeastern basins, not daily-max nitrate exceedance in tile-drained Iowa row-crop basins. Streamflow has strong, slowly-decaying inter-site rank correlation, which is what makes donor-borrowed nonexceedance series work; nitrate concentration rank correlation between Iowa basins decays much faster and is driven by local N application and tile hydrology. Any transfer of the copula/QPPQ machinery to nitrate needs that assumption tested directly, and the project's existing cross-site donor feature (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1, the top permutation-importance feature) is the closest existing analogue and does work.
- DONOR REQUIREMENT IS SATISFIED, NOT VIOLATED. FDC/copula methods need concurrent DONOR gauges, not target-site history. Iowa has ~85 nitrate sensors as donors. So the deployment constraint the claim invokes (zero observations at the pin) is not the binding constraint for this family of methods.
- DIRECTIONALLY, THE METHOD ADDRESSES THE PROJECT'S ACTUAL DEFICIT. The project is "a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker" (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21). FDC-based methods decompose exactly along that seam: the marginal/FDC carries the absolute level (the failing term) and the copula carries the timing (the working term). Framing this paper as a reason not to pursue level correction is backwards.

WHAT SURVIVES. Only this much of the claim is supportable: post-hoc calibration that requires the TARGET SITE'S OWN observations (site random intercepts fit to local data, quantile mapping against a local empirical distribution) is unusable at an arbitrary pin — but that follows from the deployment definition, not from this paper, and the paper is not needed to establish it. Citing Worland et al. 2019 as the authority for it is a misattribution.

Its ungaged (zero target observation) regime IS tested and is reported as "competitive albeit nondominating" — not as a failure regime and not as below the tested range. The paper therefore does NOT establish a years-scale threshold before target-site data becomes useful; it establishes only that the copula's relative edge over rival FDC methods emerges at "several years" (unquantified) of target record. votes.evidence:
PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED, EXACT. Source is Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis & Franz (2020), "Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach," Scientific Data 7, at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7406500/. All quoted figures match verbatim: "Validation of AgTile-US with 16000 ground truth points indicated 86.03% accuracy at the CONUS-scale"; "The AgTile-US failed to identify tile drainage at about 13.97% of ground-truth locations"; "Over the heavily tile-drained midwestern regions of the U.S., the accuracy ranges from 82.7% to 93.6%"; "Iowa (5.7 Mha), where we have identified 5253 ground truth points, and the AgTile-US showed 91.1% accuracy." ESRI multi-resolution basemap (15 m, 1 m, 0.6 m, 0.3 m) confirmed; imagery dates 10/2/2012-4/23/2017. No misattribution or exaggeration in the numbers themselves.

THE INFERENCE IS REFUTED ON THREE GROUNDS, ALL FROM THE PAPER'S OWN TEXT.

(1) POSITIVE-ONLY VALIDATION; COMMISSION ERROR NEVER MEASURED. Authors: "We limited the tile drainage ground-truth identification mostly to fallow croplands where the tile drainage signature is easily detectable," and list "uncertainty in croplands without tile drainage" as a primary limitation of the validation approach. The 16,000 points are tile-drained locations only. Hence 86.03%/91.1% are producer's accuracy (recall) for the tile class, NOT balanced overall accuracy. False-positive rate is unreported and unmeasurable from this design. The claim's "roughly 9% pixel-level misclassification" is therefore incorrect: it is ~8.9% OMISSION among visually-confirmed tiled parcels, plus an unknown commission rate. A map over-painting tile drainage across untiled cropland would score identically.

(2) NON-RANDOM SAMPLE. Points restricted to fallow fields where tile signatures are visible in imagery, so even the omission rate does not generalize to the pixel population.

(3) DECISIVE: ERROR STRUCTURE IS COUNTY-BLOCKED, SO AGGREGATION DOES NOT AVERAGE IT OUT. AgTile-US is not an independent per-pixel classifier. It is a deterministic downscaling that allocates USDA Census of Agriculture 2017 COUNTY-LEVEL tile area totals onto NLCD-2016 cropland pixels via SSURGO v2.0 drainage class (7 categories) and SRTM 30 m slope, iterating the slope threshold (1% steps, then 0.1% refinement) until the county total is matched. Errors are spatially correlated at county scale by construction. Authors quantify the binding constraint: "The average error in tile drainage estimates based on the Census of Agriculture 2017 is 19.8%," and state "Any uncertainty in these datasets will lead to inaccuracies in the model estimated tile drainage map." Basin-level aggregation averages WITHIN-county placement error but inherits the ~19.8% county census error essentially undiluted, since an Iowa basin spans few counties. Aggregation averages independent noise; it cannot average out systematic bias. The claim's central assertion — "a per-basin aggregate would average much of that out, making basin-level tile fraction a low-noise attribute" — is thus unsupported and directionally wrong.

ADDITIONAL: NLCD-2016 underrepresents census cropland by -18.15% CONUS, compounding the project's known inner-join undercount for multi-state basins. Map is a static 2017 snapshot (not time-varying). Therefore 86.03%/91.1% are producer's accuracy (recall) on a detectability-biased positive subsample, NOT overall pixel classification accuracy. The claim's inference that the Iowa raster "carries roughly 9% pixel-level misclassification" is unsupported: the false-positive rate is unmeasured in the source, so total pixel misclassification is unbounded from above by anything the paper reports.

Systematic/correlated error does not average out with area - it becomes a persistent PER-BASIN BIAS, which is exactly the between-site term (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24) the project is trying to improve. The claim's conclusion ("low-noise attribute") thus does not follow even from its own premise.

votes.evidence:
PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED — the numbers are NOT fabricated. Source is Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis & Franz (2020), "Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach," Scientific Data 7:257, PMC7406500. Confirmed verbatim: "an overall accuracy of 86.03% for the CONUS with an omission error of 13.97%"; 16,000 points from ESRI multi-resolution aerial imagery (acquisition 2012-10-02 to 2017-04-23); Iowa 91.1% on 5,253 points; Midwest range 82.7-93.6%; 30 m resolution, CONUS, year 2017. So the claim is not misattributed or garbled at the level of quoted statistics.

WHAT IS REFUTED IS THE OPERATIVE INFERENCE — "roughly 9% pixel-level misclassification ... a per-basin aggregate would average much of that out, making basin-level tile fraction a low-noise attribute." Four independent defects, each sufficient:

(1) POSITIVES-ONLY GROUND TRUTH — 91.1% IS RECALL, NOT ACCURACY. The authors "manually identified 16000 tile drainage ground-truth points," i.e. all 16,000 are known-drained locations. Commission error / false-positive rate is reported NOWHERE. Note 100 − 86.03 = 13.97 exactly: the paper's "omission error" is just the complement of its "accuracy," which is arithmetically what you get when the sample contains no negatives. A basin tile FRACTION is (drained pixels)/(basin pixels) and its error depends on commission at least as much as omission. The paper places no bound whatsoever on commission, so "9% pixel-level misclassification" is not a misclassification rate of the raster.

(2) THE SAMPLE IS NON-RANDOM AND SELECTED FOR DETECTABILITY. Authors' own limitation: "we limited the tile drainage ground-truth identification mostly to fallow croplands where the tile drainage signature is easily detectable." 91.1% is an optimistic upper bound on recall within the easiest-to-see subset, not an unbiased pixel accuracy over Iowa cropland.

(3) CALIBRATION/VALIDATION CIRCULARITY. The same 16,000 points were used "to validate the AgTile-US and to set the upper limit of slope in the geospatial model" (the 20% slope cap). Validation data parameterized the model — the accuracy figure is partly in-sample and inflated. The claim's stated protocol ("not-applicable, image-interpretation ground truth, not a train/test split") is therefore wrong: there IS a train/test issue, and it is a leak.

(4) DECISIVE FOR OUR USE — ERRORS ARE COUNTY-LEVEL SYSTEMATIC AND DO NOT AVERAGE OUT. AgTile-US is not a per-pixel classifier with independent errors; it is a deterministic greedy fill. It ranks NLCD-2016 cropland pixels by SSURGO drainage class (starting at D=7, very poorly drained, slope S=0), then relaxes slope in 1% steps to 20%, then steps down drainage class, "until the estimated tile drainage area exceeded the USDA census tile drainage area" for the county. Every pixel in a county is therefore tied to one shared constraint — the county Census of Agriculture tile acreage — and to SSURGO polygon geometry. The claim's averaging argument requires error independence; the dominant error term here is a per-county bias shared by all pixels, so a basin overlapping a handful of counties inherits that bias wholesale with no cancellation. The authors quantify it: "The average error in tile drainage estimates based on the Census of Agriculture 2017 is 19.8%," with state-level errors reaching −79.06% (New Mexico) and −42.38% (West Virginia). The relevant noise floor for a basin-mean aggregate is that ~19.8% systematic census error, not 9%. Authors also flag "underestimation ... mainly due to underrepresentation of croplands in NLCD land cover 2016" and that "any uncertainty in these datasets will lead to inaccuracies."

UNVERIFIED SUB-CLAIM: "highest per-state validation density in the paper." Iowa's 5,253/16,000 (33%) is plausibly the largest raw COUNT, but I could not recover per-state point counts for the other nine states, and "density" (points per unit area or per cropland area) was never established. Treat as unsupported.

TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET — mixed, and better than the refutation implies. Positives: AgTile-US is genuinely operational for an arbitrary Iowa map pin (CONUS coverage, so multi-state basin portions are covered; 30 m static raster, single 2017 epoch; free public download; no auth; no local history needed) and it is a STATIC BETWEEN-SITE attribute, which is exactly the deficit our diagnostics point to (between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42) and exactly the class of feature that has historically won on this project while every temporal feature failed. It also embeds a real observed quantity — county USDA census tile acreage — which is authentic between-site information not currently in the 68 features. Negatives to state plainly: (a) because it is a deterministic function of SSURGO drainage class + slope + NLCD cropland + county total, basin-mean tile fraction is substantially a re-encoding of basin soil/topography plus a county indicator, so it will be partly collinear with lat/lon (already the #2 and #3 features) — some of its apparent gain may be the model re-learning geography it already has; (b) the single 2017 epoch means no temporal variation, so it cannot help the timing task at all, only the level task; (c) THE n=19 CONSTRAINT BITES HARD — one new static covariate is being asked to explain between-family variation across 19 independent units, and because the error is county-correlated rather than independent, the effective information content is closer to the number of distinct county-groups spanned by those 19 families, likely well under 19. This is a one-degree-of-freedom-ish addition evaluated at n=19; expect a noisy LOFO estimate and treat any single-split improvement under ~0.02 PR-AUC as indistinguishable from zero.

BOTTOM LINE: use the feature if you like — the underlying reasoning for wanting a tile-drainage attribute is sound and this is the best free CONUS product available — but do NOT justify it with "91.1% Iowa accuracy so ~9% noise that averages out." That premise is wrong in three ways (positives-only recall, detectability-biased sample, self-calibrated threshold) and the averaging step is invalid because the errors are county-systematic. Budget for a ~20% systematic bias in basin tile fraction that survives aggregation, and validate the feature empirically under LOFO rather than assuming it is low-noise.

CAVEATS ON THIS VERIFICATION: all reading was WebFetch-summarizer-mediated against a single source; the session's web-search budget (200/200) was exhausted before I could cross-check against the dataset landing page, the HydroShare/UCAR distribution record, or independent papers citing AgTile-US accuracy. I did not obtain the exact download URL, license, or the full per-state table.

ABSTRACT, VERBATIM: "We developed a long short-term memory (LSTM) model using high-frequency sensor data from across the conterminous US to predict daily nitrate concentrations, achieving strong temporal validation performance (median KGE = 0.60). The three quoted numbers (0.60 temporal, 0.18 CONUS spatial, 0.34 MRB spatial) are EXACT and correctly attributed. The refutation is not about the numbers; it is about what produced them.

REFUTATION 1 — THE CLAIM SWAPS THE INTERVENTION (fatal). The claim's own first sentence says "restricting spatial VALIDATION to the MRB," which is correct. Its second sentence then asserts this is "direct evidence that transfer performance improves when the TRAINING POOL is restricted to hydroclimatically similar basins." Those are different interventions and the study performed only the first. The abstract describes ONE model ("a long short-term memory (LSTM) model using high-frequency sensor data from across the conterminous US"), singular throughout, and 0.34 is that same CONUS-trained model's spatial-holdout skill computed over the MRB SUBSET of held-out basins. "Guiding the model's targeted application to the MRB" makes the logic explicit: spatial validation was used to diagnose WHERE the continental model is trustworthy, and MRB was the answer. No MRB-only-trained model is described anywhere in the abstract, and therefore no CONUS-trained-vs-MRB-trained contrast exists to support "a regionally-specialized model over a continental one." The 0.34 was produced BY a continental model — if anything the paper is a demonstration that a continentally-pooled training set transfers acceptably into the MRB, which points the opposite way from the claim's conclusion.

REFUTATION 2 — THE DESCRIPTIVE 0.18→0.34 GAP IS CONFOUNDED, so it does not isolate "hydroclimatic similarity." At least three alternatives are not excluded: (a) TRAINING DENSITY — high-frequency nitrate sensors are concentrated in the Corn Belt, so a held-out MRB basin has far more near-neighbor training basins than a held-out arid-West or coastal basin; that is a data-density effect, not a homogeneity effect, and it predicts the same result. (b) SIGNAL AMPLITUDE / METRIC ARTIFACT — KGE combines correlation, variance ratio and bias ratio, and rewards series with large, strongly seasonal variance. MRB nitrate has far higher mean and seasonal amplitude than low-nitrate western streams, so MRB sites can score higher KGE at equal fractional error. Part of +0.16 may be signal-to-noise, not transferability. (c) The subgroup was chosen post hoc as the region of interest; comparing a favorable subset against the all-basin median is a selected-subgroup comparison, not a controlled contrast.

REFUTATION 3 — N AND UNCERTAINTY ARE UNSTATED. The claim itself concedes the MRB basin count is unknown; the abstract states no site count and no dispersion, CI, or significance test for either median. A difference of medians between two subsets of unknown (possibly small) size with no spread reported does not meet the bar of "direct evidence." I also could NOT verify the spatial-holdout protocol design from the methods — specifically whether nested / upstream-downstream basin pairs were grouped when held out. This matters directly: the Corn Belt is where monitored basins most densely nest, so an ungrouped leave-basin-out split would inflate the MRB figure precisely where the claim wants to read it as transfer skill. I flag this as unverified rather than asserting it.

REFUTATION 4 — TRANSFERABILITY TO THIS PROJECT IS NEAR-ZERO EVEN IF THE CLAIM WERE TRUE. (a) TARGET MISMATCH: median KGE on continuous daily nitrate concentration is not commensurable with our binary daily exceedance AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634; per protocol rule 1 and metric appropriateness, no number here can be compared to ours. (b) MECHANISM MISMATCH: their skill comes from an LSTM over meteorological forcing TIME SERIES; on this project essentially every temporal/lagged-forcing feature has already failed (lagged weather 0.116→0.019, rolling precip/water balance, advective routing, rolling and z-score targets). (c) NO DECISION IS ON THE TABLE: our product is already Iowa-only and entirely inside the MRB. Taken at face value the claim recommends what we have already done and changes nothing. (d) N=19 CUTS THE OTHER WAY: our binding constraint is too FEW independent units, not too heterogeneous a pool. A paper whose central move was pooling all CONUS sensors to get enough training data, then applying the result in the MRB, argues for ENLARGING our pool with out-of-state MRB sensor basins (IL, MN, MO, OH via NWIS/Water Quality Portal), not restricting it. Using this paper to justify further regional restriction inverts its own methodology.

That is a finding about the BETWEEN-SITE mean level, which is exactly our diagnosed deficit (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21), and tile drainage is our known-missing dominant control for which no source has yet been identified. Since this is a CONUS-scale model, it necessarily used some wall-to-wall tile-drainage layer covering all of Iowa AND the multi-state parts of our basins. Chasing that layer's identity (the data-availability statement in the full text, obtainable after the 2026-08-09 PMC release, or by emailing corresponding author Golden/Husic) is a far higher-value follow-up than the regional-restriction argument. I did not verify which layer they used and am not asserting one.

VERDICT: numbers exact, attribution correct, causal interpretation unsupported. The claim as written asserts a training-pool experiment the paper did not run, and its recommendation ("regionally-specialized over continental") is contradicted by the paper's own design.
