votes.evidence:
PAPER IDENTITY CONFIRMED. Crossref + OpenAlex + Semantic Scholar on DOI 10.1029/2018WR024463 all resolve to: Worland, Steinschneider, Asquith, Knight, Wieczorek (2019), "Prediction and Inference of Flow Duration Curves Using Multioutput Neural Networks," Water Resources Research 55(8):6850-6868. Wiley full text is Cloudflare/402-blocked; no repository copy exists (OpenAlex `any_repository_has_fulltext: false`). I therefore verified against the AUTHORS' OWN CODE AND PROJECT DOCUMENTATION, which is primary and in some ways better than the paper text: GitHub `scworland/restore-2018` (the USGS RESTORE FY2018 project this paper came out of).

VERBATIM ABSTRACT (via OpenAlex inverted index) confirms only: "multioutput neural network models to predict flow-duration curves (FDCs) in 9,203 ungaged locations in the Southeastern United States for six decades between 1950 and 2009", combined loss enforcing "monotonically increasing quantiles", dropout for posterior-predictive distributions, and "test model performance under cross validation". The abstract contains NO gage count, NO predictor count, NO quantile count, and NO error metric.

REFUTATION 1 — THE SPLIT PROTOCOL IS NOT A SPATIAL HOLDOUT (decisive; this is the load-bearing error). `scripts/Worland/remake_scripts/keras_funs.R`, function `sw_k_foldcv`, lines 15-18:
    N <- nrow(data)
    set.seed(1)
    indices <- sample(1:N)
    folds <- cut(indices, breaks = k, labels = FALSE)
This is a RANDOM k=10 fold over ROWS of a site-decade table, with no grouping by `site_no`. Each gage contributes up to 6 decade-rows (1950-2000), and `build_mnn_quantile.R` returns results keyed `distinct(site_no, decade, variable)`. So the SAME GAGE appears in both training and test folds in different decades. That is textbook pseudoreplication / spatial leakage: the reported CV skill measures interpolation to a new DECADE at a LARGELY-SEEN GAGE, not transfer to an ungaged basin. The production model in `build_final_fdc_model.R` uses Keras `validation_split=0.1`, which takes the LAST 10% of rows — also non-spatial. The 9,203 HUC12 pour-point predictions in `predict_fdc_all.R` are pure unvalidated extrapolation; there is no held-out-ungaged evaluation anywhere in the workflow. Under our Rule 1 this number is NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820, and the claim's "Reported split protocol: spatial-holdout" is simply false.

REFUTATION 2 — 27 QUANTILES, NOT 15. Both `build_mnn_quantile.R` and `build_final_fdc_model.R` define an explicit vector literally named `f27` with 27 entries (f0.02, f0.05, f0.1, f0.2, f0.5, f01, f02, f05, f10, f20, f25, f30, f40, f50, f60, f70, f75, f80, f90, f95, f98, f99, f99.5, f99.8, f99.9, f99.95, f99.98), and `loss_weights <- c(rep(1,10), rep(1e-2,17))` (10+17=27). `predict_fdc_all.R` confirms: `viol <- sum(yhat$viol)/(nrow(yhat) * 27)`.

REFUTATION 3 — ~956-962 GAGES, NOT 688. `data/FactsAboutSiteLists.txt` (project's own documentation): "there are 962 streamgages of the original 1,290 for which at least one complete decade of the six decades listed exists, and 2,816 decades are represented." I downloaded `scibase/gage/all_gage_covariates.csv`: 5,736 rows x 48 columns, 956 unique `site_no`, 6 unique `decade` (956 x 6 = 5,736 exactly). Note `combine_all_vars.R` already applies `drop_na()` before this file is written, so no further row loss. The effective modeling set is ~2,816 site-decades over ~950-962 gages. The figure 688 is unsourced and does not appear in any retrieved primary material.

REFUTATION 4 — NO EFFECT SIZE EXISTS. The claim itself concedes no NSE/RMSE/R2 could be retrieved, and I could not retrieve one either. Under Rule 2 the claim therefore carries zero actionable content: it cannot support any inference about how well attribute-to-distribution regionalization actually performs. "Design and counts" without a metric, where the counts are wrong and the protocol is misreported, is not usable evidence.

PARTIAL — "40 basin characteristics" is plausible but unconfirmed. The covariate table has 48 columns of which ~42 are basin attributes (minus comid/site_no/huc12/decade/lat/lon), and the model selects the contiguous block `select(d, major:flood_storage, -basin_area)`, whose exact width I cannot pin without the .feather. Caution: 40 is ALSO the width of the second hidden layer (`layer_dense(units = 40, activation="relu")`), a very plausible source of a garbled full-text-fragment read.

TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR PROJECT — fails on four counts:
(a) n. The real evidence base is ~956 gages / 2,816 site-decades, so our 19 independent basin families is ~50x smaller, not the 36x the claim states. The architecture (40 inputs -> dense 28 -> dropout 0.27 -> dense 40 -> dropout 0.70 -> 27 separate linear heads) has on the order of 2-3k parameters. Utterly infeasible at n=19.
(b) The paper provides NO evidence for the one thing the claim wants it for. Because CV was random over rows, the study never demonstrates ungaged-basin transfer. Citing it as support for "arbitrary Iowa map pin works" would import exactly the leaky protocol our CV design was built to avoid — the paper made the very mistake our 19-family grouping prevents.
(c) Target mismatch flatters the paper. Y is `log10((q + 0.001) / basin_area)`, i.e. area-normalized specific discharge. Basin area is a near-deterministic predictor of streamflow magnitude, so much of the apparent attribute-to-distribution skill is the area scaling baked into the response transform. Nitrate CONCENTRATION has no analogous normalizer; our between-site level problem has no free ride of this kind.
(d) The paper's own headline finding is a MILD NEGATIVE for this application: "basin characteristics are most useful for predicting smaller quantiles, whereas bias terms from neighboring quantiles are most informative for predicting higher quantiles." Static basin attributes were LEAST informative at the HIGH quantiles. Our target is a high-quantile exceedance (daily max >= 10 mg/L, top ~26%). So the study's own result argues that static attributes degrade precisely in the regime we care about.

SALVAGEABLE (worth passing on despite refutation): (1) The multioutput monotone-quantile architecture — one shared trunk, many quantile heads, joint loss enforcing monotonicity — is genuinely attribute-only and needs no local history, so it is structurally deployment-compatible even though it cannot be trained at n=19 in this form. (2) More actionable: the repo is a concrete free inventory of NHDPlus-accumulated static basin attributes we do NOT currently have and which speak directly to our between-site deficit — `bfi` (base-flow index), `twi` (topographic wetness index), `rdx`, `soller` (surficial geology), `aquifers`, `bedperm` (bedrock permeability), `hlr` (hydrologic landscape regions), `physio`, `ecol3`, `strm_dens` (stream density), `sinuosity`, `flood_storage`/`nid_storage` (dam storage). These are free from NHDPlus/EPA StreamCat, cover the full CONUS (so they handle our multi-state basin portions), and are static — matching our project's finding that the only wins came from geometry and static geography. That is a real lead, but it is a lead from the repo's attribute list, NOT support for the claim as written.

(2019), WRR 55(8):6850-6868, doi:10.1029/2018WR024463, trained multioutput neural networks on approximately 956-962 USGS streamgages (~2,816 site-decade records) in the Southeastern US, predicting 27 (not 15) FDC quantiles simultaneously from a block of roughly 40 static basin characteristics, then applied the fitted model to 9,203 ungaged HUC12 pour points for six decades 1950-2009. CONFIRMED BY VERBATIM ABSTRACT: "We develop multioutput neural network models to predict flow-duration curves (FDCs) in 9,203 ungaged locations in the Southeastern United States for six decades between 1950 and 2009." Also confirmed: multiple response variables in the output layer corresponding to individual FDC quantiles; combined loss enforcing monotonicity; dropout for posterior-predictive distributions; LIME for interpretation; MNN beats single-output NN.

REFUTATION 1 - THE SPLIT PROTOCOL IS WRONG, AND THIS IS DISQUALIFYING UNDER RULE 1. The claim states "spatial-holdout". The abstract says only "test model performance under cross validation" - no spatial language. The authors' code is explicit: scripts/Worland/remake_scripts/keras_funs.R, function sw_k_foldcv, does `N <- nrow(data); set.seed(1); indices <- sample(1:N); folds <- cut(indices, breaks = k, labels = FALSE)`, called from build_mnn_quantile.R as `sw_k_foldcv(build_model, k=10, epochs=500, batch_size=100, ...)`. That is RANDOM 10-fold CV over ROWS, not over gages or regions. The rows are gage-DECADES: each gage contributes up to 6 rows (1950,1960,1970,1980,1990,2000) whose static basin characteristics are near-identical. Random row-wise folds therefore place the same gage's other decades in the training set - textbook pseudoreplication/level-memorization leakage, exactly the failure mode Rule 1 exists to catch. The identical random-fold code is repeated in dropout_runs.R for the uncertainty quantification. No leave-one-gage-out, leave-one-region-out, or PUB-protocol appears anywhere in the repo's neural-net path (a separate GAM path does produce all_gage_looest_*.feather leave-one-out files, but those are Asquith's L-moment GAMs, not the MNN). Conclusion: these numbers are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820. The claim's headline framing - "applied to 9,203 ungaged pour points" - describes the PREDICTION step, not the validation step, and the claim conflates the two.

REFUTATION 2 - "15 quantiles" IS WRONG FOR THE PUBLISHED MODEL. build_mnn_quantile.R and build_snn_quantile.R both use a 27-quantile vector f27 = f0.02, f0.05, f0.1, f0.2, f0.5, f01, f02, f05, f10, f20, f25, f30, f40, f50, f60, f70, f75, f80, f90, f95, f98, f99, f99.5, f99.8, f99.9, f99.95, f99.98, with `loss_weights <- c(rep(1,10), rep(1e-2,17))`. A 15-quantile vector exists ONLY in scripts/Worland/keras_training/cloudml/two_layer_keras_model.R, an early Google CloudML hyperparameter-tuning script (dated by its job IDs to June 2018) that uses plain `validation_split = 0.25` and is not the production model.

REFUTATION 3 - "688 streamgages" IS UNSUBSTANTIATED AND CONTRADICTED BY THE AUTHORS' OWN DATA RELEASE. I downloaded the released training tables: scibase/gage/all_gage_covariates.csv = 5,736 rows, 956 unique site_no, 949 unique comid, exactly 956 per decade x 6 decades. scibase/gage/all_gage_flow_stats.csv = 2,804 rows, 956 unique site_no (1950:363, 1960:485, 1970:484, 1980:453, 1990:455, 2000:564). The repo's data/FactsAboutSiteLists.txt independently states 1,290 screened gages overall and "962 streamgages" with complete 1950-2000 decades. Nothing yields 688. The effective training set is ~2,804 gage-decade rows from ~956 gages - which also means the model was fit on ~2,804 rows, not 688 units.

REFUTATION 4 - "40 basin characteristics" IS UNVERIFIED AND LOOKS LIKE A LIKELY TRANSCRIPTION ARTIFACT. The predictor block in code is `select(d, major:flood_storage, -basin_area)`; the released covariate file has 48 columns of which 44 are non-ID (comid, site_no, huc12, decade excluded), including categorical geology/ecoregion/physiography factors coerced with as.numeric(as.factor(.)). So "~40" is plausible in magnitude but I could not confirm the exact figure. Note that "40" also appears in the code as a HIDDEN-LAYER WIDTH (`layer_dense(units = 40)` in build_mnn_quantile.R; `flag_integer("dense_units1", 40, ...)` in the tuning script) - a plausible source for a garbled paraphrase.

REFUTATION 5 - THE CLAIM'S "NO EXACT ERROR METRIC" ADMISSION IS ITSELF GROUNDS FOR REFUSAL UNDER RULE 2. There is no NSE/RMSE/R2 to compare. The one quantitative-direction result recoverable from the verbatim abstract cuts AGAINST the claim's usefulness to us: "basin characteristics are most useful for predicting smaller quantiles, whereas bias terms from neighboring quantiles are most informative for predicting higher quantiles." That is a published NEGATIVE result for attribute-only regionalization of the UPPER TAIL: for high quantiles the LIME surrogates were dominated by the intercept/bias rather than by basin attributes, i.e. static attributes carried little information about the extreme end of the distribution. Our target - violation = daily max >= 10 mg/L at a 0.263 base rate - IS an upper-tail exceedance. The paper's own finding predicts that attribute-only prediction of our tail will be weakest exactly where we need it.

TRANSFERABILITY ASSESSMENT (independent of the above, all against the arbitrary-map-pin deployment target):
(a) The claim's structural analogy is HALF right. The MNN input side is genuinely attribute-only - no local observations, no gauged neighbor, no discharge at the target - so it does clear the deployment-target bar in principle, and NLDI is even used in the repo (nldi_funs.R). But the TARGET is a DECADAL flow-duration curve: one row per gage-decade, a 10-year aggregate distribution. It is not a daily time series and contains no timing. Mapped onto our decomposition, it addresses ONLY the between-site level term (our between_rate_r2 0.24 / between_r2 0.21), and provides no mechanism for the daily "when" that our model already does well. Adopting it means abandoning daily resolution, which the product requires.
(b) SAMPLE SIZE, RULE 5. Even accepting the smaller of the candidate counts, the evidence base is ~956 gages / ~2,804 independent-ish units. Our n=19 independent basin families is ~50x smaller than the gage count and ~150x smaller than the row count. A ~40-input, 2-hidden-layer (28 and 40 units), 27-output network is on the order of 2,500+ parameters; at n=19 effective units this is hopeless. The claim's own NOTE concedes this, which is to its credit, but conceding infeasibility does not make the cited evidence supportive - it makes the citation inert for our decision.
(c) DOMAIN. Southeastern US / Gulf RESTORE region: humid, forested-to-mixed, no artificial subsurface tile drainage. The covariate set (bfi, twi, rdx, soller surficial geology, statsgo, ecoregion, physiography, dams/flood_storage, NLCD classes, ppt/temp mean+sd) contains nothing analogous to tile drainage density or nitrogen surplus. Streamflow FDCs are also far more strongly attribute-controlled (area and precipitation alone explain most of the variance; note the code divides all quantiles by basin_area before log10, i.e. the dominant scaling is removed a priori) than nitrate concentration is. Transferring an "attributes predict the distribution" conclusion from unit-area streamflow to nitrate concentration is not supported by anything in this paper.
(d) DEPLOYMENT. Nothing here requires the target site's own observations - that part of the claim is accurate and is the claim's one genuinely useful content. But it is also the trivial part: our current model is already attribute-plus-weather with no local history.

BOTTOM LINE: the paper exists and 9,203 / six decades / 1950-2009 / multioutput-NN / attribute-only-input are correct, but the two numbers that would make it evidence for us are wrong or unverifiable (protocol is random row-wise 10-fold CV with same-gage leakage, NOT spatial holdout; 15 quantiles is actually 27; 688 gages is contradicted by the authors' released 956 gages / 2,804 gage-decades; 40 predictors unverified and possibly confused with a hidden-layer width), and there is no retrievable error metric of any kind. Under Rules 1, 2, and the stated default, this is refuted.

X is built only from static/decadal basin characteristics (basin_slope, elev_mean, bfi, rdx, twi, length_km, sinuosity, strm_dens, aquifers, bedperm, ecol3, hlr, physio, soller, statsgo, ppt_mean/sd, temp_mean/sd, major, ndams, nid_storage, norm_storage, flood_storage, developed + 11 NLCD land-cover fractions). THE ONE ERROR — SPLIT PROTOCOL IS NOT SPATIAL HOLDOUT. util_funs.R::sw_k_foldcv, verbatim:
    N <- nrow(data)
    set.seed(1)
    indices <- sample(1:N)
    folds <- cut(indices, breaks = k, labels = FALSE)
This is RANDOM k-fold over ROWS. Rows are gage-decades, and 688 gages supply 2,009 rows (mean 2.9 decades/gage; decade counts 1950:257, 1960:343, 1970:346, 1980:325, 1990:341, 2000:397). With k=5 (the MNN call: sw_k_foldcv(build_model, k=5, epochs=400, batch_size=467)) a held-out row's OWN GAGE is also in the training fold unless all its sibling decades land in the same fold — for a 3-decade gage that probability is (1/5)^2 = 4%, so ~96% of test rows have their own gage represented in training. There is no grouping by site, basin, HUC, or region anywhere in the archive. The single-output comparison model uses k=3, same random splitter. tune_layers.R uses validation_split=0.1 (Keras tail split), also non-spatial. This is exactly the leakage mode our rule 1 forbids comparing to LOFO 0.820: the net can memorize a gage's area-normalized flow LEVEL from its other decades, so the reported CV measures temporal/decadal interpolation at KNOWN gages, not transfer to unknown basins.

METRICS: no NSE/RMSE/R2 exists in the retrievable material. Keras loss is MSE with metrics="mae" on log10(q/area); plot_funs.R contains no skill-metric function. The r2 at fdc_est.R:416 is fit2$dev.ratio of the LIME local glmnet SURROGATE (explanation fidelity), NOT predictive skill. The claim's "no exact error metric could be retrieved" is accurate and I independently reproduce that finding.

NO VALIDATION OF THE UNGAGED APPLICATION: the model deployed to the 9,203 HUC12s is trained on all 688 gages and its predictions are never checked against held-out basins. ScienceBase adds an unflagged extrapolation caveat, verbatim: "The neural network was trained using streamflow data at sites with records that contained only non-zero streamflow values. However, the model was used to make predictions for every HUC12 pour point. Some of these predictions are likely for sites that have streamflow values equal to zero." The 688 training gages are by construction perennial; the 9,203 targets include intermittent streams. That is an acknowledged, unquantified domain shift.

TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR PROJECT — largely negative:
1. n: 688 gages / 2,009 records vs our 19 independent basin families. 36x fewer units, as the claim itself flags. The 40->35->31->15 net has ~3,300 parameters fit on 2,009 rows (~0.6 rows/param, already thin); at n=19 families it is not merely underpowered, it is unfittable. Correctly flagged by the claim.
2. Target mismatch: the response is a DECADAL FDC — a 10-year aggregate distribution, one row per gage-decade, area-normalized. It contains zero daily dynamics. So the analogue is our BETWEEN-site term ONLY; the paper offers no evidence at all about daily event timing. It does not address our primary target (daily binary violation >= 10 mg/L) and gives no classification metric.
3. Domain: RESTORE study area is the Gulf Coast states (per gis/GulfStates.zip, restore_bnd.zip), coastal-plain hydrology, NOT tile-drained Corn Belt. Predictor set has BFI, TWI, dam storage, aquifer/bedrock permeability classes — none of which are in our feature set, and it has no tile-drainage proxy either.
4. Data-availability asymmetry: FDCs are computable at every USGS gage from free daily discharge, which is why n=688 was reachable. Nitrate concentration-duration curves require multi-year nitrate records, which is precisely the scarcity (19 families) that caps our project. The method's feasibility rests on the very abundance we lack.
5. Deployment-target verdict: structurally the setup IS right for an arbitrary ungauged map pin (static attributes in, distribution out, no local history). That structural point in the claim is correct and is the claim's real value. But the paper supplies NO validated ungauged-basin skill number, so it cannot be cited as evidence that such regionalization WORKS — only that it has been ATTEMPTED at scale and published.

VERDICT: refuted=false. Every factual count is exact and the structural characterization is right; the claim is wrong only on the protocol field, which I correct below. Under rule 1 the correction is load-bearing: this paper yields no number comparable to our LOFO 0.820 and must not be cited as spatial-holdout evidence.
votes.correction:
The claim's counts and design are all exactly correct and independently reproducible from the authors' own model archive (688 gages, 40 basin characteristics, 15 FDC quantiles, 9,203 ungaged HUC12 pour points, six decades 1950-2009, attribute-only predictors, multioutput NN). Two corrections:

(1) THE SPLIT PROTOCOL IS NOT SPATIAL HOLDOUT — change the field to "random k-fold, site-level leakage". The released util_funs.R uses `set.seed(1); indices <- sample(1:N); folds <- cut(indices, breaks=k)` — random 5-fold over gage-decade ROWS with no grouping by site, basin, or region. The 688 gages contribute 2,009 gage-decade rows (~2.9 decades/gage), so ~96% of held-out rows have their own gage present in the training fold. The reported cross-validation therefore measures decadal interpolation at KNOWN gages, not transfer to unknown basins, and is NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 under rule 1. The 9,203-point application is genuine spatial extrapolation but is entirely unvalidated — no held-out-basin skill number is reported anywhere in the paper or its data release.

(2) The correct unit of analysis is 2,009 gage-decade records from 688 gages, not 688 independent samples — the effective independent-unit count is 688, and pseudoreplication across decades is exactly what the random folds fail to control.

Additional caveats worth carrying: the target is a DECADAL area-normalized flow-duration curve (a 10-year aggregate climatology), so this paper speaks only to our between-site term and says nothing about daily event timing or about binary exceedance classification; the study area is the Gulf Coast RESTORE region, not tile-drained Corn Belt; and ScienceBase discloses that the 688 training gages were screened to perennial (non-zero-flow) records while predictions were emitted for all 9,203 HUC12s including intermittent streams — an acknowledged, unquantified domain shift. Use this citation as evidence that attribute-to-distribution regionalization is a published, structurally valid framing for an ungauged map pin — NOT as evidence of its out-of-sample accuracy, and not as a method importable at n=19 families (a ~3,300-parameter network fit on 2,009 rows does not scale down 36x).

SOURCE IDENTIFIED AND PARTIALLY ACCESSIBLE. The DOI resolves to: Pandit, Golden, Christensen, Lane & Husic (2025), "Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin," Water Resources Research 61(8), e2024WR039207, CC-BY-NC. Wiley returns 403/402 to automated fetch; the PMC deposit (PMC12425153) is an EPA author manuscript still under EMBARGO, so only the abstract is retrievable (verified via Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, and NCBI efetch — all four return the identical abstract text). Unpaywall lists no PDF at any location. Full text (Methods, results tables) could NOT be obtained.

WHAT THE ABSTRACT ACTUALLY SAYS, VERBATIM:
"We developed a long short-term memory (LSTM) model using high-frequency sensor data from across the conterminous US to predict daily nitrate concentrations, achieving strong temporal validation performance (median KGE = 0.60). Spatial validation—or prediction in unmonitored basins—yielded lower performance for nitrate concentration (median KGE = 0.18). Nonetheless, spatial validation was crucial in quantifying the impact of current data gaps and guiding the model's targeted application to the MRB where spatial validation performance was stronger (median KGE = 0.34)."

ROW 1 OF THE CLAIM IS EXACT. Nitrate concentration 0.60 -> 0.18, drop 0.42, spatial-holdout / prediction-in-unmonitored-basins protocol: verbatim correct, correct protocol label, correct metric (median KGE across sites).

ROWS 2 AND 3 ARE UNSUBSTANTIATED. The abstract describes a single-target model — an LSTM "to predict daily nitrate concentrations." Nothing in any accessible text indicates that streamflow or nitrate yield were separately modeled and scored with KGE under both a temporal and a spatial protocol. The purported streamflow 0.78 -> 0.65 and nitrate yield 0.59 -> 0.32 pairs appear in no retrievable part of the record. Nitrate yield in this paper is a DERIVED quantity used for the mass-balance analysis (the "19 ± 4% of surplus" export fractions, Iowa wet-year 42 ± 24% vs dry-year 6 ± 6%), not a separately validated prediction target with its own KGE. The entire load-bearing structure of the claim — "degradation was strongly TARGET-DEPENDENT," "concentration degrades ~3x more than discharge" — rests on those two unverified rows. Four of six numbers cannot be substantiated.

n=95 IS UNVERIFIED. The abstract says only "high-frequency sensor data from across the conterminous US" and gives no site count. I could not confirm 95, and could not confirm that the temporal and spatial evaluations used the same site set.

MATERIAL OMISSION THAT REVERSES THE CLAIM'S IMPLICATION FOR US. The claim quotes 0.18 and suppresses the paper's own explicit finding that spatial validation was nearly TWICE as good inside the Mississippi River Basin (median KGE = 0.34). Iowa is in the MRB and is the paper's featured region. The in-domain number, not the continental one, is the relevant analogue for an Iowa-only model. The claim cherry-picks the worst-case figure.

METHODOLOGICAL OBJECTION EVEN IF THE MISSING NUMBERS EXISTED. Comparing raw KGE drops across streamflow and concentration is not a clean measure of "transferability difficulty." KGE bundles correlation, a variance ratio and a mean-bias ratio; streamflow is far more seasonally forced and autocorrelated than concentration, and the two targets have different signal-to-noise and different dynamic ranges. A larger KGE drop for concentration is partly an artifact of the metric and the target's statistics, not purely evidence about between-site transferability.

TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR SETTING. (a) The protocol is the right analogue — prediction in unmonitored basins is exactly our arbitrary-map-pin deployment target, and the study requires no target-site observations. That is genuinely relevant. (b) But the metrics are not comparable: median daily-concentration KGE vs our binary exceedance AUC/PR-AUC under LOFO. No numeric read-across is possible. (c) Sample size: this is a continental LSTM trained across the full CONUS sensor network (count unknown but plainly far more than 19 families, and spanning many hydroclimates). Our n=19 independent basin families cannot support an LSTM of that kind, so their achieved spatial KGE is not a ceiling or floor we can import. (d) The genuinely actionable item is elsewhere in the same abstract: Shapley analysis identified TILE DRAINAGE, roadway density and wetland cover as the key spatial drivers of MEAN nitrate concentration, with non-linear thresholds. That is direct, primary-source support for our own diagnosis that the deficit is static between-site information and that missing tile-drainage density is a prime suspect — a stronger and better-sourced claim than the one being asserted here.
votes.correction: The defensible version, stripped of the unverifiable comparison: "Pandit et al. (2025, WRR, doi:10.1029/2024WR039207) trained a CONUS-wide LSTM on high-frequency nitrate sensor data to predict daily nitrate CONCENTRATION. Under temporal validation the median KGE was 0.60; under spatial validation (prediction in unmonitored basins) it fell to median KGE 0.18 — a drop of 0.42, confirming that the between-site absolute level of nitrate concentration transfers poorly even for a deep model with continental training data. The claim's "yield 0.32" is suspiciously adjacent to a real number in the abstract - the MRB-subset spatial CONCENTRATION KGE of 0.34 - which is the signature of a garbled paraphrase, i.e. a real figure re-labeled as a different target.

n=95 IS UNVERIFIED. The abstract says only "high-frequency sensor data from across the conterminous US" with no site count. I could not reach any text stating 95.

FULL TEXT WAS INACCESSIBLE BY EVERY FREE ROUTE ATTEMPTED, so the unverified components remain unverified rather than disproven: Wiley doi/epdf/full all HTTP 402; PMC12425153 landing page HTTP 403 and PMC-by-PMID served a reCAPTCHA; Europe PMC search returns isOpenAccess "N", inEPMC "N", pmcid null, fullTextUrl "Subscription required"; Europe PMC fullTextXML 404; NCBI efetch db=pmc returned 10KB of front matter only with the embedded comment "The publisher of this article does not allow downloading of the full text in XML form"; NCBI BioC pmcoa endpoint returned no article; PMC OA service returned error idDoesNotExist; ESS Open Archive 403; IA Scholar 0 hits; fatcat API connection refused. WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before this task, so no further discovery was possible. Per the standing rule that inability to verify is grounds for refutation, the two unsubstantiated pairs and n must be treated as unsupported.

MATERIAL OMISSION THAT REVERSES THE CLAIM'S APPLICABILITY TO US. The claim stops at 0.18, but the abstract's immediately following sentence reads: "Nonetheless, spatial validation was crucial in quantifying the impact of current data gaps and guiding the model's targeted application to the MRB where spatial validation performance was stronger (median KGE = 0.34)." Iowa is inside the Mississippi River Basin, and the paper singles Iowa out by name in its export analysis. The deployment-relevant spatial-transfer figure for our setting is therefore 0.60 -> 0.34 (drop 0.26), not the CONUS-wide 0.42, which is inflated by transfer into hydroclimatically dissimilar regions we will never serve. The claim selects the pessimistic global number and drops the regional number that is closer to our actual use case.

THE HEADLINE INFERENCE RESTS ENTIRELY ON THE UNVERIFIED NUMBERS. "Concentration degrades ~3x more than discharge" is 0.42/0.13, a ratio of differences whose denominator I could not substantiate at all. Even if the flow number exists, ratio-of-KGE-drops is a weak construct: KGE decomposes into correlation, bias and variability ratio terms that behave very differently for a high-dynamic-range flux (discharge) than for a bounded, chemostatically-buffered concentration, so the two drops are not on a common scale and their ratio is not an effect size.

METHODOLOGY / TRANSFERABILITY ASSESSMENT OF WHAT DOES SURVIVE. (a) Sample size: if the site count really is ~95 CONUS high-frequency nitrate sensors, this is NOT a 531-basin CAMELS-scale result - it is comparably data-poor to our own 85 sites / 19 independent families, which makes it more relevant to us but also means the reported medians are over few held-out basins and carry wide, unreported uncertainty. Note also that Iowa's IWQIS network is one of the densest high-frequency nitrate networks in the US, so a large share of their CONUS sites are plausibly OUR sites - raising a real pseudoreplication/overlap concern if their spatial folds did not account for nested Iowa basins the way our basin-family CV does. Unverifiable without full text. (b) Metric mismatch: their KGE is on daily continuous concentration; our primary target is a binary 10 mg/L exceedance scored by AUC/PR-AUC. KGE 0.18 and AUC 0.820 are not comparable quantities, so this claim cannot be used to argue our numbers are good, bad, or near a ceiling. (c) The genuinely actionable content of this paper for us is not the KGE table at all - it is the Shapley result that "tile drainage, roadway density, wetland cover" are the dominant SPATIAL drivers of mean nitrate concentration with non-linear thresholds. That is independent corroboration, from a deep model with continental data, that our known missing static covariate (tile drainage density) sits exactly where our known deficit is (the between-site term), and it is consistent with our own pattern that only geometry and static geography have produced wins.
votes.correction: Salvageable, defensible version: "Pandit et al. (2025, WRR, doi:10.1029/2024WR039207) trained an LSTM on high-frequency nitrate sensor data across the conterminous US to predict DAILY NITRATE CONCENTRATION - a single target, not a multi-target study. Under spatial holdout (prediction in unmonitored basins, the same protocol class as our LOFO and the correct analogue for our ungauged-map-pin deployment), median KGE fell from 0.60 under temporal validation to 0.18 CONUS-wide. Restricted to the Mississippi River Basin, which contains Iowa and which the authors highlight for Iowa specifically, spatial-holdout performance was materially better: median KGE 0.34 (drop 0.26). Site count is not stated in the abstract and the full text is paywalled; the widely-quoted n=95 is unverified. The paper reports NO streamflow KGE and NO separately-modeled nitrate-yield KGE that I could substantiate - the frequently-cited 'streamflow 0.78->0.65' and 'nitrate yield 0.59->0.32' should not be used, and the 'yield 0.32' figure appears to be a mis-labeling of the real MRB concentration figure 0.34. Consequently the popular framing that 'concentration degrades ~3x more than discharge' is NOT supported by anything retrievable from this source and should be dropped. What the paper does legitimately support for us: (i) between-basin transfer of nitrate CONCENTRATION level is hard even for a deep model with continental training data and the temporal-vs-spatial gap is large, which corroborates our own within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21 diagnosis rather than indicating a defect in our modeling; (ii) via Shapley analysis, the dominant SPATIAL controls on mean nitrate concentration are tile drainage, roadway density and wetland cover - direct third-party support for prioritizing tile-drainage density as our highest-value missing static feature. Caveats to state whenever citing this: their metric is KGE on continuous daily concentration and is not comparable to our AUC/PR-AUC on a 10 mg/L exceedance; their effective number of independent held-out basins is likely small and unreported; and because Iowa's IWQIS network is among the densest US nitrate sensor networks, their CONUS training set plausibly overlaps our own sites, so their CONUS numbers are not an independent external benchmark for us."

votes.evidence:
PAPER IDENTITY CONFIRMED. DOI 10.1029/2024WR039207 = Pandit, A., Golden, H.E., Christensen, J.R., Lane, C.R., & Husic, A. (2025), "Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin," Water Resources Research 61(8), e2024WR039207. Confirmed independently via Crossref API, Semantic Scholar API, OpenAlex, and Europe PMC.

VERIFIED PORTION (2 of 6 numbers). The Europe PMC core record returns the abstract verbatim: "We developed a long short-term memory (LSTM) model using high-frequency sensor data from across the conterminous US to predict daily nitrate concentrations, achieving strong temporal validation performance (median KGE = 0.60). Spatial validation-or prediction in unmonitored basins-yielded lower performance for nitrate concentration (median KGE = 0.18)." The nitrate-CONCENTRATION pair (0.60 -> 0.18, drop 0.42) is therefore EXACT and citable, as is the protocol label (spatial holdout = prediction in unmonitored basins).

UNSUBSTANTIATED PORTION (4 of 6 numbers, including the claim's entire comparative backbone).
(a) Streamflow 0.78 -> 0.65: no accessible text mentions streamflow/discharge as a modeled LSTM target. The abstract describes a single-target model predicting daily nitrate concentration. The 0.13 drop is the denominator of the claim's headline "concentration degrades ~3x more than discharge," so the central comparative assertion rests entirely on an unverified figure.
(b) Nitrate yield 0.59 -> 0.32: unverified. The abstract does discuss nitrate YIELDS and export fractions, but as derived/diagnostic quantities (interannual yields, wet-year 42 +/- 24% vs dry-year 6 +/- 6% export fractions), not as a validated prediction target with a reported KGE.
(c) n = 95 sites: unverified. The abstract says only "across the conterminous US" with no site count. The claim's "all 95 CONUS sites" is not supported by any source I could access.
(d) The framing "in the same study, degradation was strongly TARGET-DEPENDENT across three targets" is a structural assertion about the paper's design that no accessible text supports.

ACCESS ATTEMPTS (exhaustive; WebSearch budget was already spent at 200/200 before this task began, so verification was WebFetch-only): Wiley landing page HTTP 402; Wiley /doi/full HTTP 402; PMC HTML article PMC12425153 HTTP 403; Europe PMC fullTextXML HTTP 404; NCBI PMC OA package API returns "identifier PMC12425153 does not exist" (i.e. not in the OA bulk set despite OpenAlex listing it); scholar.archive.org no results; ESS Open Archive preprint search HTTP 403; EPA Science Inventory no record. Per the standing rule that inability to verify is grounds for refutation rather than charity, the unverified two-thirds of the claim must be treated as unsupported.

MATERIAL OMISSION THAT CHANGES THE CLAIM'S MEANING FOR THIS PROJECT. The same abstract continues: "spatial validation was crucial in quantifying the impact of current data gaps and guiding the model's targeted application to the MRB where spatial validation performance was stronger (median KGE = 0.34)." The Mississippi River Basin is the region containing Iowa. The claim quotes the pessimistic CONUS-wide 0.18 as the transferability ceiling for our target while suppressing the fact that the paper's own spatial-holdout performance in OUR region is 0.34 -- roughly double. Used as written, the claim would overstate the difficulty of between-site concentration transfer in Iowa by about a factor of two.

METHODOLOGY. The split protocol is correctly labeled and is genuinely the right kind: spatial holdout, explicitly defined by the authors as prediction in unmonitored basins, which matches our LOFO and matches the arbitrary-map-pin deployment target (no local nitrate history required). That part of the claim is sound. However KGE is reported as a MEDIAN ACROSS SITES of a continuous daily-concentration skill score; it is not commensurable with our AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 / MCC 0.466 on a binary exceedance target. No numerical comparison between the paper's KGE values and our LOFO metrics is licensed in either direction. Without the site count I also cannot assess pseudoreplication or whether basins nest (the exact issue that collapses our 85 sites to 19 families).

TRANSFERABILITY / n=19 CONSTRAINT. Even granting the verified concentration pair, this is an LSTM trained on continental-scale multi-site sensor data; "across the conterminous US" implies on the order of 100+ sites, versus our 19 independent basin families. Any inference of the form "even a deep model with continental training data only reaches KGE 0.18, so our between-site ceiling is low" is a directional intuition, not a transferable bound, because (i) the site count is unverified, (ii) the metric is incommensurable with ours, and (iii) the regionally relevant number is 0.34, not 0.18.

INCIDENTAL FINDING MORE USEFUL THAN THE CLAIM. The verified abstract states: "Interpretable Shapley values identified key spatial drivers influencing mean nitrate concentrations-tile drainage, roadway density, wetland cover-and quantitative, non-linear thresholds in their influence." This is peer-reviewed, spatially-validated external corroboration that TILE DRAINAGE is a dominant driver of the BETWEEN-SITE MEAN concentration -- precisely the term identified as holding essentially all remaining headroom in this project, and precisely the feature listed as missing with no data source identified. Pandit et al. evidently obtained a CONUS-extent tile-drainage covariate, so their data/methods section is a concrete lead for sourcing one (and would cover the multi-state portions of large basins, unlike Iowa-only products). Note this is a static geographic covariate, consistent with the project's observed pattern that geometry and static geography win while temporal features fail.
